scoring.rule: Five statements, each true or false, 1 point each. The student checks the statements they believe are true. A statement scores 1 point if it is checked and true, or unchecked and false; otherwise 0.

questions.stem: Candidates for a game-programming job are asked what the words scene, level and map mean in the three big engines. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: In Unity, more than one scene can be open at the same time, which is called additive loading.
statements.explanation: Additive loading opens a scene on top of the scenes already open, which is how levels are built from several parts.

statements.label: B
statements.text: In Unity, "scene" means a reusable object that is instanced many times, in the way a prefab is.
statements.explanation: A Unity scene is a container of GameObjects for a level or screen; the reusable, instanced object is the prefab.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A Godot scene can be a single weapon, a character or a whole level, so "scene" does not mean "one screen of the game".
statements.explanation: A Godot scene is a saved tree of nodes of any size, which is why one mechanism serves small objects and whole levels.

statements.label: D
statements.text: In Godot, "level" is a special engine type that is different from a scene.
statements.explanation: Godot has no separate level type; a level is a scene, usually one that instances smaller scenes.

statements.label: E
statements.text: In Unreal, a level is a saved map that holds the Actors placed in one part of the world.
statements.explanation: In Unreal the level (map) file stores the Actors placed in it.

questions.stem: Engines package a reusable game object once and then place many copies of it. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: In Unreal, a Blueprint class is an asset that defines a custom Actor type, and each Actor placed in a level from it is an instance of that class.
statements.explanation: A Blueprint class is the definition; each placed copy is an instance of that class.

statements.label: B
statements.text: In Unity, a prefab is an asset that serves as a template, and each copy placed in a scene is a prefab instance linked to that asset.
statements.explanation: The prefab asset is the template; instances in scenes are linked copies of it.

statements.label: C
statements.text: In Unity, a scene and a prefab are the same kind of asset, so loading a prefab replaces the current level.
statements.explanation: Scenes and prefabs are different asset types; opening a prefab does not replace the level.

statements.label: D
statements.text: In Godot, a saved scene can be instantiated inside another scene, so one mechanism covers a whole level and a reusable object such as an enemy.
statements.explanation: In Godot a scene file is both the level format and the reusable-object format, and scenes nest.

statements.label: E
statements.text: In Unity, a prefab instance in a scene and the prefab asset are one object, so deleting the instance from the scene deletes the asset file.
statements.explanation: The instance is a separate object in the scene; removing it leaves the asset untouched.

questions.source: Translating engine words in an instruction
questions.stem: A developer working in a Godot project types to a coding agent: "Make the coin a prefab and spawn ten of them along the track." (Prefab is a Unity word.) Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A Godot scene plays the role a prefab plays in Unity, so the agent can read "prefab" as "a saved scene that is instanced".
statements.explanation: A saved Godot scene is the reusable template that Unity calls a prefab, so the word translates.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Spawning ten coins means making one coin node and ten references to it, so the ten share a single position.
statements.explanation: Each instance is a separate node with its own position; references to one node would be the same object.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Instantiating the coin's loaded scene ten times gives ten separate node trees, each of which can be given a different position.
statements.explanation: Each call to instantiate produces a fresh, independent tree of nodes.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Godot has a built-in prefab file type, and the agent has to create one before it can spawn a coin.
statements.explanation: Godot has no prefab file type; the scene file is the mechanism.

statements.label: E
statements.text: After instantiate has been called, the coin runs in the game even if it has not been added as a child of a node.
statements.explanation: An instance becomes part of the running game after it is added as a child in the scene tree.

questions.stem: An enemy template (a Unity prefab, an Unreal Blueprint class or a Godot scene) is instanced 50 times in a level. On 3 instances the developer sets a different move speed on the instance itself. Later the developer changes the move speed default in the template. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: An override is a value stored on the instance, and the new template default replaces it.
statements.explanation: An override is stored on the instance, so a change to the default does not replace it.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Instances are unlinked copies made at placement time, so later edits to the template do not reach them.
statements.explanation: Instances stay linked to the template in all three engines; that link lets edits flow to them.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The instances whose speed was left at the template value follow the new default.
statements.explanation: A property that is not overridden keeps following the template's value.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The 3 instances with their own speed value keep it, because an override on an instance wins over the template's default.
statements.explanation: The override is the instance-level value, and it wins over the default until it is reverted.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Adding a new child object or component to the template shows up in the instances without editing them one by one.
statements.explanation: Structural changes made to the template, such as an added child node or component, appear in its instances.

questions.stem: A candidate is asked how objects get behaviour in each of the three engines. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: In Unreal, the base Actor Component type carries a transform and can be attached to other components in a hierarchy.
statements.explanation: Transform and attachment belong to Scene Components; the plain Actor Component has no place in the world.

statements.label: B
statements.text: In Unreal, an Actor can be placed in a level or spawned during play, and its location, rotation and scale come from its root component.
statements.explanation: An Unreal Actor has no transform of its own; it takes one from its root component.

statements.label: C
statements.text: In Godot, the idiom for giving one object several unrelated abilities is to attach several components to a single node, as with Unity's GameObjects.
statements.explanation: Godot builds behaviour by arranging nodes in a tree and instancing scenes; its nodes are not components in the Unity sense.

statements.label: D
statements.text: In Unity, a GameObject has a Transform, and rendering, physics and scripts are added to it as components.
statements.explanation: A GameObject has a Transform, and other behaviour comes from components.

statements.label: E
statements.text: In Unity, a GameObject that holds scripts can exist without a Transform, because the Transform is added when something needs a position.
statements.explanation: A GameObject has a Transform from the moment it exists.

questions.stem: Games label objects so that code can find or filter them, such as all enemies. Engines give those labels different rules. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: In Godot, a group is a collision rule that decides which objects touch each other, so joining a group changes what a node can hit.
statements.explanation: Collision filtering uses layers and masks; groups are lookup labels.

statements.label: B
statements.text: In Unity, a GameObject has one tag, so one object carries a single tag and not both "Enemy" and "Flying" at the same time.
statements.explanation: Unity gives a GameObject a single tag (and a single layer).

statements.label: C
statements.text: In Godot, a node can belong to several groups, and the scene tree can list a group's members or call a method on them.
statements.explanation: Groups work like tags with many allowed per node, and the scene tree can query them.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Adding a group or tag to an object helps code look it up; by itself it changes neither how the object looks nor how it moves.
statements.explanation: A lookup label has no built-in effect on rendering or physics.

statements.label: E
statements.text: In Unity, a GameObject's tag and its layer are two names for the same property, so setting one sets the other.
statements.explanation: Tags and layers are separate properties; layers drive filtering such as rendering and physics, tags are for lookup.

questions.stem: A designer wants a health bar to float 40 units above an enemy's head, follow the enemy as it walks and turns, and still be right when the enemy is scaled up to be a boss. The bar is made a child of the enemy. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A local position of (0, 0) places the child at the world origin.
statements.explanation: A local position of (0, 0) is the parent's own origin, wherever the parent is in the world.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The bar's local position is measured relative to its parent, so a fixed local offset of 40 units up stays the same while the bar's world position changes as the enemy walks.
statements.explanation: A local position is stored relative to the parent and does not change when the parent moves.

statements.label: C
statements.text: When the parent is rotated, the engine rotates the child's local offset with it, so the bar swings around the enemy.
statements.explanation: The world position is built from the chain of parent transforms, including rotation.

statements.label: D
statements.text: When the parent is scaled up, the child's local offset is scaled with it, so the bar sits farther away unless scale inheritance is handled.
statements.explanation: Parent scale applies to the child's offset, so a boss at scale 2 puts the bar twice as far away.

statements.label: E
statements.text: World (global) space measures positions from the parent object's own origin.
statements.explanation: World space is measured from the world origin; local space is measured from the parent.

questions.stem: A developer tells a coding agent: "Raise the platform by 100 units." The agent edits position values in three engines. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: In Unreal, y is the up axis, so raising an Actor means increasing its y.
statements.explanation: Unreal's up axis is z, not y.

statements.label: B
statements.text: In Unreal, positive z points up, so raising an Actor means increasing its z.
statements.explanation: Unreal is z-up, so increasing z raises the Actor.

statements.label: C
statements.text: In Unity the up axis is y, with positive y pointing up, so decreasing a GameObject's y raises it.
statements.explanation: In Unity positive y is up, so decreasing y lowers the object.

statements.label: D
statements.text: In Godot's 2D space the y axis points down the screen, so raising a 2D node means decreasing its y position.
statements.explanation: Godot 2D uses screen-style coordinates in which y grows downward.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Unity and Unreal use the same real-world length for one unit by default, so "100 units" is the same distance in both.
statements.explanation: Unity treats a unit as a metre by convention, while Unreal treats a unit as a centimetre, so "100 units" differs.

questions.stem: A developer tells a coding agent: "Move the player to where I click." In a 2D game the click arrives as a position inside the viewport, and the camera may be moved or zoomed. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The raw click position is a screen (viewport) coordinate, and the agent can treat it as the same thing as a world coordinate.
statements.explanation: Screen and world coordinates are different spaces, and a conversion is needed.

statements.label: B
statements.text: When the camera is panned or zoomed, the same screen position corresponds to a different world position.
statements.explanation: The camera defines the mapping, so moving or zooming it changes which world point sits under a screen position.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Screen coordinates are measured in the viewport, usually from its top-left corner, while world coordinates locate a point in the game world.
statements.explanation: Screen space belongs to the display, and world space belongs to the game world.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A precise instruction asks the agent to convert the click from screen coordinates to world coordinates through the camera, then move the player to that world position.
statements.explanation: Naming both spaces and the conversion removes a guess that would put the player in the wrong place.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The camera has no role in relating screen space to world space.
statements.explanation: The camera is what relates the two spaces.

questions.stem: Check each statement about frames, ticks and delta time.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A tick is one update step of a subsystem such as physics, while a frame is one pass of the main loop ending in a rendered image, so the counts can differ.
statements.explanation: Physics ticks and rendered frames are counted separately and need not be equal.

statements.label: B
statements.text: In Godot, the delta passed to the physics callback follows the fixed physics rate, so it does not stretch when a rendered frame takes longer than usual.
statements.explanation: Godot's physics callback runs at a fixed rate, and its delta follows that rate.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Frame rate is the number of fixed physics steps that run each second, which is why the two numbers match.
statements.explanation: Frame rate counts rendered frames per second; the fixed-step rate is a separate setting.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The delta passed to a per-frame callback is a fixed 1/60 s, because 60 frames per second is the standard rate games are built for.
statements.explanation: The per-frame delta varies with how long each frame took on that machine.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Delta time is the time elapsed since the previous call of the update callback, usually measured in seconds.
statements.explanation: Delta is the elapsed time between consecutive calls, which lets movement scale with real time.

questions.stem: A developer asks a coding agent: "Make the enemy move right 5 pixels every frame." The agent writes position.x += 5 in the per-frame update function, and the game is tested on a 60 Hz screen and a 144 Hz screen. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Delta time is the count of frames drawn in the last second.
statements.explanation: Delta time is a duration in seconds, not a count of frames.

statements.label: B
statements.text: position.x += 5 is movement per frame, so the enemy covers more distance per second when more frames are drawn each second.
statements.explanation: A fixed step per frame makes speed depend on the number of frames per second.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Movement of 5 pixels per frame is frame-rate independent, so the enemy looks the same speed at 60 and at 144 frames per second.
statements.explanation: A per-frame step is the textbook example of movement that is not frame-rate independent.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Asking for "move right at 300 pixels per second" and writing position.x += 300 * delta gives the same on-screen speed at 60 and at 144 frames per second.
statements.explanation: A rate in units per second scaled by the time per frame covers the same distance per second at any frame rate.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Multiplying a step by delta changes its unit from "per frame" to "per second", so the number 5 may need to be raised to keep the old speed.
statements.explanation: With delta, the number is a rate per second, so a per-frame value needs converting.

questions.stem: An interviewer asks why movement that involves the physics engine belongs in the fixed-step callback (Unity's FixedUpdate, Godot's _physics_process) and not in the per-frame callback (Update, _process). Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Putting movement in the fixed-step callback makes the on-screen frame rate constant.
statements.explanation: Frame rate depends on rendering and load; the fixed step only decouples physics from it.

statements.label: B
statements.text: In Godot, the physics callback is the right place for cosmetic effects such as a flickering light, because it runs more often than the per-frame callback.
statements.explanation: The physics callback runs at its own fixed rate, which can be lower or higher than the frame rate; cosmetic effects belong in the per-frame callback.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The physics engine advances the world in fixed-size steps, so forces and velocities applied in the callback tied to that step line up with the simulation.
statements.explanation: Fixed-size steps keep the simulation's time unit constant.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Gravity, forces and body movement belong in the fixed-step loop, while camera smoothing and UI animation belong in the per-frame loop.
statements.explanation: Visual smoothing follows the rendered frames, while physics follows the fixed step.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Physics driven by the variable per-frame delta depends on how fast the machine renders, so the same input can give different jump arcs on different machines.
statements.explanation: A varying step makes collisions and jump heights less repeatable between machines.

questions.stem: A game's fixed-step callback is set to a constant rate, and rendering is not capped. When a frame takes long, the engine runs extra fixed steps to catch up. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: After a frame that lasted several times the step length, the engine runs several fixed steps to catch up.
statements.explanation: The engine accumulates elapsed time and spends it in whole fixed steps.

statements.label: B
statements.text: When frames are shorter than the step length, some rendered frames run no fixed step.
statements.explanation: On short frames the accumulated time has not yet reached a full step.

statements.label: C
statements.text: When the frame rate rises, the length of the fixed step shrinks so that each step lines up with one frame.
statements.explanation: The step length is a setting and does not change with the frame rate.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Each catch-up call of the fixed-step callback receives the delta of the whole long frame.
statements.explanation: Each call receives the constant step length; several calls together cover the long frame.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The fixed-step callback runs once per rendered frame, so the two loops alternate one to one.
statements.explanation: The two loops run at independent rates, so they do not alternate one to one.

questions.stem: A scene holds 2000 enemies, and each runs a per-frame update that checks whether the player is near. A developer asks an agent to cut that cost. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Reacting to an event costs more per frame than polling for idle objects.
statements.explanation: An event has no per-frame cost for idle objects.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Switching off the per-frame callback on idle enemies removes their polling cost until they are switched back on.
statements.explanation: An object without a per-frame callback pays nothing for it.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Event-driven code runs when something happens, so idle objects add nothing per frame.
statements.explanation: Events invoke code at the moment of change.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Polling checks a condition on each update even when nothing has changed, so its cost grows with the number of objects.
statements.explanation: Polling repeats the same check at the update rate whether or not the answer changed.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Polling and event-driven are two names for the same technique.
statements.explanation: Polling asks again and again; an event is pushed when the change occurs.

questions.stem: Most engines give an object a hook that runs once when it is ready to be used (Godot's _ready, Unity's Start, Unreal's BeginPlay) and a hook that runs repeatedly (Godot's _process, Unity's Update, Unreal's Tick). Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A hook that runs one time is unsuitable for starting a looping timer, because the hook does not repeat.
statements.explanation: A once-only hook can start a repeating process; it starts it once.

statements.label: B
statements.text: In Godot, _ready is called again each time a node is removed from the scene tree and added back.
statements.explanation: _ready is called once per node unless it is explicitly requested again.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A per-frame hook is the right place to build the player's starting inventory, because it keeps retrying until it succeeds.
statements.explanation: Setup in a per-frame hook repeats each frame or needs a guard flag; setup belongs in the once-only hook.

statements.label: D
statements.text: In Godot, children's _ready callbacks run before the parent's, so the parent can rely on its children being set up.
statements.explanation: Children are ready first, then the parent.

statements.label: E
statements.text: In Unity, Start is called before the script's first frame update, and when the script instance is enabled.
statements.explanation: Start runs before the first frame update for an enabled script.

questions.stem: Godot calls it a signal, Unity programmers use C# events or UnityEvent, and Unreal has delegates and Event Dispatchers. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Signals, events and delegates hold the message in a queue until each listener checks it once per frame.
statements.explanation: Listeners are called by the announcer when the event happens; a Godot signal calls connected functions immediately unless deferring is requested.

statements.label: B
statements.text: In Godot, emitting a signal that nothing is connected to is not an error; it calls nothing.
statements.explanation: An empty list of listeners is legal; emitting then does nothing.

statements.label: C
statements.text: In the three engines, the code that announces an event does not need to name the objects that react to it.
statements.explanation: Listeners register themselves, so the announcer stays unaware of who is listening.

statements.label: D
statements.text: In Godot, a listener can connect to a signal on a node it has a reference to; a parent and child relationship is not required.
statements.explanation: A connection links a signal to a callable on any object; the tree layout does not restrict it.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A callback is a function that a listener hands over so the announcing object can call it when the event happens.
statements.explanation: The callback is the function passed to the signal, event or delegate.

questions.source: Signals versus polling and direct calls
questions.stem: A developer wants the health bar (HUD) to redraw when the player takes damage. The requirements for the coding agent are that the player's code does not need to know the HUD exists and the HUD does not check the player every frame. A statement is true when the request it quotes meets both requirements.

statements.label: A
statements.text: "Have the player emit a health-changed signal, and have the HUD connect to it and redraw in the handler."
statements.explanation: The player announces the change and the HUD listens, so neither requirement is broken.

statements.label: B
statements.text: "Give the player a reference to the HUD and have the player call the HUD's redraw function when it takes damage."
statements.explanation: A direct call needs the player to hold a reference to the HUD, which breaks the first requirement.

statements.label: C
statements.text: "In the HUD's per-frame update function, read the player's health and redraw if it changed."
statements.explanation: Reading the health in a per-frame update is polling, which breaks the second requirement.

statements.label: D
statements.text: "Store health in a global variable that the player writes and the HUD reads in its per-frame update function."
statements.explanation: The HUD still polls the shared value, which breaks the second requirement.

statements.label: E
statements.text: "Have the HUD declare a signal, and have the player connect to it and emit it whenever health changes."
statements.explanation: The player would have to reference the HUD to connect to its signal, which breaks the first requirement.

questions.stem: A Unity script subscribes one of its methods to a C# event on a long-lived manager object. The script's GameObject is later destroyed without the script unsubscribing. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Event systems keep weak references to subscribers, so a long-lived emitter drops a destroyed subscriber without an unsubscribe call.
statements.explanation: A C# event holds a normal reference to each subscriber, so a missing unsubscribe causes stale calls.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The usual remedy is symmetrical: subscribe when the object is enabled and unsubscribe when it is disabled or destroyed.
statements.explanation: Pairing subscribe and unsubscribe with enable and disable (or destroy) is the standard discipline.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The engine queues the event until the next frame, by which time the destroyed object has been cleaned up and no error follows.
statements.explanation: A C# event calls its subscribers in the line that raises it; nothing is queued.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The manager's list of subscribers still holds the destroyed script's method, so the next time the event is raised a call can be made on an object that no longer exists.
statements.explanation: A stale subscription stays in the list and is called on the next raise.

statements.label: E
statements.text: In Godot, when a node whose method is connected to a signal is freed, the engine removes that connection.
statements.explanation: Godot removes the connections of a freed object.

questions.stem: A studio interview asks why engines offer input actions instead of letting game code read raw keys. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Unity's Input System actions, Unreal's Enhanced Input actions and Godot's Input Map actions are three engine-specific forms of the same idea.
statements.explanation: Each engine maps named actions to bindings under different names and tools.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Polling and an event callback are the same thing: both push a message to the code when the input occurs.
statements.explanation: Polling reads state when asked; an event callback is pushed to the code when the input happens.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Hard-coding a check for the Space key in the movement code is the preferred way to support rebinding.
statements.explanation: A hard-coded key defeats rebinding and ties the code to one device.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Because game code asks about the action, a player can rebind the key without game code changing.
statements.explanation: Rebinding changes the mapping, not the code that reads the action.

statements.label: E
statements.text: An input action is a named intent, such as "jump", mapped to one or more physical inputs like a keyboard key or a gamepad button.
statements.explanation: The action is the game-level meaning, and bindings tie it to devices.

questions.source: Just-pressed versus held; precise input instruction
questions.stem: A designer wants jumping to happen once per button press and running to continue while a button is held. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A just-pressed query stays true for the whole time the button is held.
statements.explanation: That describes a held state; just-pressed is true on a single frame or tick.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A just-pressed query is true on the frame or tick the press began, which fits a one-shot jump.
statements.explanation: A just-pressed query fires once per press.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A precise version defines an action named jump bound to the Space key and a gamepad button, reacts once per press, and defines a separate run action read as a held state.
statements.explanation: It names the action, the bindings and the query type for each control.

statements.label: D
statements.text: "Jump when the player presses space" is a precise instruction, because it names the key.
statements.explanation: It hard-codes one key and one device, and does not say whether holding repeats the jump.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A held-state query, true for as long as the button is down, fits the run control.
statements.explanation: Running continues while the input is down, so a held state fits.

questions.stem: Developers use "asset" and "resource" loosely. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: In Godot, a Resource and a Node are interchangeable: both can be placed in the scene tree and both receive the per-frame callback.
statements.explanation: Nodes live in the scene tree and get per-frame callbacks; a resource is data.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A Godot Resource is a data container that does nothing on its own; nodes use resources to do their work.
statements.explanation: A Resource is data; behaviour comes from nodes.

statements.label: C
statements.text: In Godot, loading the same resource path twice returns two independent copies, so changing one does not affect the other.
statements.explanation: Loading a resource that is already in memory returns the same copy.

statements.label: D
statements.text: An asset, in the everyday sense, is a file in the project folder such as a PNG, a WAV or a mesh, which the engine imports before using it.
statements.explanation: Source files are imported by the editor, and the engine uses the imported form at runtime.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Unity's ScriptableObject and Unreal's Data Asset fill a similar role: a data asset that many objects can read, independent of an object in a level.
statements.explanation: Both are data assets that exist independently of objects in a level, though they are not identical features.

questions.stem: A game keeps the player's inventory in one globally reachable object: a singleton in Unity, an autoload in Godot, or an object held by the persistent Game Instance in Unreal. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Such an object is useful because it outlives a single scene or level, so what it stores survives scene changes.
statements.explanation: Lifetime beyond the current scene is the reason to put shared state in such an object.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Registering a script as an autoload makes the engine refuse to create a second copy of it, which makes it a true singleton.
statements.explanation: An autoload is still an ordinary node that could be instanced again; the engine does not enforce a single copy.

statements.label: C
statements.text: In Godot, replacing the current scene frees the autoload nodes too, and they are recreated for the new scene.
statements.explanation: Autoloads stay loaded whichever scene is running.

statements.label: D
statements.text: In Unity, an object survives a scene load when it is explicitly marked to be kept, for example with DontDestroyOnLoad.
statements.explanation: Unity destroys the objects of the replaced scene unless they are marked to survive.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Because code can reach it from anywhere, a function that quietly reads the global is harder to test alone than one handed the inventory as a parameter.
statements.explanation: A hidden dependency on a global makes a function depend on state its signature does not show.

questions.stem: A developer asks a coding agent for "a global score counter" in a Godot game that has a title scene, a level scene and a game-over scene. The agent puts the counter in a script on the root node of the level scene, and the score reads zero on the game-over scene. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Passing the score to the next scene as the scenes are switched is a way to avoid a global.
statements.explanation: The vague word "global" hid a design choice; handing the value on is a legitimate alternative.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Registering the script as an autoload would keep it alive from startup through each scene change.
statements.explanation: An autoload is a node placed under the root before the main scene and kept through scene changes.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The score variable was freed along with the level scene's nodes when the game switched scenes.
statements.explanation: A variable lives as long as the node it belongs to, and the level scene's nodes were removed.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Marking the variable with @export keeps its value when the game switches scenes.
statements.explanation: @export exposes a variable to the editor; it does not extend its lifetime.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The cause is that GDScript resets number variables to zero when a new scene is loaded.
statements.explanation: GDScript does not reset variables; the object holding the variable was removed.

questions.stem: Check each statement about the editor, a running game and a built (exported or packaged) game.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Producing a standalone game is a separate step from running it in the editor, and engines name that step export, build or package.
statements.explanation: Running in the editor and producing a standalone game are different steps with engine-specific names.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Code written to extend the editor, such as Unity code in the UnityEditor namespace, is absent from a built player.
statements.explanation: Editor-only code does not exist in the player.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A game that runs correctly from the editor runs the same in a built version, so testing the build adds little.
statements.explanation: Builds can differ from editor runs in included files, platform settings and performance.

statements.label: D
statements.text: In Godot, export templates, the prebuilt runtime for each target platform, have to be installed before a project can be exported.
statements.explanation: Export templates supply the runtime for each target platform.

statements.label: E
statements.text: In Unity, edits made to scene objects in Play mode are kept when Play mode stops.
statements.explanation: Changes made in Play mode are discarded when it ends.

questions.stem: A developer tells a coding agent: "Ship the game to my tester." The agent starts the project from the command line, sees it run, and reports it is done. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The tester needs the editor installed to open an exported game.
statements.explanation: A built game is meant to run without the editor.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A precise instruction names the export (or build, or package) step and the target platform, and asks for the built artifact to be launched and checked.
statements.explanation: Naming the step, platform and check removes the guesses.

statements.label: C
statements.text: "Ship" is the engines' own name for the export step, so the instruction is precise.
statements.explanation: Engines say export, build or package; "ship" leaves the step and the target open.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Running the project from the command line produces a standalone file the tester can open without the engine.
statements.explanation: Running a project launches it with the engine and creates no standalone game.

statements.label: E
statements.text: An export includes the files its settings select, so a file that loads in the editor can be missing from the build.
statements.explanation: The editor reads the project folder directly, while an export contains selected files.

questions.source: Vague request rewrite: frame-rate independence and global state
questions.stem: A developer gives a coding agent this instruction: "Add a global thing so the enemies chase the player every frame at speed 4." Check each statement that is true about the wording.

statements.label: A
statements.text: "Each frame" is precise, because it fixes how fast the enemies move on screen.
statements.explanation: A per-frame step makes speed depend on the frame rate.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A better version asks for movement toward the player at a stated rate in units per second, with the step scaled by delta in the per-frame callback.
statements.explanation: A rate per second scaled by delta is frame-rate independent.

statements.label: C
statements.text: "Speed 4" has no unit and no time base, so it could mean 4 units per frame or 4 per second.
statements.explanation: A number without unit and time base leaves the real speed to the agent.

statements.label: D
statements.text: "Global thing" does not say whether the object is a script on a level node, a manager node or an autoload that survives scene changes.
statements.explanation: The location and lifetime of shared state change what happens at a scene change.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Replacing "global thing" with "global variable" makes the location and lifetime precise.
statements.explanation: "Global variable" is as vague about location and lifetime as "global thing".

questions.stem: A level contains 30 copies of a crate. The designer wants the crates in one corner to be heavier, and wants every crate to play a new sound when hit. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The 30 crates are unrelated hand-made copies that share a name.
statements.explanation: Instances are linked to one template and are not unrelated copies.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Adding the sound to the template once gives it to the 30 instances without editing them one by one.
statements.explanation: A change to the template reaches its linked instances.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Changing the weight on the corner instances alone creates an override, a value stored on the instance rather than in the template.
statements.explanation: An override is the instance-level value.

statements.label: D
statements.text: If the template's default weight is changed later, the overridden crates keep their own weight until the override is reverted.
statements.explanation: Overrides persist until they are reverted, while the other instances follow the default.

statements.label: E
statements.text: To make the corner crates heavier, the designer edits the template's weight.
statements.explanation: Editing the template would make every crate heavier, not just the corner ones.

questions.stem: A developer who knows Unity starts working on Godot and Unreal projects. Check each statement that is true about how Unity terms map to the other engines.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A C# event corresponds to a Godot autoload.
statements.explanation: A C# event matches a Godot signal or an Unreal delegate; an autoload matches a singleton.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A Godot scene does the work of both a Unity scene and a Unity prefab.
statements.explanation: A Godot scene is both the level format and the reusable-object format.

statements.label: C
statements.text: An agent told to "do it the Unity way" in Godot can add components to a node in the same way as to a GameObject.
statements.explanation: Godot nodes are not Unity components, so a literal translation builds something Godot does not use.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Unity's ScriptableObject corresponds roughly to a Godot Resource and to an Unreal Data Asset.
statements.explanation: All three are data assets independent of objects in a level.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Unity's FixedUpdate corresponds roughly to Godot's physics callback.
statements.explanation: Both run at a fixed rate for physics work.

questions.source: Signal, event and delegate versus direct call
questions.stem: A game has a player, a HUD, an audio manager and an achievement system, and the four have to react when the player picks up a coin. A junior developer makes the coin script call each of the four directly. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A direct call is the better choice when a parent commands a child it owns, or when a return value is needed.
statements.explanation: A direct call fits a single known target and a needed return value.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A redesign has the coin emit a "coin collected" signal, and each system connects its own callback.
statements.explanation: The emitter announces what happened and each listener registers itself.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Events suit asking another object for an answer, because they return a value to the emitter.
statements.explanation: Events announce what already happened; they are not a way to ask for an answer.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Direct calls couple the coin to the four systems: it needs a reference to each and changes when a system is added or removed.
statements.explanation: A direct call ties the caller to its target.

statements.label: E
statements.text: With signals, the emitter has to name its listeners when it emits.
statements.explanation: Listeners register themselves, so the emitter does not name them.

questions.stem: A designer says, "We use MCP so the AI can drive our editor." Which statements use the terms protocol, model and inference correctly? Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: MCP is the model that does the inference.
statements.explanation: Inference is done by the language model; MCP is the connection standard around it.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Inference is the step where the language model produces output from its input.
statements.explanation: Inference means running the trained model to get a reply.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Connecting an MCP server retrains the model on the project's assets.
statements.explanation: Connecting a service does not change model weights.

statements.label: D
statements.text: MCP is a rendering technique for the editor viewport.
statements.explanation: MCP says nothing about drawing; it connects applications to tools and context.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A protocol is an agreed set of message formats and behaviours between applications.
statements.explanation: That is the meaning of protocol, and MCP is one.

questions.stem: An assistant application uses a connector to reach a service that exposes editor operations. Which statements name the roles correctly? Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A server can run as a local process on the same machine.
statements.explanation: Server names a role, not a location.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The client is the part of the host that holds the connection to a server.
statements.explanation: A client maintains one connection to a server on the host's behalf.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The host is the assistant application the user works in.
statements.explanation: The host contains the user interaction and the clients.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The client is the player character in the level that calls the service.
statements.explanation: The client is the protocol connector, not an in-game character.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The server is the service that exposes tools, resources and prompts.
statements.explanation: Exposing capabilities is the server role.

questions.stem: A teammate writes, "The MCP server in the Claude app calls our editor client to run commands." Which statements correct the wording? Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The Claude app is the host, not the server.
statements.explanation: The assistant application is the host.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Host and server are synonyms, so the note needs no fix.
statements.explanation: They are different roles with different jobs.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The editor-facing service that offers the commands plays the server role.
statements.explanation: It supplies the external capabilities.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The editor plugin that offers the commands is the client.
statements.explanation: The service offering commands is the server.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The part of the host that opens the connection is the client, and it calls the server.
statements.explanation: Clients call servers, not the reverse.

questions.stem: Which statements give the correct meaning of the three server primitives? Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A tool is an operation the model can invoke with arguments, and it may have side effects.
statements.explanation: Tools perform actions.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A prompt is a reusable message or workflow template that a server offers.
statements.explanation: Prompts are templates the client can retrieve.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A tool is readable content identified by a URI.
statements.explanation: That describes a resource.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A prompt is the text the model writes back to the user.
statements.explanation: That is the model's reply, not a prompt primitive.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A resource is an operation that changes the scene when it is called.
statements.explanation: A resource supplies readable context; it is not an action.

questions.stem: A hypothetical editor server offers a spawn operation with arguments, a scene manifest at a URI, and a reusable lighting-review template. Which statements name the primitives correctly? Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The review template is a prompt.
statements.explanation: Prompts are reusable templates.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Retrieving the review template counts as running the review.
statements.explanation: Getting instructions does not carry them out.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The review template is a tool because it can be reused.
statements.explanation: Reusable message templates are prompts.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The spawn operation is a tool.
statements.explanation: It is invoked with inputs to do something.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The scene manifest is a resource.
statements.explanation: It is URI-addressed content that a client reads.

questions.stem: An agent remembers a tool name from a tutorial, but the connected server does not list it. Which statements are correct? Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Tool discovery means asking the server for the tools it advertises and then calling one of those.
statements.explanation: Discovery grounds the call in the live server.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A name remembered from a tutorial substitutes for the advertised tool definition.
statements.explanation: Names and arguments differ between integrations.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Two servers can advertise differently named or shaped tools for the same goal.
statements.explanation: Tool catalogs are implementation-specific.

statements.label: D
statements.text: An input schema is the list of tools a server has installed.
statements.explanation: A schema describes one tool's arguments.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Renaming a scene object to the tutorial's tool name makes the server advertise that tool.
statements.explanation: Object names do not register server operations.

questions.stem: A move tool's input schema lists object_id (a string) and distance (a number). It gives no units or coordinate space. Which statements are correct? Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Reading back the resulting transform checks the effect beyond schema validity.
statements.explanation: A read-back is verification of the outcome.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Units and coordinate space are semantics that come from the tool contract or an inspected example.
statements.explanation: They are not in the type.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Because distance is a number, the unit is metres by default.
statements.explanation: A type does not carry a unit.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A request that passes schema validation targets the intended object.
statements.explanation: Identity is checked separately.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Schema validation checks the type and shape of arguments, not what the values mean.
statements.explanation: Semantics are outside what a type check covers.

questions.stem: A trace shows JSON-RPC messages between a client and a server. Which statements use the terms correctly? Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The id is the index of the target actor in the level.
statements.explanation: The id correlates messages; it is not an engine identity.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A well-formed JSON message shows the requested edit succeeded.
statements.explanation: Syntax says nothing about the operation's result.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A response carries the same id as the request it answers.
statements.explanation: The id pairs a reply with its request.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A missing response to a notification shows the connection is broken.
statements.explanation: No reply is expected for a notification.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A notification carries no id and gets no response.
statements.explanation: Notifications are one-way messages.

questions.stem: Two integrations carry MCP messages over stdio and over Streamable HTTP. Which statements are correct? Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Switching transport translates Unity components into Unreal components.
statements.explanation: A transport does not convert engine data.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A transport carries messages and does not define the editor operations.
statements.explanation: Delivery and scene-editing semantics are separate layers.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A transport fault can stop a valid request from reaching the server.
statements.explanation: Delivery can fail before execution.

statements.label: D
statements.text: With stdio, the client launches the server as a subprocess and exchanges messages over its standard streams.
statements.explanation: That is how the stdio transport works.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Streamable HTTP can reach a server on the same machine.
statements.explanation: HTTP does not imply a remote service.

questions.stem: A tool call returns a structured reply saying the named scene object could not be found. Which statements describe the failure correctly? Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: This is a transport failure, so the next step is changing the network port.
statements.explanation: The reply arrived, so delivery worked.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The object identity is irrelevant to the next investigation.
statements.explanation: The error concerns the target, so identity and scene state are next.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Reinstalling the language model is the first diagnosis the evidence supports.
statements.explanation: Nothing points at the model.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A structured reply shows that the object was modified.
statements.explanation: The reply states the opposite.

statements.label: E
statements.text: This is a tool execution error: the operation ran and reported failure in its result.
statements.explanation: Domain failure travels inside a successful exchange.

questions.stem: A client and a server both say they support MCP, yet initialization fails. Which statements are correct? Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A small call that reads without modifying is a low-risk interoperability check before edits.
statements.explanation: It tests communication without changing the scene.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Each side declares the protocol revision it supports during initialization.
statements.explanation: Revision is negotiated at the start of the connection.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A tutorial's handshake sequence is enough evidence of the current requirements.
statements.explanation: Lifecycle rules change between revisions.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A capability is a rendering feature of the engine exposed to the client.
statements.explanation: Capabilities are optional protocol features each side declares.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The MCP name guarantees both sides support the same revision.
statements.explanation: A product label is not a compatibility guarantee.

questions.stem: A resource read returned a list of lights, and a designer then deleted one. Which statements are correct? Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The deletion turns the earlier response into a protocol error.
statements.explanation: The response was valid when produced.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Re-resolving the target means looking the object up again by identifier before editing.
statements.explanation: It confirms the object still exists.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A stale snapshot is data that no longer matches the live scene.
statements.explanation: Staleness is the mismatch with current state.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Reading a resource locks the scene against later editor changes.
statements.explanation: A read does not freeze the scene.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The returned list is a snapshot of the scene at read time.
statements.explanation: It records state at one moment.

questions.stem: Two engine servers both advertise a tool described as creating an object. Which statements are correct? Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Creating an object may yield an Actor in Unreal and a GameObject in Unity, which are different engine concepts.
statements.explanation: The same intent maps to different engine objects.

statements.label: B
statements.text: MCP standardizes communication, not a universal game-editor API.
statements.explanation: Operations stay engine-specific.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The argument schemas of the two tools can differ.
statements.explanation: Each server defines its own tool contract.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Matching descriptions mean matching side effects.
statements.explanation: Behaviour must be checked, not inferred from a description.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A shared protocol makes asset files loadable in both engines.
statements.explanation: Asset formats are outside the protocol.

questions.stem: An operator sets a limit of ten edit attempts for an agent that edits and tests a scene. Which statements use the terms correctly? Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Reaching the limit shows the scene is correct.
statements.explanation: A limit stops work; it does not accept the result.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Dropping a failing requirement satisfies it.
statements.explanation: Changing the target hides the failure.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Comparing observed state with the requested outcome after an edit is verification.
statements.explanation: Verification checks the result, not just that a call was made.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A stopping condition is the same thing as an acceptance criterion.
statements.explanation: Acceptance asks whether the outcome meets the request; stopping asks when to quit.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A retry limit is a stopping condition that bounds the repair loop.
statements.explanation: It ends repeated attempts.

questions.stem: Check each statement that correctly separates inference, tool execution and gameplay execution. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Inference is the language model producing its reply.
statements.explanation: The model computes the reply.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Where the server is deployed is separate from where inference runs.
statements.explanation: Local or remote deployment is a configuration choice.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Gameplay execution is the MCP server running the player's scripts as the game is played.
statements.explanation: Gameplay runs in the game runtime.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Tool execution is the server carrying out an operation in the editor.
statements.explanation: The server performs the requested operation.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Tool execution is the language model predicting the next token.
statements.explanation: That is inference.

questions.source: mapping a vague request to primitives
questions.stem: A designer asks an agent, "Hook the AI up to the lighting stuff." Which statements are exact rewrites? Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Expose create-light as a tool with arguments for target scene and intensity.
statements.explanation: An operation with inputs is a tool.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Expose the scene inventory as a resource.
statements.explanation: Readable context fits the resource primitive.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Reading the inventory resource first lets the agent choose where to call the create-light tool.
statements.explanation: Context informs the action.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Expose the review checklist as a resource that runs the review when read.
statements.explanation: Reading a resource supplies content and does not run a review.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Expose the reusable checklist as a prompt template.
statements.explanation: Reusable templates are prompts.

questions.stem: A move-object tool is specified for an editor where several objects share a display name. Which statements are correct? Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: An unambiguous identifier should select the target, not the display name.
statements.explanation: Display names can repeat.

statements.label: B
statements.text: An offset moves relative to the current position, while an absolute destination sets the final position.
statements.explanation: They are different input meanings.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The contract states units and coordinate space.
statements.explanation: Without them the number is ambiguous.

statements.label: D
statements.text: An offset and an absolute destination give the same result regardless of the starting position.
statements.explanation: They agree only by coincidence.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A display name is a unique identifier.
statements.explanation: Several objects share it.

questions.stem: A tool call reached the server but nothing appears in the editor. Which symptoms are matched to the right layer? Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A rejection saying a required argument is missing is an argument validation failure.
statements.explanation: Validation checks the arguments before execution.

statements.label: B
statements.text: An edit applied in the wrong scene is found by verification against the request.
statements.explanation: Verification compares the scene with the requested outcome.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A connected status indicator shows the operation executed.
statements.explanation: Connection status says nothing about execution.

statements.label: D
statements.text: An engine error logged while the operation ran is a delivery failure.
statements.explanation: That is an execution failure.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A request with no matching response points first at delivery.
statements.explanation: Responses are matched by id.

questions.stem: A studio uses a cloud-hosted model with a local Unity editor server. Which statements are correct? Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Sending project context to the remote model crosses a data-disclosure boundary.
statements.explanation: Content leaves the machine.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Context filtering is the control for the permission boundary.
statements.explanation: Filtering limits disclosure; scoped tools limit permission.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The two boundaries are one boundary, so one control covers both.
statements.explanation: Disclosure and permission are distinct.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A local server keeps project context off the remote model.
statements.explanation: Context passed through the host still reaches the model.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Invoking a tool that edits the local project crosses a permission boundary.
statements.explanation: An action needs authorization.

questions.stem: A plugin works with client X but fails with client Y. Which statement describes a sound investigation? Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Comparing a minimal trace of read calls separates transport, discovery and capability problems.
statements.explanation: It isolates the layer without changing the scene.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Retesting on the production scene gives the lowest risk.
statements.explanation: An isolated project limits risk.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Recording the supported protocol revisions is unnecessary evidence.
statements.explanation: Revision differences are a common cause.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Failing with client Y shows the plugin does not implement MCP.
statements.explanation: It works with client X.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Inventing a method the specification does not define is a valid way to force a connection.
statements.explanation: Unsupported methods hide the mismatch.

questions.stem: A human and an agent edit the same level, and the agent planned from an inventory read minutes earlier. Which statements are correct? Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A lock is unnecessary when the agent is faster than the human.
statements.explanation: Speed does not prevent conflicting writes.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The inventory is a stale observation, not the current authority.
statements.explanation: The scene may have changed since the read.

statements.label: C
statements.text: On a conflict the agent should stop or replan from fresh state.
statements.explanation: It avoids overwriting the human's work.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A precondition check compares current state with the snapshot before a write.
statements.explanation: It detects conflicting changes.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Silently overwriting counts as resolving a conflict.
statements.explanation: It discards the other edit.

questions.stem: A checkpoint-placing workflow is shared between Unity and Unreal. Which statements are correct? Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Creating objects and referencing assets belongs to the shared layer.
statements.explanation: Those are engine-specific.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Tool names and argument meanings can be reused between adapters without checking.
statements.explanation: Each adapter's contract differs.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The shared layer holds intent, such as count, locations and activation behaviour.
statements.explanation: Intent is engine-neutral.

statements.label: D
statements.text: An adapter maps the shared intent onto an engine's own operations.
statements.explanation: Adapters hold the engine-specific part.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Passing verification in one engine shows the other engine passes.
statements.explanation: Gameplay is verified in each engine separately.

questions.stem: Unity Spark is described as a browser-based game-creation experience, and a Unity MCP integration exposes editor capabilities to an external assistant. Which statements are correct? Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Installing an MCP server gives access to Spark.
statements.explanation: An interface does not grant a separate product.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Two products from one vendor share the same project workflow.
statements.explanation: Workflow compatibility needs evidence.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Spark names a product experience, while an MCP integration names an interface to editor capabilities.
statements.explanation: They are different kinds of thing.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Spark is the expanded name of the acronym MCP.
statements.explanation: MCP stands for Model Context Protocol.

statements.label: E
statements.text: What an installed MCP server can do is found by inspecting the tools it advertises.
statements.explanation: Capabilities come from discovery, not from a product name.

questions.stem: A teammate says, "Unity Spark is Unity's MCP, so installing an MCP server gives us Spark." Which statements correct the wording? Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Evaluating an installed MCP integration begins by opening Spark in a browser.
statements.explanation: An integration is evaluated through its own tools.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Installing an interface gives access to a separate product experience.
statements.explanation: Access to a product is not a side effect of an interface.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Spark is evaluated by listing its MCP tools.
statements.explanation: Spark is a product experience judged on the games it produces.

statements.label: D
statements.text: MCP stands for Model Context Protocol.
statements.explanation: That is the expansion of the acronym.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Spark is a creation experience, not a protocol.
statements.explanation: The two words name different categories.

questions.stem: A vendor note says an older in-editor MCP server is deprecated and a CLI-hosted MCP server replaces it. Which statements are correct? Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Deprecating one server retires the MCP protocol.
statements.explanation: A component lifecycle is not a protocol lifecycle.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A replacement server's tool catalog can differ, so tool names and contracts are checked again.
statements.explanation: Names and arguments are not carried over by assumption.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Deprecated means still present but discouraged and planned for removal.
statements.explanation: It is a lifecycle label for a component.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A pilot in a small project is unnecessary once a vendor note exists.
statements.explanation: A pilot exposes compatibility problems before production.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Deleting the project's scenes is the first migration step.
statements.explanation: Migrating a connection does not touch game content.

questions.stem: A team plans to migrate from an older MCP server to its replacement. Which statements use the terms correctly? Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A query that reads is the riskiest first test of a new connection.
statements.explanation: Reading is low risk compared with writing.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A reversible edit is a change that is impossible to undo.
statements.explanation: Reversible means it can be undone.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A checkpoint is a recoverable snapshot of the project and configuration taken before the change.
statements.explanation: It lets the team return to a known state.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A query that reads changes the scene slightly.
statements.explanation: A query reads and does not modify.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A rollback route is a documented way to return to the previous setup.
statements.explanation: Rollback undoes the migration.

questions.stem: A Unity automation package offers direct command-line commands and an MCP interface to the same editor operations. Which statements are correct? Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Both routes need the editor operation's result checked.
statements.explanation: The interface does not prove correctness.

statements.label: B
statements.text: An MCP tool advertises an input schema that describes its arguments.
statements.explanation: The schema is part of the tool definition.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Direct commands can automate a task without a language-model inference.
statements.explanation: A script can call known operations directly.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Which route is usable depends on whether the agent host supports MCP tools or can run shell commands.
statements.explanation: Hosts differ in the interfaces they offer.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Direct commands need no authorization because no MCP message is sent.
statements.explanation: They can still change project state.

questions.stem: Two Unity projects are open and each has a scene named Arena. An agent is asked to add a light to one project's Arena. Which statements are correct? Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The most recently opened editor is the target.
statements.explanation: Recency is not user intent.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A scene name is ambiguous across projects, so an asset path within a named project is a better selector.
statements.explanation: Qualified identifiers remove the ambiguity.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A successful tool connection identifies the intended project.
statements.explanation: Connectivity does not show the user's intent.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A light in either Arena satisfies the request.
statements.explanation: The destination project is part of the request.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The agent verifies project identity as well as scene identity.
statements.explanation: A shared scene name is ambiguous.

questions.stem: A scene has twenty instances of a lamp prefab, and one named lamp should turn blue. Which statements use the terms correctly? Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Reverting an override returns the instance to the prefab's value.
statements.explanation: Revert discards the per-instance difference.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A prefab instance is a placed copy in the scene that stays linked to its prefab asset.
statements.explanation: Instances derive from the prefab asset.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Deleting the prefab asset is a way to isolate one lamp.
statements.explanation: That damages the reusable asset.

statements.label: D
statements.text: An override changes a value on one instance without changing the prefab asset.
statements.explanation: Overrides are per-instance differences.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Applying an override to the prefab keeps the change on one instance.
statements.explanation: Applying writes the change into the prefab asset, so other instances pick it up.

questions.stem: Twenty lamps reference one material asset, and one lamp should be blue. Which statements are correct? Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A MaterialPropertyBlock overrides properties for one renderer without editing the material asset.
statements.explanation: It is a per-renderer property override.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A material instance is a per-renderer copy, so changing it leaves the other lamps alone.
statements.explanation: Instancing separates one renderer from the shared asset.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Moving a lamp makes its material reference independent.
statements.explanation: Transform changes do not clone materials.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Looking at the selected lamp shows that the other lamps are unchanged.
statements.explanation: Unchanged lamps need their own check.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Editing the shared material asset changes each renderer that references it.
statements.explanation: The reference is shared.

questions.stem: An agent changes one wall's material colour, and several other walls change too. Which statements are correct? Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Moving the changed wall gives its material an independent copy.
statements.explanation: A transform does not clone a material.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The walls reference the same material asset, which explains the propagation.
statements.explanation: One definition feeds each consumer.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Editing the shared material is the correct fix whatever the intended scope.
statements.explanation: The intended scope decides whether to edit the asset or use a per-object approach.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The extra changes show a transport fault in the MCP connection.
statements.explanation: Shared asset semantics already explain them.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A screenshot of the selected wall shows the scope was correct.
statements.explanation: It does not show unintended changes elsewhere.

questions.stem: An agent edits a script to add a field, then tries to set it on the component, and the editor shows compilation errors. Which statements are correct? Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Hiding the console errors makes the new component definition usable.
statements.explanation: Display filtering does not fix compilation.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Repeating the field assignment repairs a compiler error.
statements.explanation: The cause is in the code or dependencies.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A serialized field is a field Unity stores with the component, such as a public field.
statements.explanation: Serialization is what makes a field settable in the editor.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The field is available as soon as the script file is saved.
statements.explanation: Saved bytes do not mean the code compiled.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A compilation error means the new script version is not loaded, so the component keeps its old layout.
statements.explanation: The old compiled definition stays in use.

questions.stem: After a script change, an agent plans its repair steps. Which statements use the terms correctly? Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Suppressing the error message counts as addressing the diagnostics.
statements.explanation: The cause remains.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The sequence is compile, reload, inspect the component, set the field, read it back, then test the behaviour.
statements.explanation: Each step depends on the one before.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A read-back means reading the value from the editor after setting it.
statements.explanation: It confirms the stored state.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Compiler diagnostics are the messages that name the location and cause of an error.
statements.explanation: They guide the code fix.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Reading the script file's text is equivalent to a read-back from the component.
statements.explanation: The component's loaded state is a different thing.

questions.stem: A tool reports a successful scene edit, but after closing and reopening the project the change is gone. Which statements are correct? Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A success result can describe a completed mutation without a completed save.
statements.explanation: The tool contract defines what success covers.

statements.label: B
statements.text: In-memory state is the scene as the open editor holds it, and saved state is the scene file on disk.
statements.explanation: They can differ until a save.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The missing change shows the language model forgot the scene.
statements.explanation: Persistence is an editor and storage matter.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Reopening the saved scene is a persistence check.
statements.explanation: It tests whether the change survives a reload.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A dirty scene is one with unsaved changes.
statements.explanation: The editor marks such scenes as dirty.

questions.stem: A texture file was copied into a Unity project and the editor is still importing it. Which statements are correct? Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: An import error shows that the file was not copied.
statements.explanation: Copying and importing are separate steps.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The file's presence on disk shows the asset is ready.
statements.explanation: Filesystem presence and engine readiness differ.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Copying the file again is a way to wait for import.
statements.explanation: Duplicates add ambiguity.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Assigning a placeholder proves the requested texture imported.
statements.explanation: A placeholder is a different asset.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A file on disk becomes an asset the engine can use once the editor imports it.
statements.explanation: Import is the processing step.

questions.stem: A parent object is translated ten units along one axis with identity rotation and scale, and its child has local position zero. Which statements are correct? Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A child's local transform is applied relative to its parent's transform.
