statements.text: Import converts source assets into the engine's runtime formats and stores them in the cache folder.
statements.explanation: The engine uses the imported copy at runtime, not the raw PNG or WAV.

questions.stem: A coding agent has edited several files in a project tracked in a repository. Before accepting anything, the developer wants to know what changed. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A repository is the project's files together with the recorded history of earlier versions.
statements.explanation: Version history lets "what changed?" have an exact answer.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A diff shows, line by line, how one version differs from another, such as the working files versus the last commit.
statements.explanation: A diff records added, removed and changed lines.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A commit pushes the change to a shared server so teammates receive it immediately.
statements.explanation: A commit records a snapshot in local history; sharing is the separate push step.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A diff with a few changed lines proves the change works, because a diff lists lines that ran successfully.
statements.explanation: A diff records what changed, not whether it behaves correctly.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Reading the diff before committing is unnecessary when the agent's own report lists the files it changed.
statements.explanation: The report is a claim; stray edits show up in the diff.

questions.stem: A developer lets a coding agent run shell commands without asking when they match an allow rule. The developer writes one rule for commands starting with `env` and another for commands starting with the game engine's program name. The engine can run a script file given on its command line, and that script may start other programs. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A permission prompt is a chance to review the command or script, not a formality.
statements.explanation: The prompt is where a human can catch a command broader than intended.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A broad engine rule also lets through code in a script the agent wrote, including code that starts other programs.
statements.explanation: An allow rule decides which program starts, not what a script run by that program does.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A rule allowing one exact command with fixed arguments is a narrower grant than a wildcard on the program name.
statements.explanation: The fewer variations a rule matches, the less it grants.

statements.label: D
statements.text: `env` runs the command given as its arguments, so an `env` rule also allows the program that follows it.
statements.explanation: `env NAME=value program` starts the named program, so the rule is as wide as "run a program".

statements.label: E
statements.text: An allow rule limits what an allowed program does internally once it is running, for example which files it opens.
statements.explanation: Allow rules decide which commands start without asking; they do not constrain a running program.

questions.stem: A coding agent runs in a sandbox that lets it write inside the project folder. During an import step the engine prints an error that it cannot save its settings file, which lives in the user's home directory, yet the import still produces a usable project. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Inside this sandbox the agent can still delete project files, including test output it produced earlier.
statements.explanation: Deleting is a kind of write, and writes inside the workspace are allowed.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Running in a sandbox confirms that the code the agent writes is correct.
statements.explanation: A sandbox limits damage; it says nothing about correctness.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A sandbox and a permission prompt are one mechanism under two names.
statements.explanation: A prompt asks a human before a command runs; a sandbox enforces limits on what a running command can touch.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A sandbox is a technical limit on what a process may read, write or reach.
statements.explanation: Sandboxes restrict capabilities at the operating-system level.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The error fits a sandbox blocking a write outside the project folder while writes inside it succeed.
statements.explanation: The settings file is outside the project folder, and the cache is inside it.

questions.stem: Two developers ask a coding agent for a score counter in a two-player paddle game. Developer X writes "add a nice score system". Developer Y lists the observable behaviour (a point goes to the right player when the ball leaves through the left edge), what must not change, which files to read first, how to run the existing checks, and "show me the real command output; do not commit". Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Y's request works as a spec: required behaviour, constraints and a way to check the result.
statements.explanation: A spec makes "done" decidable; a bare prompt does not.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Asking for real command output instead of a summary matters: a description is a claim, output can be inspected.
statements.explanation: Output can be checked against a rerun; a summary cannot.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Adding adjectives such as "robust" and "clean" to X's request turns it into a precise spec.
statements.explanation: Adjectives add mood, not checkable behaviour or constraints.

statements.label: D
statements.text: X's request leaves the agent to choose where the score is shown, which event changes it and what counts as finished.
statements.explanation: Each unstated decision is a place where the agent can build something other than what was meant.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Stating what stays fixed helps, because an agent that is not told may alter related behaviour.
statements.explanation: Explicit constraints keep the change bounded.

questions.stem: Yesterday a developer spent an hour in one session teaching a coding agent how to run a project's checks, which need a special flag. Today the developer starts a new session in the same repository and says: "run the checks and fix what fails". No instruction file in the repository mentions the flag. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The agent remembers the flag, because the same underlying model is used and the project is the same.
statements.explanation: The same model does not carry over a past session's content.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The agent deduces the missing flag from the project's name.
statements.explanation: A project-specific flag is written down or discovered; a name does not reveal it.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A larger context window lets the agent recall yesterday's session.
statements.explanation: Window size does not matter; yesterday's text is not in today's context.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The new session starts without yesterday's conversation; the agent knows what it is given or can read.
statements.explanation: Context is the text available now, and a fresh session starts without earlier conversations.

statements.label: E
statements.text: If the agent runs the checks without the flag and they fail, the failure is evidence that the game is broken.
statements.explanation: The failure may come from running the checks the wrong way.

questions.stem: A developer asks a coding agent to add a pause feature: pressing the pause key stops the ball, and pressing it again resumes. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A test that sets the game's `paused` variable to true and then checks it is true is a strong acceptance test of the pause key.
statements.explanation: It does not exercise the key press, so it passes even if the key is not connected.

statements.label: B
statements.text: If the new test fails, loosening its checks until it passes gives the same evidence as a pass of the original checks.
statements.explanation: A weakened test certifies less.

statements.label: C
statements.text: An acceptance test checks the agreed behaviour from the outside, the way a player would exercise it.
statements.explanation: Acceptance is judged on observable behaviour.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The agent takes the test's expected results from what its finished code does, so the test fits what was built.
statements.explanation: Expected results copied from the code confirm the code; they should come from the required behaviour.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A stronger test sends the pause key through normal input handling and checks that the ball's position stays put.
statements.explanation: It follows the real chain from input to observable state.

questions.stem: A coding agent finishes a change and reports: "Done. All tests pass." The developer considers what each item establishes. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A diff shows which lines changed but not that the changed code behaves correctly.
statements.explanation: A diff describes the change, not its correctness.

statements.label: B
statements.text: After one person plays the game for five minutes, the change counts as verified for other players and machines.
statements.explanation: A playtest shows one person's experience on one machine.

statements.label: C
statements.text: If the agent pastes the test output, the developer treats the result as verified without rerunning anything.
statements.explanation: Pasted output may come from a differently configured run; reproducing it is the check.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A passing automated test with the time step pinned shows the tested state is right under that scripted input; it does not show the game is fun or readable.
statements.explanation: A test speaks to the state it reads, under the inputs it feeds.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The agent's report is a claim; running the same command yourself and seeing the same output is evidence.
statements.explanation: Evidence is something the developer can reproduce and inspect.

questions.stem: A test presses the up key for 600 frames and then checks that a paddle has reached the top wall. The paddle's movement is speed times delta, where delta is the real time since the previous frame. With no change to code or test, it passes on 7 of 10 runs on a busy laptop and on 10 of 10 on an idle one. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: This test is flaky: its outcome varies between runs with no change to code or test.
statements.explanation: Flaky means the result varies with no change to the code or the test.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A test that passes ten times in a row is proven deterministic.
statements.explanation: Ten passes are consistent with a failure that is rare or load-dependent.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Re-running until the test passes and keeping that run is a sound fix.
statements.explanation: It hides the variation instead of removing its cause.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Seeding the random number generator removes this variation, because the variation comes from randomness.
statements.explanation: The unpinned quantity is frame timing, which a random seed does not control.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A plausible cause is that frame length varies with machine load, so 600 frames span different amounts of game time.
statements.explanation: The test counts frames while the game advances in seconds.

questions.stem: A game moves a paddle by adding speed times delta each frame, where delta is the game time one frame represents. A test holds the up key for a number of frames. The engine is started with an option that forces a fixed frame rate, so each frame represents the same game time, and the engine does not wait on the wall clock between frames. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: With a higher forced frame rate and the same frame count, the same game time is simulated.
statements.explanation: More frames per second means less game time per frame, so the same frame count covers less game time.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Holding the key for a stated amount of game time, instead of a frame count, removes the dependence on the frame rate.
statements.explanation: A test written in game seconds covers the same time at any frame rate.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Pinning the time step removes the machine-dependent quantity from the test.
statements.explanation: The pinned step removes the load-dependent frame length.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Forcing the frame rate makes a frame-counting test repeatable, because each frame is the same game time on each machine.
statements.explanation: A pinned time step makes frames equal in game time.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Because the frame length is pinned, the test takes as many real seconds to run as the game time it simulates.
statements.explanation: Game time per frame is pinned, but the run takes as long as the machine needs.

questions.stem: A developer wants a coding agent to fix a bug and prove the fix. Several instructions are considered. Check each statement that is true about whether the quoted instruction is precise enough to be checked.

statements.label: A
statements.text: "Do what it takes to get the test suite green." This is precise, because "green" is a measurable state.
statements.explanation: The state is measurable, but the instruction permits weakening tests to reach it.

statements.label: B
statements.text: "Do not commit; leave the changes uncommitted so I can read the diff." This keeps acceptance with the developer.
statements.explanation: It separates making the change from accepting it.

statements.label: C
statements.text: "Run the regression test headless at a fixed 60 fps; it has to exit 0; paste the command and its full output." This fixes conditions, pass criterion and evidence.
statements.explanation: Each element can be verified by rerunning the command.

statements.label: D
statements.text: "Make sure it works now." This is checkable, because "works" covers the test, the build and how the game feels.
statements.explanation: The word has no pass condition, so readers can interpret it differently.

statements.label: E
statements.text: "If an existing test fails, report which and stop; do not edit tests." This blocks the shortcut of rewriting a failing test.
statements.explanation: It forbids the cheapest way to turn red into green.

questions.stem: A studio decides whether a coding agent can work on its scene files. One engine saves scenes as human-readable text; another saves its main scene format as binary files. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: An agent that hand-edits a text scene can tell the engine will load it, by re-reading the file.
statements.explanation: A hand-edited scene can read as well-formed text and still fail to load; the engine is the judge.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A binary scene can be reviewed with an ordinary text diff as clearly as a text one.
statements.explanation: A line diff of binary data is not readable.

statements.label: C
statements.text: An agent can judge what a binary image looks like by reading its bytes as text in a terminal.
statements.explanation: Pixel content is not recoverable by reading bytes as characters.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A binary scene file is stored without history in version control, so a bad change has to be repaired by hand.
statements.explanation: Version control stores binary files and can revert them; it cannot show a readable line diff.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A text scene shows up in a version-control diff line by line, so a reviewer sees which node or property changed.
statements.explanation: Text formats are what line-based diffs are built for.

questions.stem: A developer types to a coding agent: "Add a score to my two-player paddle game and make sure everything still works." Check each statement that is true about rewriting this as a precise instruction.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A new test for the score writes the score variable directly and then asserts it, which exercises the real behaviour.
statements.explanation: A test that sets the asserted value cannot fail for the right reason; it should drive the game through normal input.

statements.label: B
statements.text: "Everything still works" is a checkable constraint, because it names the paddle and ball behaviour that has to stay fixed.
statements.explanation: "Everything" names nothing; the rewrite has to list the behaviour that stays fixed.

statements.label: C
statements.text: "A score" is vague; observable behaviour names which player gets a point, for which edge, and where both scores are displayed.
statements.explanation: Observable terms leave less to guess.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The original wording lets "works" mean "it runs", lets a test be weakened to pass, and lets unrelated behaviour change.
statements.explanation: Each is a way the vague wording can go wrong.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A precise rewrite names the command that runs the checks (headless, frame rate pinned, under a timeout, exit 0 as the pass condition) and asks for the real output.
statements.explanation: Conditions, a pass criterion and evidence make the check repeatable.

questions.source: Flaky tests and fixed frame rate
questions.stem: A regression test passes on one laptop and fails on another, and sometimes fails then passes on the same laptop with no change to the code. The test presses keys for a fixed number of frames, and the game moves objects by speed times delta. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Another fix is to express the test in game seconds instead of counting rendered frames.
statements.explanation: A game-seconds test does not depend on how many frames are drawn.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A deterministic test gives the same result on each run from the same code and inputs.
statements.explanation: Determinism means the same inputs give the same result.

statements.label: C
statements.text: One fix is to run the engine with a fixed frame rate so each frame is the same game time.
statements.explanation: A pinned frame rate removes the machine-dependent step.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The mismatch is that the test counts frames while the game advances in seconds of delta.
statements.explanation: Frame length depends on load, so the same frame count covers different game time.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Before blaming the game code, change several variables at once so the cause shows up faster.
statements.explanation: Changing one variable at a time, under the pinned configuration, is what separates a flaky test from a code bug.

questions.stem: A developer wants a coding agent to import a game project and run its headless tests, but not to run arbitrary commands. Three options are considered: (a) an allow rule for commands starting with the engine's program name; (b) allow rules for exact commands with fixed arguments; (c) running everything in a sandbox that can write inside the project folder. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Option (a) is wide, because an engine that runs a script file runs whatever code the script contains.
statements.explanation: A program-name rule is not a boundary on behaviour.

statements.label: B
statements.text: An allow rule decides which commands run without asking a human, while a sandbox technically limits what a running process can reach.
statements.explanation: A permission grant and a sandbox are different mechanisms.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Option (b) is narrower and easier to reason about, though an exact-match rule needs updating when the command changes.
statements.explanation: A narrow grant is easier to read, at the cost of upkeep.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Even with these options the developer still reads new commands and scripts before approving them and reviews the diff before committing.
statements.explanation: Human review is not replaced by either mechanism.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Option (c) stops the agent from deleting or overwriting project files.
statements.explanation: A sandbox that allows writes inside the folder allows deletion there too.

questions.stem: A coding agent ran a project's regression test the wrong way, the test failed, and the agent gave a confident but wrong explanation. The developer then added a short section to a standing instruction file in the repository, and the same request produced a correct run. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Project-specific facts such as required flags and setup steps are known to the agent without being written down.
statements.explanation: What is not written down is guessed, and the guess can look plausible but be wrong.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A fluent explanation is evidence, and the instruction file guarantees identical design choices on each run.
statements.explanation: A fluent explanation is not evidence, and an instruction file does not fix design choices; the developer still verifies.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The section should list exact commands, required options, setup steps such as the import step, the expected result and a time limit.
statements.explanation: These details make the run repeatable.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The file should say what stays a human decision or is off limits to edit.
statements.explanation: Limits belong in the file as well.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Context is the text available to the agent now, such as instructions, files it has read and command output, and it is limited in size.
statements.explanation: A new session starts without earlier conversations.

questions.stem: A developer wants to verify, without opening a window, that a score label shows the correct number after the ball leaves the left edge. Check each statement that is true about a good headless test.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The test sets the score variable directly and then reads it back to confirm it.
statements.explanation: Writing the asserted value directly proves nothing about the game.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The test reports through its exit code, 0 for pass and nonzero for fail, plus a readable report.
statements.explanation: The exit code is the machine-readable verdict.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The test reads observable state, such as the score counter and the label's text, and pins the time step so the run is repeatable.
statements.explanation: State plus a pinned time step gives a repeatable check.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The test shows how the number looks when rendered, including legibility and overlap.
statements.explanation: Headless mode draws no frame, so appearance needs a person looking at a rendered image.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The test loads the real game scene and drives it through normal input events or by letting the game play until the ball leaves.
statements.explanation: Driving the real game exercises the real behaviour.

questions.stem: A coding agent reports "Done, all tests pass." Check each statement that is true about what an item shows.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A reasonable minimum before accepting is reading the diff, rerunning the pinned test, checking that no test was weakened, and a human playtest for anything about feel.
statements.explanation: These checks cover the change, the test and the feel.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The agent's report shows that the agent produced a message, and the developer's own rerun is evidence.
statements.explanation: A report is a claim; a reproduced result is evidence.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A clean import and parse check shows that files load and scripts parse, not that behaviour is right.
statements.explanation: Loading and parsing say nothing about behaviour.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A person playing shows what the game does on other machines.
statements.explanation: A playtest shows one person's experience on one machine.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A build running on the target platform shows the game survives packaging, not that anyone wants to play it.
statements.explanation: A packaged run tests the build, not the experience.

questions.stem: A Godot beginner is asked to define the basic terms of the engine. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: An instance is a saved scene file stored on disk.
statements.explanation: An instance is the set of nodes created from a scene, not the file.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The scene tree is the saved scene file that Godot loads at startup.
statements.explanation: The scene tree is the live hierarchy of nodes in the running game.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A scene file is limited to a single node.
statements.explanation: A scene holds any number of nodes arranged in a tree.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A node is the basic building block of a scene, and its type decides what it can do.
statements.explanation: Godot builds everything from nodes, such as Sprite2D or Timer, and the type gives the abilities.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A scene is a saved arrangement of nodes in a tree that can be reused.
statements.explanation: A scene is a tree of nodes saved as a file that other scenes can reuse.

questions.stem: A developer has a saved Character scene (body, sprite, collision shape) and wants a Magician that is mostly the same with one extra staff node. Check each statement that is true about the terms.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Instancing and inheriting are two names for the same operation.
statements.explanation: Instancing nests a scene inside another; inheriting builds a new scene on a base.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Instancing places a scene as a node inside another scene and keeps it linked to its source file.
statements.explanation: An instance appears as one node and edits to the source scene reach it.

statements.label: C
statements.text: An instanced scene appears as several unlinked top-level nodes.
statements.explanation: An instance appears as one node, the root of the instanced scene, still linked to its file.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Adding the staff to a Magician that inherits from Character means editing the Character scene itself.
statements.explanation: An inherited scene can add the staff without changing the base.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Inheriting creates a new scene that extends a base scene, can add nodes of its own, and follows later changes to the base.
statements.explanation: An inherited scene builds on a base scene and can extend it.

questions.source: Instancing a scene for repeated objects
questions.stem: A developer tells a coding agent: "Add ten enemies to the level." The agent duplicates the enemy's nodes ten times directly inside the level scene, and later the developer changes the enemy sprite. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Duplicated nodes are independent copies with no link to a shared enemy scene.
statements.explanation: Plain duplicates are unlinked, so each needs the edit by hand.

statements.label: B
statements.text: "Instance the Enemy scene ten times in the level, at these positions" is a precise version of the instruction.
statements.explanation: It names the term (instance), the scene and the placement.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Instancing one saved Enemy scene ten times lets an edit to that scene reach each instance.
statements.explanation: Instances stay linked to the scene file they came from.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The word "add" does not say whether to duplicate nodes or to instance a scene, which leaves open a choice that affects maintenance.
statements.explanation: Duplicating and instancing give different results later, so the verb needs to be exact.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Instances of one scene share a single position because they share one scene file.
statements.explanation: Each instance has its own transform.

questions.stem: A Main scene has a root Main with one child Player, and Player has one child Sprite. Each node has a script that prints a message from _enter_tree and from _ready. Check each statement that is true about the order of the callbacks.

statements.label: A
statements.text: In Main's _ready, the Player and Sprite have already been through their _ready.
statements.explanation: Main is the last node to be ready.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The _ready of a node is called after the _ready of its children.
statements.explanation: _ready goes from the leaves up, so children are ready first.

statements.label: C
statements.text: _ready is called before the node has entered the scene tree.
statements.explanation: _ready is called once the node and its children are in the tree.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The _enter_tree of Sprite is called before the _enter_tree of Player.
statements.explanation: A child enters the tree after its parent.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The _enter_tree of a parent is called before the _enter_tree of its children.
statements.explanation: Entering the tree goes from the root down to the leaves.

questions.stem: A developer describes three callbacks of one Godot node. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: _process is called once per rendered frame.
statements.explanation: The frame rate can change, and so can the number of _process calls per second.

statements.label: B
statements.text: _physics_process is called at a fixed rate that does not follow the frame rate.
statements.explanation: The physics step is fixed, so physics-driven movement uses this callback.

statements.label: C
statements.text: _ready is called again on each frame.
statements.explanation: _ready is called once per node unless it is requested again.

statements.label: D
statements.text: _process is called at the fixed physics rate.
statements.explanation: The fixed rate belongs to _physics_process.

statements.label: E
statements.text: _ready is called once when the node and its children have entered the scene tree.
statements.explanation: One-time setup belongs in _ready.

questions.stem: A coding agent writes var label = $Label at the top of a script on a node with a child named Label. At startup the console says the node was not found, and label is null later. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A member initializer runs when the script instance is created, before the children are available.
statements.explanation: The children do not exist at that moment, so the lookup fails.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Godot finds a child by number and does not find it by name.
statements.explanation: A child is found by name or by path; the cause here is the timing.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Repeating the $Label lookup in _process each frame is the right fix for the null reference.
statements.explanation: A lookup once at ready time is enough and a lookup each frame repeats work.

statements.label: D
statements.text: _init is the constructor, and it runs when the object is created, before the node is in the tree.
statements.explanation: Assigning children in _init has the same timing problem.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Marking the variable @onready defers its initialization until right before _ready.
statements.explanation: @onready is the annotation for a variable that is assigned when the node is ready.

questions.stem: Check each statement about GDScript and about how a script relates to a node.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The signal keyword declares a signal that other scripts can connect to.
statements.explanation: Declaring a signal makes it part of the node's interface.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A script that begins with extends Node2D builds on that node type and can use its properties and methods.
statements.explanation: extends names the base type that the script is built on.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Python runs GDScript files inside the engine.
statements.explanation: GDScript looks like Python but has its own interpreter in the engine.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Member variables belong to each script instance, so each node has its own copy.
statements.explanation: Variables declared at the top of a script are per instance, not global.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Attaching a script to one node gives the same behaviour to other nodes of the same type.
statements.explanation: A script applies to the node it is attached to.

questions.stem: A coin script has @export var value: int = 1, and the coin scene is instanced three times in a level. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A value set in the Inspector is stored in the scene file.
statements.explanation: Exported properties are saved with the scene.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Each instance can carry its own exported value.
statements.explanation: The script supplies the default and each instance can override it.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A variable that is not exported is hidden from other scripts.
statements.explanation: Export concerns the editor, not access from code.

statements.label: D
statements.text: @export makes the variable global, so one change reaches each instance.
statements.explanation: Exported variables are still per-instance members.

statements.label: E
statements.text: @export exposes the variable in the editor's Inspector.
statements.explanation: Export is about editor visibility.

questions.stem: A developer tells a coding agent: "Let the designer tune run speed and jump height without touching code." Check each statement that is true about the terms.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A group stores numeric values for the nodes in it.
statements.explanation: A group is a tag for finding nodes, not a place for values.

statements.label: B
statements.text: An exported variable of a Resource type lets the designer pick the tuning file in the Inspector.
statements.explanation: An exported slot of a Resource type lets the file be assigned in the editor.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A Resource is added to the scene tree as a child node.
statements.explanation: A Resource is not a node and does not enter the scene tree.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A constant at the top of a script can be edited in the Inspector.
statements.explanation: A constant is part of the script text and is not exposed.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A custom Resource is a data container saved as a file that can be edited and shared.
statements.explanation: A custom Resource with exported fields is a data file.

questions.stem: Three enemies point at the same saved EnemyStats Resource through an exported variable. During play, a script lowers stats.health on one enemy. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Runtime state such as current health is kept in the node, or the Resource is duplicated for each enemy.
statements.explanation: Per-enemy state needs per-enemy storage.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Changing the value in memory rewrites the saved file at once.
statements.explanation: The file changes only if the game saves the resource.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A Resource is a data object, not a node.
statements.explanation: Resources are containers for data.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Loading the same resource path returns the same in-memory object, so the change is seen by each enemy.
statements.explanation: A shared resource is shared state.

statements.label: E
statements.text: @export gives each enemy its own copy of the Resource.
statements.explanation: Export exposes the slot; it does not copy.

questions.stem: A Door node has a child Lock, and the Lock should tell the Door when it has been picked. Check each statement that is true about the usual advice "call down, signal up".

statements.label: A
statements.text: A shared ancestor can connect or mediate between sibling scenes.
statements.explanation: An ancestor that knows both siblings can wire them.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A parent can call a method on a child it owns.
statements.explanation: Calls go down to children that the parent knows.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A Lock that emits an unlocked signal can be reused where there is no Door.
statements.explanation: The emitter does not need to know what listens.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A Lock that calls get_parent().open() is tightly coupled to the layout of the tree above it.
statements.explanation: Coupling is a dependency on structure that is not guaranteed.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Sibling scenes should hold direct references to each other.
statements.explanation: Direct sibling references tie scenes together.

questions.stem: A script declares signal health_changed(new_value) and emits it from several places. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Emitting calls the connected functions and passes them the arguments.
statements.explanation: Emit sends the arguments to each connected function.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A deferred connection runs its function at the end of the frame instead of at once.
statements.explanation: Deferred mode postpones the call.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Emitting a signal with no connected function raises an error.
statements.explanation: A signal without listeners calls nothing.

statements.label: D
statements.text: By default connected functions run at the end of the frame.
statements.explanation: The default is immediate; deferred is the option that waits.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Connecting in the editor's Signals dock and with connect in code both make a connection.
statements.explanation: The dock and code are two ways to make the same kind of link.

questions.stem: A coding agent builds player controls from the instruction "Make Space jump and A and D move." Check each statement that is true about input terms.

statements.label: A
statements.text: An input action names an intent, such as jump, and maps to bindings in the Input Map.
statements.explanation: Code asks about the action and not about a key.

statements.label: B
statements.text: is_action_just_pressed is true on the frame the press began, and is_action_pressed is true while it is held.
statements.explanation: Just pressed and pressed are different tests.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A binding by physical key stays at one keyboard position on other layouts, and a binding by printed character follows the character.
statements.explanation: Physical bindings suit WASD-style controls.

statements.label: D
statements.text: An action holds one input event.
statements.explanation: An action can group several events, such as a key and a gamepad button.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Reading the Space key directly is as flexible as using an action.
statements.explanation: A hard-coded key cannot be rebound without editing code.

questions.stem: A pause menu of Control nodes opens over gameplay. Check each statement that is true about input callbacks.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Polling Input.is_action_pressed in _process is blocked while a menu is open.
statements.explanation: Polling reads the current state of the action.

statements.label: B
statements.text: _input is called before the GUI processes the event.
statements.explanation: _input can see events before a button uses them.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Marking an event as handled stops it from reaching later nodes.
statements.explanation: Handled events stop propagating.

statements.label: D
statements.text: _unhandled_input is called before _input.
statements.explanation: _input comes first, and _unhandled_input gets what is left.

statements.label: E
statements.text: _unhandled_input gets events that no earlier callback or Control consumed.
statements.explanation: Gameplay code there ignores a click that a button consumed.

questions.stem: A level has twelve guard nodes in several scenes, and an alarm must put them on alert. A developer proposes a group named guards. Check each statement that is true about groups.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Using a group means the alarm code keeps a list of guard references by hand.
statements.explanation: Avoiding a hand-kept list is the purpose of a group.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A group is a name tag, and adding a node to it does not change its parent.
statements.explanation: The nodes stay where they are in the tree.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A group is a node type.
statements.explanation: A group is a label, not a type of node.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A node can belong to more than one group.
statements.explanation: A guard can also be in an enemies group.

statements.label: E
statements.text: One call on the scene tree can call a method on each member of a group.
statements.explanation: A group call addresses the members together.

questions.stem: A project registers a script as an autoload and a developer inspects the live scene tree during play. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: An autoload is added after the main scene has finished loading.
statements.explanation: Autoloads are loaded before the main scene.

statements.label: B
statements.text: An autoload is freed and recreated when the current scene is replaced.
statements.explanation: An autoload persists across scene changes.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A script has no way to refer to an autoload by the name it was registered with.
statements.explanation: A GDScript can use the registered name.

statements.label: D
statements.text: An autoload node is a child of the root, added before the main scene is loaded.
statements.explanation: Autoloads come first, with the current scene added after them.

statements.label: E
statements.text: An autoload is safe to remove with queue_free at runtime.
statements.explanation: Freeing an autoload at runtime can crash the engine.

questions.stem: A script calls get_node("UI/Panel/ScoreLabel") inside _process, so the lookup runs on each frame. Check each statement that is true about node paths.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A hard-coded path keeps working after a node on that path is renamed.
statements.explanation: Paths break when a node on the path is renamed or moved.

statements.label: B
statements.text: get_node on a path that leads nowhere returns an empty node and reports no error.
statements.explanation: An invalid path gives an error and a null result.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Storing the reference in a variable once the node is ready avoids repeating the lookup.
statements.explanation: Caching the reference is the usual practice.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A relative path starts at the calling node, and an absolute path starts at the root with a slash.
statements.explanation: The leading slash marks an absolute path.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A unique name set on a node lets %Name reach it from within its scene, wherever it sits.
statements.explanation: A unique name is a lookup that does not depend on position.

questions.stem: A bullet node must be removed when it hits a wall. Check each statement that is true about freeing nodes.

statements.label: A
statements.text: queue_free queues the node for deletion at the end of the current frame.
statements.explanation: The node can still be accessed until then.

statements.label: B
statements.text: free deletes the object at once, so older references to it become invalid.
statements.explanation: Immediate deletion can leave dangling references.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Freeing a node leaves its children behind in the tree.
statements.explanation: Freeing a node also frees its children.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Calling queue_free twice on one node is an error.
statements.explanation: Repeating queue_free is safe.

statements.label: E
statements.text: After queue_free the node's other callbacks stop in the same frame.
statements.explanation: Deletion happens at the end of the frame.

questions.stem: A developer tells an agent: "Spawn a bullet when the player fires." Check each statement that is true about the terms in a precise version.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A bullet added under the level root moves in the player's local space.
statements.explanation: Under the level root, the bullet moves in the level's space.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A PackedScene is a loaded scene resource that can be instantiated.
statements.explanation: A PackedScene is the loaded form of a scene file.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Instantiating creates nodes that are not in the scene tree until they are added as a child of a node that is.
statements.explanation: add_child is the step that puts the nodes in the tree.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A child inherits its parent's transform, so a bullet added under the player moves with the player.
statements.explanation: Transforms are inherited down the hierarchy.

statements.label: E
statements.text: An instance that was not added to the tree still runs its _ready.
statements.explanation: Callbacks run when the node enters the tree.

questions.stem: A coin script runs get_parent().get_parent().add_score(10), and it breaks in a level with a different tree layout. Check each statement that is true about the terms in the redesign.

statements.label: A
statements.text: To emit a signal is to register a function that will be called.
statements.explanation: Emit sends the signal and connect registers the function.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A coin that emits a collected signal does not need to know who listens.
statements.explanation: The emitter is decoupled from its listeners.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A script that reaches two parents up is tightly coupled to the layout of the tree.
statements.explanation: The script works only where the ancestors are arranged as expected.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Connecting a function to a signal can be done in the editor or in code.
statements.explanation: Both ways make a connection.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Signals carry information down the tree and calls carry it up.
statements.explanation: The usual advice is the other way round: call down, signal up.

questions.stem: An agent moves a node with position.x += 5 in _process and loads a settings file in _process. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The fixed-step callback suits physics-driven movement.
statements.explanation: A constant step gives stable physics.

statements.label: B
statements.text: delta is the time since the previous frame or tick.
statements.explanation: Delta is the length of the last step.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Loading a settings file once is one-time setup that belongs in _process.
statements.explanation: One-time setup belongs in _ready.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Adding a fixed amount in _process makes speed depend on the frame rate.
statements.explanation: More frames per second means more distance per second.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Multiplying a per-second speed by delta gives movement that is independent of the frame rate.
statements.explanation: Scaling by delta ties movement to real time.

questions.stem: A designer wants enemy stats in a shared Resource with exported fields. Check each statement that is true about when values arrive.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A Resource slot shared by several enemies holds separate copies automatically.
statements.explanation: Users of one loaded resource share one object.

statements.label: B
statements.text: _ready fails to read the values that were set in the Inspector.
statements.explanation: _ready can read the designer's values.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Exported values are assigned after _init has run and before _ready.
statements.explanation: Editor values are applied between construction and ready.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A custom Resource extends the Resource type and is saved as a file.
statements.explanation: A custom Resource is a data file defined by a script.

statements.label: E
statements.text: _init sees the values that were set in the Inspector.
statements.explanation: _init sees only the defaults from the script.

questions.source: Physical versus labelled keys, input callbacks
questions.stem: Players on an AZERTY keyboard say WASD movement feels wrong, and clicking Resume on a pause menu also fires a shot. The agent read key labels directly and handled the mouse in _input. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A binding by printed label keeps the same key positions on other layouts.
statements.explanation: A labelled binding follows the character to a new position.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Handling fire in _unhandled_input receives just the events that no Control consumed.
statements.explanation: _unhandled_input is for gameplay events left after the GUI.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A binding by physical key position keeps the WASD hand shape on other layouts.
statements.explanation: Physical bindings refer to location.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Handling fire in _input lets the gameplay code see a click that the Resume button also uses.
statements.explanation: _input comes before the GUI.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A precise instruction can leave out which callback handles the mouse event.
statements.explanation: The callback decides the order, so a precise instruction names it.

questions.stem: A game needs an alarm that reaches the guards, a score that survives a scene change, and a door that opens when its lock child is picked. Check each statement that is true about choosing a mechanism.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A score kept in a node of the level scene survives the change to a game-over scene.
statements.explanation: Nodes of the level are freed with the level.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A signal lets a child announce an event without knowing its parent.
statements.explanation: The child stays reusable.

statements.label: C
statements.text: An autoload is a node that persists across scene changes, which suits a score.
statements.explanation: An autoload is not freed with the scene.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A misspelled group name raises an error at the call.
statements.explanation: A misspelled group name silently matches nothing.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A group addresses many nodes by a shared tag.
statements.explanation: A call on the group reaches each member.

questions.stem: An agent summarised Godot behaviour in several claims. Check each statement that is a correct claim.

statements.label: A
statements.text: queue_free removes the node at the end of the frame, and the node can be used until then.
statements.explanation: Deletion is deferred to the end of the frame.

statements.label: B
statements.text: _ready is called once for a node unless it is requested again.
statements.explanation: _ready follows the node entering the tree.

statements.label: C
statements.text: @export var speed stores one value in the script that the instances share.
statements.explanation: Each instance can carry its own exported value.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Emitting a signal with no listeners raises an error.
statements.explanation: An emit without connections calls nothing.

statements.label: E
statements.text: An autoload is recreated when the current scene is replaced.
statements.explanation: An autoload persists.

questions.stem: A developer wants the vocabulary for 2D art straight before instructing a coding agent. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Resolution is the pixel dimensions of an image, written as width by height.
statements.explanation: A 32 by 48 image has a resolution of 32 by 48 pixels.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Texture and sprite are synonyms for one thing.
statements.explanation: The two words name different things.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A sprite is a 2D image, or one frame of one, drawn as an object in the game scene.
statements.explanation: A sprite is a drawn 2D object.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Aspect ratio is the total pixel count of an image.
statements.explanation: Aspect ratio is the proportion of width to height.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A texture is image data applied to a surface or drawn, and a sprite is drawn using a texture.
statements.explanation: Texture names the image data and sprite names the thing drawn from it.

questions.stem: An image generator returns a nearly square picture, and the game uses a wide 16:9 viewport. Check each statement that is true about placing it.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A 16:9 viewport and a nearly square picture have the same aspect ratio.
statements.explanation: 16:9 is much wider than near-square.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Enlarging a low-resolution picture by interpolation adds real detail that was missing.
statements.explanation: Interpolation creates pixels but not information.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Scaling it uniformly to fit keeps the aspect ratio and leaves unused space on one axis.
statements.explanation: Uniform scaling keeps the shape, so one dimension does not fill the viewport.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Stretching the picture to the viewport size distorts it because the aspect ratios differ.
statements.explanation: Non-uniform scaling changes the proportions.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Interpolation estimates new pixel values from neighbouring pixels.
statements.explanation: The new values are guesses based on nearby pixels.

questions.stem: A developer asks an image generator for a character sprite "on a transparent background" and gets hero.jpg. In the engine the sprite sits inside a white rectangle. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Lowering the sprite node's opacity makes just the white rectangle transparent.
statements.explanation: Node opacity fades the whole image, character and background.

statements.label: B
statements.text: JPEG has no alpha channel, so it does not hold transparency.
statements.explanation: PNG stores alpha and JPEG does not.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Removing a background by colour key can leave light fringe pixels along the edge.
statements.explanation: Anti-aliased edge pixels blend the character with the old background.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A white background painted into the pixels counts as transparency.
statements.explanation: Painted white is colour content, not an alpha value.

statements.label: E
statements.text: An alpha channel stores opacity for each pixel.
statements.explanation: Alpha is the extra channel for opacity.

questions.stem: A 32 x 32 pixel-art sprite looks crisp at its original size but looks blurry when shown at four times its size in the game. Check each statement that is true about texture filtering.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Linear filtering blends neighbouring texels when a texture is enlarged, which softens hard edges.
statements.explanation: Linear interpolates between neighbouring texels.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Nearest filtering takes the colour of the single closest texel, so enlarged pixel art keeps hard edges.
statements.explanation: Nearest samples one texel per screen pixel.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The instruction "make it sharper" names the setting that should be changed.
statements.explanation: "Sharper" names a result, not the filter setting.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A filter set on one sprite applies to that sprite, while a project default applies to sprites that do not set their own.
statements.explanation: Scope follows where the setting is placed.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Regenerating the sprite at a higher resolution fixes the blur while linear filtering stays on.
statements.explanation: The cause is the sampling mode, not the source size.

questions.stem: A pixel-art game is drawn in a 640 x 360 viewport with nearest filtering and scaled up to fill the window. Check each statement that is true about scaling.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Switching to linear filtering removes the uneven widths with no other change to the look.
statements.explanation: Linear filtering hides the unevenness by blurring everything.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A non-integer scale is harmless to pixel art as long as nearest filtering is on.
statements.explanation: Nearest filtering makes the unevenness visible.

statements.label: C
statements.text: At a non-integer scale with nearest filtering, pixels show uneven widths.
statements.explanation: Some source pixels cover more screen pixels than others.

statements.label: D
statements.text: At an integer scale each source pixel becomes a whole-number block of screen pixels.
statements.explanation: A scale of 2 makes each pixel a 2 by 2 block.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Integer scaling needs linear filtering to look right.
statements.explanation: Integer scaling pairs with nearest filtering.

questions.stem: A developer chooses among a sprite sheet, a texture atlas, a tileset and a tilemap. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A tileset is a library of reusable tiles, and a tilemap is the level grid whose cells reference them.
statements.explanation: The tileset supplies the pieces and the tilemap places them.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A sprite sheet and a tileset can both be one PNG in a grid and differ in how the engine uses the cells.
statements.explanation: Sheet cells are played as frames, and tileset cells are placed on a map.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A sprite sheet is one image holding the frames of an animation, often in equal grid cells.
statements.explanation: The engine slices a sheet into frames played in order.

statements.label: D
statements.text: An atlas packs many separate images, often of different sizes, into one texture with a record of each rectangle.
statements.explanation: An atlas is a packing of many images into one texture.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A tilemap is the image file of tile artwork, and a tileset is the painted level layout.
statements.explanation: The two terms are swapped.

questions.source: Tileset or tilemap in an instruction
questions.stem: A designer tells a coding agent "make me a cave tilemap" and wants to paint rooms with 16 x 16 tiles for floor, wall, ceiling and corners. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The reusable tile artwork is a tileset, and a tilemap is the painted grid.
statements.explanation: Tileset names the library and tilemap names the layout.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The wording could be met by one fixed picture of a finished room.
statements.explanation: A fixed picture matches the words but cannot be rearranged.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The tile size can be left out, because the engine infers it from the image.
statements.explanation: The engine is told the size of one tile to cut the image.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A precise request gives the tile size, the tile types, the edge-matching rule and the file format.
statements.explanation: Each item removes a guess.

statements.label: E
statements.text: "Cave tilemap" is a precise request because it fixes tile size and edge rules.
statements.explanation: The phrase leaves out size, types and edge rules.

questions.stem: An image generator is asked for a four-frame walk cycle in one row and returns one 800 x 200 image. The developer slices it into 4 columns and 1 row. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Equal slicing assumes the figures are spaced evenly in the image.
statements.explanation: Slicing cuts at fixed positions.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Frames of one cycle share a baseline and a scale so that they play as one motion.
statements.explanation: A shifting baseline makes the animation bob.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Equal slicing centres each figure in its cell.
statements.explanation: Unevenly spaced figures are cut apart or shifted.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Playback speed is set in the engine on the animation, not stored in the image.
statements.explanation: Frames per second is an animation setting.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A frame count of 4 shows that the figures are poses of one character.
statements.explanation: A count says how many cells, not who is drawn.

questions.stem: An interviewer asks why packing 64 separate sprite images into one atlas can make a 2D game run better. Check each statement that is true about a sound answer.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Padding between packed sprites prevents colour bleed when filtering samples near an edge.
statements.explanation: Without padding, sampling can read a neighbour sprite's pixels.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Packing sprites into an atlas changes their drawn size.
statements.explanation: An atlas changes where pixels are stored, not how large the sprite is drawn.

statements.label: C
statements.text: An atlas stores fewer pixels than the separate images it replaces.
statements.explanation: Padding and unused space can make an atlas larger.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Sprites that share one texture can be batched into fewer draw calls.
statements.explanation: No texture switch is needed between them.

statements.label: E
statements.text: An atlas reduces texture switches rather than reducing the number of pixels stored.
statements.explanation: The gain is fewer state changes.

questions.stem: A developer will repeat a 256 x 256 grass image over a large ground plane. Check each statement that is true about seamless textures.

statements.label: A
statements.text: An image that looks good as a single picture is therefore seamless.
statements.explanation: One view says nothing about how the edges meet their copies.

statements.label: B
statements.text: With repeat mode the image tiles, and with clamp mode the edge pixels stretch.
statements.explanation: Repeat and clamp are the two wrap behaviours.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Placing copies side by side tests whether a texture is seamless.
statements.explanation: A seam is the join between copies.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A seamless (tileable) texture has opposite edges that match, so copies show no visible join.
statements.explanation: Seamlessness is a property of the image's edge content.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A seamless texture shows no visible repetition over a large area.
statements.explanation: Distinctive features recurring at a regular spacing still form a pattern.

questions.stem: A pixel-art game restricts its art to a 16-colour palette, and a script counts the distinct colours in a generated enemy sprite. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A script can count distinct colours and test each against the palette.
statements.explanation: The test is exact and can be automated.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Anti-aliased edges add in-between colours that are not in the palette.
statements.explanation: Blended edge pixels are extra colours.

statements.label: C
statements.text: An image generator guarantees it will respect a request for these 16 colours.
statements.explanation: Generators approximate such constraints, so the result is checked.

statements.label: D
statements.text: An indexed-colour image stores a palette plus an index per pixel, so editing palette entries recolours the sprite.
statements.explanation: The index data stays the same when palette entries change.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A palette is a fixed set of colours the art draws from, and sharing one helps assets look consistent.
statements.explanation: A shared palette gives visual consistency.

questions.stem: In Godot, an imported PNG has import settings stored in a small file beside it. A developer asks an agent to "make the sprite crisp". Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Mipmaps are pre-shrunk copies of a texture used when it is drawn smaller.
statements.explanation: They help with minified drawing.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The settings file records the import choices for that image and belongs in version control with the asset.
statements.explanation: A clone without it falls back to default import settings.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Lossless compression is the recommended mode for pixel art, because VRAM compression shows artifacts in 2D.
statements.explanation: Compression artifacts are visible on small 2D images.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Mipmaps sharpen a sprite that is drawn at its native size.
statements.explanation: Mipmaps add memory and do not sharpen.

statements.label: E
statements.text: "Make the sprite crisp" names the import settings to change.
statements.explanation: The phrase names a result, so the agent may change the wrong setting.

questions.stem: A sound effect is stored as uncompressed PCM audio with a sample rate, a bit depth and a number of channels. Check each statement that is true about these terms.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Sample rate is the number of samples taken per second.
statements.explanation: Sample rate is how finely time is sampled.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The highest frequency a sample rate can represent is half of it, which is the Nyquist limit.
statements.explanation: A signal above half the rate cannot be represented correctly.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Raising the sample rate makes the sound louder.
statements.explanation: Sample rate does not set loudness.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Stereo has one channel and mono has two.
statements.explanation: Stereo has two channels and mono has one.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Bit depth sets the number of samples taken per second.
statements.explanation: Bit depth is the precision of each sample's level; samples per second is the sample rate.

questions.stem: A model generates an 8-bar music track at a steady tempo in 4/4 time to loop behind a level. Check each statement that is true about looping.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A fade-out baked into the end of the file is harmless in a loop.
statements.explanation: The fade makes a dip and then a jump back up at the join.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A sharp jump between the last and first sample can be heard as a click.
statements.explanation: A discontinuity in the waveform is audible.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A track that sounds smooth played once will loop seamlessly.
statements.explanation: A single play does not test the join.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Cutting the loop at a bar line keeps the rhythm unbroken across the join.
statements.explanation: A loop that ends mid-bar shifts the beat on each repeat.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The loop point is the position where the track fades out before repeating.
statements.explanation: A loop point is where playback jumps back to, and a fade-out at that point would be audible.

questions.source: Lossless versus lossy; one-shot versus loop
questions.stem: A developer chooses file formats and playback behaviour for a coin-pickup effect and a three-minute background track. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A one-shot plays once per trigger, and a loop repeats until stopped.
statements.explanation: One-shot and loop are playback behaviours.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Lossless audio such as WAV or FLAC keeps the samples, and lossy audio such as Ogg Vorbis or MP3 discards detail permanently.
statements.explanation: Lossy encoding trades information for size.

statements.label: C
statements.text: FLAC is a lossy format because it is compressed.
statements.explanation: Compressed does not mean lossy.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Re-encoding a lossy file to another lossy format loses no further detail at the same bit rate.
statements.explanation: Each lossy generation discards more detail.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The original uncompressed audio can be rebuilt in full from a lossy file.
statements.explanation: The discarded detail is gone.

questions.stem: A game routes sound effects to a bus named SFX and music to a bus named Music, and both feed a Master bus. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A bus is a channel that audio is routed through before output, and its volume and effects apply to the sources routed to it.
statements.explanation: Buses group sources for shared control.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A bus at 0 dB is silent.
statements.explanation: Silence is a very large negative decibel value.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Clipping happens when summed sounds pass the digital maximum, which causes distortion.
statements.explanation: Simultaneous sounds add, and the sum can exceed the limit.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A change of about 6 dB roughly doubles or halves the amplitude.
statements.explanation: The decibel scale is logarithmic.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A bus at 0 dB passes the signal with no change in level.
statements.explanation: 0 dB is unity gain.

questions.stem: A coin sound is played by one audio player limited to a single simultaneous voice. Three quick pickups produce one clipped blip. A developer says "make the coin sound better". Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: With a limit of one voice, a new play request cuts off the sound still playing.
statements.explanation: Exceeding the limit drops the earlier sound.

statements.label: B
statements.text: "Make the coin sound better" names the voice limit as the problem.
statements.explanation: The phrase names no problem.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Raising polyphony cuts off overlapping copies of the sound sooner.
statements.explanation: More voices lets overlapping plays sound together instead of cutting each other off.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Making the file louder fixes the cut-off.
statements.explanation: Loudness is unrelated to cut-off.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Polyphony is the number of voices that can sound at the same time.
statements.explanation: Polyphony counts simultaneous voices.

questions.stem: A studio reviews sprites from an image generator for a pixel-art game. Check each statement that is true about pixel art.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Pixel art means an image with a retro colour scheme.
statements.explanation: The term describes how the image is built.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Pixel art is authored at low resolution on a grid, with each pixel placed deliberately.
statements.explanation: Control over each pixel defines the style.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Pixel art is shown at an integer scale with nearest filtering so each art pixel stays a crisp block.
statements.explanation: Uneven scaling or blending would destroy the pixel shapes.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A generated image can look like pixel art while lacking a true pixel grid.
statements.explanation: Blocky look does not guarantee the pixels sit on a grid.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A smoothed, JPEG-compressed picture becomes clean pixel art when shrunk with linear filtering.
statements.explanation: Shrinking blends the artifacts and does not restore a grid.

questions.stem: A developer ships a game with an AI-generated sprite and an AI-generated music track. Check each statement that is true about licensing and provenance.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Provenance is the record of an asset's origin: tool and version, prompt and settings, terms, references and edits.
statements.explanation: Provenance is the evidence trail for an asset.

statements.label: B
statements.text: An unrecorded reference image can leave its licence doubt attached to the result.
statements.explanation: A result derived from an unknown reference inherits the doubt.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A tool's terms can restrict use, for example to non-commercial work.
statements.explanation: Some services carry non-commercial terms.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A provenance record helps regenerate or replace an asset later.
statements.explanation: Recorded settings make an asset reproducible.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Writing the prompt gives the developer full copyright in the output.
statements.explanation: Ownership of output depends on the terms and the jurisdiction.

questions.stem: A developer tells an image generator and a coding agent: "Make me a cool pixel-art enemy with a walk animation, plus a jump sound and some background music that I can ship." Check each statement that is true about making this precise.

statements.label: A
statements.text: "That I can ship" is a licensing requirement that a provenance record supports.
statements.explanation: Shipping needs terms and origin to be known.

statements.label: B
statements.text: "Background music" does not say whether it loops, and "looping track cut on a bar boundary" does.
statements.explanation: Loop and one-shot are different playback behaviours.

statements.label: C
statements.text: "Pixel-art" becomes precise when the size in the viewport and the palette are stated.
statements.explanation: Size and palette remove guesses.

statements.label: D
statements.text: "Cool" tells the generator the viewpoint and the on-screen size.
statements.explanation: "Cool" names a taste, not a viewpoint or size.

statements.label: E
statements.text: "Walk animation" is imprecise, and "four-frame walk cycle as a sprite sheet in equal cells" is precise.
statements.explanation: The precise phrase fixes frame count and layout.

questions.stem: Pixel art looks crisp in an image viewer but smeared when enlarged in the running game. Check each statement that is true about causes and checks.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Changing the filter mode edits the PNG file.
statements.explanation: The filter is an engine setting, not a change to the image.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Texture filtering applies when the texture is sampled at draw time.
statements.explanation: Filtering happens when pixels are drawn.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Import settings apply when the source file is converted for the engine.
statements.explanation: Import happens before the game runs.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Checking at several window sizes tests the effect of scale.
statements.explanation: Non-integer scales show uneven pixels.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A JPEG-compressed source with blocky artifacts becomes clean pixel art once nearest filtering is chosen.
statements.explanation: Filtering cannot repair a source that is not on a pixel grid.

questions.source: Choosing sheet, atlas, tileset or tilemap
questions.stem: A game has an eight-frame walking character and a cave level built from forty reusable wall and floor pieces. Check each statement that is true about which term fits.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The cave pieces are a tileset that is painted into a tilemap.
statements.explanation: The tileset holds pieces and the tilemap places them.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The eight-frame character is described with a sprite sheet.
statements.explanation: A sheet holds animation frames.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The cells of a tileset are played in order as frames.
statements.explanation: Sheet cells play in order and tileset cells are placed individually.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The walking character is described with a tilemap.
statements.explanation: A tilemap is a level grid, not a character animation.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A texture atlas is chosen mainly to reduce texture switches and draw calls.
statements.explanation: Packing images into one texture reduces state changes.

questions.stem: A game needs a short coin sound, an ambient loop and a three-minute music piece. Check each statement that is true about formats and playback.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Long music is often a lossy file, to save space, that is streamed.
statements.explanation: Streaming plays from disk rather than loading the whole file.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A short effect is a one-shot that is triggered by an event and may overlap itself.
statements.explanation: One-shot describes playback once per trigger.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Keeping a lossless master rules out a later re-export.
statements.explanation: A lossless master is what allows a later re-export without generation loss.

statements.label: D
statements.text: An ambient loop should have a fade-out baked into its end.
statements.explanation: A fade-out would make a dip at each repeat.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Sample rate changes loudness.
statements.explanation: Sample rate sets time resolution and the highest frequency.

questions.stem: A student ships an AI-generated sprite made from a reference picture of unknown source, and a music track from a tool whose terms were not read. Check each statement that is true about provenance.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A provenance record lets a problem be traced after the fact.
statements.explanation: Recorded origin makes tracing possible.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A good log entry lists the tool and version, the prompt and settings, references with licences, the terms and the edits.
statements.explanation: The log is the evidence trail for the asset.

statements.label: C
statements.text: An unknown-source reference stops affecting the result once it is deleted from the project.
statements.explanation: The uncertainty stays with the generated asset.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Ownership of generated output follows automatically from writing the prompt.
statements.explanation: Ownership depends on terms and jurisdiction.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Some terms require attribution as a duty.
statements.explanation: Attribution is a condition of use in some licences.

questions.stem: A developer covers a large ground surface with a 256 x 256 texture. Check each statement that is true about repeating textures.

statements.label: A
