statements.explanation: A mip chain adds memory rather than saving it.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Block compression reduces video memory use.
statements.explanation: Block formats stay compressed in video memory.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Anisotropic filtering sharpens a road seen at a shallow angle.
statements.explanation: Shallow angles stretch the footprint, which anisotropic filtering handles.

questions.source: Material instance in an agent prompt
questions.stem: A game has many enemies that share one mesh and one shader. A coding agent is told: "Make a red version of the enemy material and flash the hit enemy." Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Colour variants are built as material instances that override the colour parameter of one parent material.
statements.explanation: An instance reuses the parent's shader and overrides values.

statements.label: B
statements.text: "Make a red version" is ambiguous, because the agent might edit the shared material or create a material instance.
statements.explanation: Naming the intended term (material instance versus editing the shared material) removes the ambiguity.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A per-instance parameter limits the flash to the node that was hit.
statements.explanation: A per-instance parameter is stored per object.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A flash on the hit enemy is done by editing the shared material's flash parameter.
statements.explanation: Editing the shared material changes every enemy that uses it.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Four colour variants need four shader programs.
statements.explanation: Variants differ in parameter values, so one shader program serves them.

questions.source: Tiling, UV scale and atlas terms in a prompt
questions.stem: A level has a large concrete floor and many small props, each with its own small texture. A developer tells a coding agent: "make the floor texture bigger and put the prop textures together." Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: "Put the prop textures together" is a texture atlas, with UVs remapped to each cell.
statements.explanation: An atlas packs several textures into one, and each prop gets new UVs.

statements.label: B
statements.text: "Bigger" is ambiguous, because it could mean a different UV scale, a higher resolution or a different texel density.
statements.explanation: Tiling scale, resolution and density are different things that "bigger" mixes up.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Texel density is the pixel size of the image file.
statements.explanation: Texel density is texels per unit of surface.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A seamless texture is one with high resolution.
statements.explanation: Seamless means the edges match so tiling shows no joins.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Bleeding across atlas cells comes from filtering at cell borders.
statements.explanation: Filtering reads texels across a border, so padding is needed.

questions.stem: A developer reports: "The metal shield is pure black, the crevice ambient occlusion has no effect, and the glowing crystal does not light the cave wall. The textures must be broken." The scene has one directional light, no environment lighting and zero ambient light. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: An emissive crystal does not light the wall without a light or global illumination.
statements.explanation: Emission affects the surface itself, not its neighbours, unless the renderer treats it as a light.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Emission lights nearby walls by default.
statements.explanation: Lighting neighbours needs a light or global illumination.

statements.label: C
statements.text: An AO texture that modulates ambient light has no visible effect when ambient light is zero.
statements.explanation: Occlusion scales ambient light, and zero ambient leaves nothing to scale.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A metal with nothing to reflect looks black, which is a lighting problem and not a texture problem.
statements.explanation: A metal has no diffuse colour and shows only reflections, so it needs a reflection source.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Regenerating the textures is the right fix for the three symptoms.
statements.explanation: The causes are in the lighting setup, so new textures would not help.

questions.source: Compile error versus visual bug; claim versus evidence
questions.stem: A coding agent reports: "Done. The shader compiles with no errors and the existing automated tests pass." Check each statement that is true about the terms.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The agent's reply is a claim, and the compile log is evidence of valid syntax rather than of correct output.
statements.explanation: A claim is a statement, and evidence is something observed that supports it.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Existing tests that pass before and after a change show that nothing is drawn differently.
statements.explanation: Tests cover only what they check, and drawing may be outside them.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A clean compile shows that the output matches the intended look.
statements.explanation: A compiler checks syntax and types, not the design.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A shader that multiplies a colour by the wrong factor still compiles.
statements.explanation: A wrong formula is valid code, so it compiles.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A compile error means the source was rejected, while a visual bug means it built and ran but drew a wrong result.
statements.explanation: Compile errors and visual bugs are different failure types caught at different stages.

questions.stem: A continuous-integration machine has no graphics card. It runs the engine in headless mode with a dummy display driver, or alternatively with a software renderer that draws on the CPU. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A headless run with no errors shows that the shader's output colours are correct.
statements.explanation: Headless mode draws no pixels, so colours are never produced.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A frame time on the software renderer predicts the frame time on players' graphics cards.
statements.explanation: A CPU rasteriser has a different cost profile than a GPU.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A headless run can check game logic that feeds a shader, such as the value a script writes to a shader parameter.
statements.explanation: Logic runs without a display, so parameters can be inspected.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A software renderer produces an image, which can be used to check colours.
statements.explanation: A software renderer does rasterise to an image.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A software renderer's image can differ from a real GPU's in precision or filtering.
statements.explanation: Precision and filtering are implementation details that vary between renderers.

questions.stem: A team verifies a shader change with a golden-image test: a fixed scene is rendered, captured and compared with an approved reference image, using a per-channel tolerance and a limit on the fraction of different pixels. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A reference image captured from a buggy build and approved without anyone looking still lets the test report the bug.
statements.explanation: The test only reports differences from the reference, so an approved bug is baked in.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A wrong-coloured region that is small enough to stay under the allowed fraction of different pixels passes the test.
statements.explanation: The pixel-fraction threshold lets small defects pass.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A pass on a scene that does not draw the changed part shows that the change is correct.
statements.explanation: A scene that never exercises the change says nothing about it.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A golden image is an approved capture that later captures are compared against.
statements.explanation: Golden image and reference image are the same idea.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A per-channel tolerance prevents tiny rounding differences from failing the test, and also hides very small real colour shifts.
statements.explanation: Tolerance trades sensitivity for stability.

questions.source: Evidence versus a claim of success
questions.stem: An agent rewrote a shader that tints a sprite when the character is damaged and says: "Verified, it works." The developer wants evidence rather than a claim. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Rendering a fixed test scene at tint amounts 0, 0.5 and 1 and comparing pixel values with the specification's predictions is evidence.
statements.explanation: A controlled input with measured output compared with a specification is an observation.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Asking the agent to restate how sure it is gives more evidence.
statements.explanation: Restating confidence repeats the claim.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A comment in the shader saying it was verified is evidence.
statements.explanation: A comment is another claim.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A compile log is evidence of valid syntax, not of correct output.
statements.explanation: Compiling shows the source parses, nothing more.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Asking which statements were observed in a run and which were inferred from reading the code separates evidence from claim.
statements.explanation: Observed and inferred are different kinds of support.

questions.stem: Shader code works with positions in several coordinate spaces. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: View space (also called camera or eye space) measures positions relative to the camera.
statements.explanation: In view space the camera is the origin.

statements.label: B
statements.text: After the camera is moved without rotation, a point's view-space position still differs from its world-space position.
statements.explanation: Moving the camera shifts every view-space position.

statements.label: C
statements.text: World space is relative to the camera.
statements.explanation: World space is the frame shared by the scene; view space is relative to the camera.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Screen space is the same as texture coordinates (UV), so a screen position can be read as a UV.
statements.explanation: Screen space is a position on the display, while UV is a position on the mesh's surface image.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Local space (also called object or model space) measures positions from the object's own origin and axes.
statements.explanation: A vertex keeps its local position when the object moves or rotates.

questions.stem: A coding agent writes a fragment shader for a flood line: surfaces below world height 0.5 are drawn darker. The agent takes height from the vertex position as the mesh stores it and compares it with 0.5, with no transformation. A crate stands at world height 10. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The shader compares a local-space height with a world-space level, which mixes two coordinate spaces.
statements.explanation: Stored vertex positions are in local space, and the flood line is a world quantity.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Moving the one crate to world height 0 makes the effect correct for the props across the level.
statements.explanation: One crate at one spot does not fix the mixing of spaces.

statements.label: C
statements.text: View space gives a fixed flood line because it does not depend on the camera.
statements.explanation: View space moves with the camera, so the line would move too.

statements.label: D
statements.text: If the crate is turned upside down, the dark band ends up at its top in the world, because local heights turn with the object.
statements.explanation: Local coordinates are attached to the object and rotate with it.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The fix is to transform the position by the model matrix into world space before the comparison.
statements.explanation: The model matrix takes a local position to world space.

questions.stem: A surface has a tangent t and a normal n that are perpendicular. The object is then scaled non-uniformly, for example four times taller only. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Normalizing a normal after the model matrix repairs its direction under non-uniform scale.
statements.explanation: Normalizing fixes length, not direction.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The model matrix gives correct normals under a non-uniform scale, so the inverse transpose can be skipped.
statements.explanation: The model matrix only works for normals when the scale is uniform.

statements.label: C
statements.text: For a rotation or a uniform scale, applying the model matrix and then normalizing gives a normal with the right direction.
statements.explanation: Rotation and uniform scale preserve angles, so only length changes.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Carrying the normal through the inverse transpose of the model matrix keeps it perpendicular to the surface.
statements.explanation: The inverse transpose (the normal matrix) is the transform that preserves perpendicularity.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Carrying the normal through the model matrix can leave it not perpendicular to the transformed tangent.
statements.explanation: Non-uniform scale distorts directions of normals differently than surface directions.

questions.stem: Shading languages offer full precision (32-bit float) and half precision (16-bit float). Half-precision values are spaced coarser as the magnitude grows. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Half precision is fine for world positions in the thousands of units, because its range is large.
statements.explanation: Range is not the issue; spacing between values at that size is coarse.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A half-precision variable can hold the value 3001 exactly.
statements.explanation: Above 2048 the spacing is larger than 1, so 3001 is not representable.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Half precision loses fine detail on large values, because the gap between neighbouring representable values grows with magnitude.
statements.explanation: Floating-point spacing scales with magnitude.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Half precision is a routine speed-up that needs no comparison of the picture afterwards.
statements.explanation: Reduced precision changes results, so the output is compared with full precision.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Half precision is usually adequate for colours between 0 and 1.
statements.explanation: Small differences in colour are not visible.

questions.stem: A scrolling-water effect looks smooth on a desktop. On a mid-range phone, after the game runs a while, the texture moves in visible jumps. The shader keeps the texture offset (elapsed time times a speed) in a half-precision variable. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Computing the offset in full precision, or keeping the fractional part alone before storing it in half precision, is a sound fix.
statements.explanation: A smaller or more precise value avoids coarse steps.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Raising the frame rate removes the jumps.
statements.explanation: The cause is value spacing, not frame rate.

statements.label: C
statements.text: As the offset grows, half precision can represent just coarse steps, so the motion advances in jumps.
statements.explanation: Large values have wide spacing in half precision.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Many desktop GPUs run a half-precision request at full precision, which can hide the problem.
statements.explanation: Platform differences in precision can hide a bug on one device.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The smooth desktop result shows the shader is correct.
statements.explanation: The same source can behave differently depending on the hardware's precision.

questions.stem: A GPU runs fragment shaders for neighbouring pixels together in lockstep groups (called warps, wavefronts or SIMD groups). A shader has an `if` whose two sides are each expensive. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A condition from a per-pixel value such as noise costs the same as a condition from a uniform.
statements.explanation: Per-pixel conditions can diverge, uniform ones do not.

statements.label: B
statements.text: When the condition differs between pixels of a group, the `if` saves time because each pixel runs just its own side.
statements.explanation: With divergence the group pays for both sides.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A condition from a uniform is constant across the draw, so pixels in a group agree.
statements.explanation: A uniform has one value for the whole draw.

statements.label: D
statements.text: When the group agrees on the condition, it can run just the side taken.
statements.explanation: Uniform agreement lets the hardware skip the other side.

statements.label: E
statements.text: When pixels of a group disagree, the hardware runs both sides with the non-participating pixels switched off, which is called divergence.
statements.explanation: Divergence is the term for lockstep pixels disagreeing about a branch.

questions.stem: A shader declares a uniform `flash_amount` with a default of 0.0. A script sets it to 1.0 on one enemy when that enemy is hit. In play, all enemies, which share a single material, flash at once. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A uniform is a value that varies per pixel within a draw.
statements.explanation: A uniform is constant across a draw call; a varying differs per pixel.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The declared default is the value each object has until something overrides it.
statements.explanation: The default is the starting value.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A material is a shared asset, so objects referencing it see a change to its parameter.
statements.explanation: Shared resources propagate changes to every reference.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A per-instance parameter (Godot instance uniforms, Unity material property blocks) limits the flash to the enemy hit.
statements.explanation: Per-instance parameters are stored per object.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The problem is a shader compile error that was reported when the shader loaded.
statements.explanation: The shader compiled fine; the cause is sharing.

questions.stem: A damage flash fades over 33 frames, counted by adding 1 to an integer once per rendered frame. The design says the fade lasts 0.55 seconds. The developer checked it only at 60 frames per second. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A frame counter and game time agree at the frame rate the count was calibrated for.
statements.explanation: At 60 frames per second, 33 frames is 0.55 seconds.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Passing at 60 frames per second shows the fade is independent of frame rate.
statements.explanation: One setting does not show independence.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Driving the fade from elapsed game time, the sum of each frame's delta time, makes its length independent of frame rate.
statements.explanation: Game time uses delta time, which tracks real elapsed time.

statements.label: D
statements.text: At a higher frame rate, a fade counted in frames lasts longer.
statements.explanation: More frames per second finish the count sooner.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A fade counted in rendered frames lasts longer when the frame rate drops.
statements.explanation: Fewer frames per second means each frame takes longer.

questions.stem: An agent writes a new automated check for a shader and runs it on the changed code. It passes and the agent says the change is verified. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A check becomes evidence once it fails on a known-bad version and passes on a known-good one.
statements.explanation: Testing the test shows it can tell good from bad.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A check that fails on a known-good version is a false alarm, and the check needs fixing.
statements.explanation: A failure on good code is a false positive and points to the check.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A check that passes on both the known-bad and known-good versions supports the change under review.
statements.explanation: A check that cannot tell them apart carries no information (a false negative).

statements.label: D
statements.text: Running the same check again on the same changed code adds confidence that the check detects the bug.
statements.explanation: Repeating gives the same result and does not test the check.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A check written by the same agent as the change confirms the change independently of the agent's assumptions.
statements.explanation: Shared assumptions can produce a check that repeats the same mistake.

questions.stem: A shader moves a colour from a base colour toward a flash colour by an amount between 0 and 1, with output = base + (flash − base) × amount. The agent's shader has a mistake in the formula, yet the agent's test passes. A test oracle is what a test compares a result against. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: An oracle written from the specification stays valid when the shader is rewritten.
statements.explanation: A specification does not depend on the implementation.

statements.label: B
statements.text: An oracle written from the specification would have caught the mistake.
statements.explanation: An oracle independent of the code can disagree with it.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The formula is a linear interpolation, called mix in the Godot shading language and lerp in Unity's shader language.
statements.explanation: Mix and lerp are the shader-language names for linear interpolation.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A CPU calculation of the specification replaces looking at what the GPU drew.
statements.explanation: The CPU result is a prediction; the drawn image still needs checking.

statements.label: E
statements.text: An oracle copied from the code under test is preferable, because it follows changes to the code.
statements.explanation: A copied formula repeats the mistake, so the test is circular.

questions.stem: A game renders at 1920 by 1080. After the scene is drawn, three full-screen translucent layers are drawn on top: fog, a damage vignette and a colour grade. Each layer runs a fragment shader per pixel it covers. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Doubling the resolution in each dimension doubles the fragment shader invocations.
statements.explanation: Doubling both dimensions multiplies pixels by four.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A layer's cost depends mainly on its triangle count.
statements.explanation: Cost follows how many pixels are shaded, not triangles.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Three full-screen layers run the fragment shader about three times per pixel, which is overdraw.
statements.explanation: Overdraw means shading the same pixel more than once.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A value that varies linearly across a surface is cheaper computed per vertex and interpolated when fragments outnumber vertices.
statements.explanation: Fewer vertex invocations do the same job when interpolation is exact.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Combining the three effects into one full-screen pass shades each pixel once.
statements.explanation: One pass merges the work, though each shader does more.

questions.source: Controlled inputs for common shader mistakes
questions.stem: A developer prepares controlled inputs, test values chosen so correct and wrong outputs are far apart. Two suspected mistakes are alpha applied twice and a flipped vertical texture coordinate. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A test texture that is red on top and blue on the bottom exposes a vertical flip.
statements.explanation: Different top and bottom make a swap visible.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A texture that is symmetric top to bottom is as good as an asymmetric one for exposing a flip.
statements.explanation: A symmetric texture looks the same when flipped.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A vertical flip swaps left and right as well as top and bottom.
statements.explanation: A vertical flip swaps top and bottom only; a 180 degree rotation swaps both.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A fully opaque test pixel is the best input for exposing alpha applied twice.
statements.explanation: At alpha 1.0 doubling alpha changes nothing, so the bug stays hidden.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A shader that multiplies colour by alpha and is drawn with ordinary alpha blending applies alpha twice.
statements.explanation: Premultiplying and then blending applies the factor two times.

questions.source: A precise specification for an agent
questions.stem: A developer gives a coding agent a specification for a character's hit flash that can be checked on a device with any frame rate. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Stating that at amount 0 the output equals the incoming colour and at 1 equals the flash colour defines the end points of a linear mix.
statements.explanation: End points plus linear mix fully pin down the rule.

statements.label: B
statements.text: "A strong red" is vague, and a precise spec names the flash colour as exact RGB values.
statements.explanation: Exact values can be compared with measured pixels.

statements.label: C
statements.text: "Returns to normal" is a precise end condition that a test can check.
statements.explanation: "Normal" is not a measurable value; the end value should be stated.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Giving the fade length as a count of rendered frames fixes its length in real time.
statements.explanation: A frame count changes length when the frame rate changes.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Giving the fade length in seconds of game time keeps its length the same at different frame rates.
statements.explanation: Game time follows delta time, so it does not depend on frames.

questions.stem: A reviewer asks for evidence about a shader change and lists kinds of checks. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A headless run is the strongest evidence of how the shader looks.
statements.explanation: A headless run draws nothing.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A golden-image comparison detects colour changes but does not judge whether the reference was right.
statements.explanation: A golden image only compares with an approved reference.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A run on the target phone is evidence about that phone's precision and driver behaviour.
statements.explanation: Hardware-specific behaviour needs the actual hardware.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Passing existing tests shows the shader draws correctly.
statements.explanation: Existing tests may not exercise the shader.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A compile check is the weakest evidence, showing valid syntax and types.
statements.explanation: A compile check says nothing about the output.

questions.stem: A developer tells a coding agent: "Add a damage flash to the player and make sure it works." Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: "A bit red" is acceptable as the flash colour.
statements.explanation: A vague colour cannot be checked against pixels.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Saying "alpha unchanged" states what the output's transparency does.
statements.explanation: It states one part of the output rule.

statements.label: C
statements.text: "Make sure it works" gives no pass criterion that a test can check.
statements.explanation: A pass criterion needs measurable values.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A precise rewrite names a uniform with a stated range, such as 0 to 1.
statements.explanation: A named uniform with a range is a testable input.

statements.label: E
statements.text: "Flash" is precise, because it names the effect.
statements.explanation: Flash leaves colour, timing and blend rule open.

questions.stem: An agent adds a test for a fade effect by recomputing the expected value with the formula copied from the shader. The test passes on a change containing a real bug. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Varying inputs such as frame rate and amount exposes hidden dependences.
statements.explanation: Several settings test more of the behaviour.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A copied formula gives an independent oracle.
statements.explanation: A copied formula repeats the shader's mistake.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A check at a single frame rate can mislead, because behaviour may depend on frame rate.
statements.explanation: One setting can hide a frame-dependent bug.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A test oracle is what a test compares a result against.
statements.explanation: The oracle is the source of the expected value.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A check that passes on a known-bad version shows the check is trustworthy.
statements.explanation: Passing on bad code means the check cannot tell good from bad.

questions.source: Four spaces and mixing them up
questions.stem: A tester finds a bug caused by mixing two coordinate spaces in a shader. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Local space is relative to the object's origin.
statements.explanation: Local space belongs to the object.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Screen space uses the mesh's own origin.
statements.explanation: Screen space is a position on the display, usually in pixels.

statements.label: C
statements.text: World space is shared by the scene.
statements.explanation: All objects in the scene share world space.

statements.label: D
statements.text: View space has its origin at the world origin.
statements.explanation: View space has the camera at the origin.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A symptom of mixing spaces often changes when the object or camera moves.
statements.explanation: The mixed quantity depends on a transform that changes with movement.

questions.source: Precision, branching and fragment cost on mobile
questions.stem: A shader looks right and runs smoothly on a desktop, but on a mid-range phone it shows stepping and the frame rate drops. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Desktop frame time predicts phone frame time because the shader code is the same.
statements.explanation: Hardware differs in speed and precision.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Half precision on the phone can cause stepping with large values such as time.
statements.explanation: Reduced precision coarsens large values.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Stepping on the phone is a compile error.
statements.explanation: A compile error would stop the shader from loading.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Full-screen translucent layers multiply fragment invocations and can hurt the phone's fill rate.
statements.explanation: More overdraw means more pixel work.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A divergent branch can make the phone pay for both sides.
statements.explanation: Divergence runs both sides in a lockstep group.

questions.stem: A team designs a golden-image test process for a library of shaders. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Per-platform references or tolerances handle platform differences.
statements.explanation: Each platform gets its own reference or tolerance.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A fixed scene has a fixed camera, resolution, inputs and pinned clock with no randomness.
statements.explanation: Determinism makes any difference come from the shader.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A pass shows the shader is correct on hardware that was not tested.
statements.explanation: A pass says nothing about untested hardware.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A pass shows the render matches the approved reference, not that the reference is right.
statements.explanation: A golden image compares, and a person approves the reference.

statements.label: E
statements.text: One reference image from a desktop GPU is adequate for phone GPUs.
statements.explanation: Different hardware gives slightly different images.

questions.stem: A technical artist describes a campfire to a coding agent and has to pick the exact particle-effect noun for each part. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: An emitter is the source that creates particles, either steadily at a rate or in bursts.
statements.explanation: The emitter is where particles are born, and its rate or burst settings say when.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A particle is one small element that the system creates, updates and removes over time, with its own age, position and velocity.
statements.explanation: A particle is a lightweight record with a life cycle: it is born, updated each step and removed.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A particle system is the whole effect (spawning, simulation and drawing), and one system can combine several emitters.
statements.explanation: The system covers emission, simulation and drawing, and a larger effect can use more than one emitter.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A particle is a separate game object with its own script, which is why it is called a particle.
statements.explanation: Particles are data processed in bulk by the system, not individual objects with scripts.

statements.label: E
statements.text: An emitter is the name for the whole finished effect, including its drawing settings and each particle it has made.
statements.explanation: The whole effect is the particle system; the emitter is only the part that creates particles.

questions.source: Emission shape, initial velocity and spread
questions.stem: A developer separates two settings that both control where particles come from and how they move. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Emission shape (point, sphere, box or cone) sets the region where particles are born.
statements.explanation: The emission shape decides placement of births.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A larger spread makes each particle leave the emitter faster.
statements.explanation: Speed comes from the initial velocity, not from the spread.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Emission shape and initial velocity are separate settings.
statements.explanation: Placement of births and motion after birth are independent controls.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Initial velocity sets the starting speed and direction of a particle after it is born.
statements.explanation: Initial velocity is the speed and direction a particle has at birth.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Spread is the exact word for the launch speed of a particle.
statements.explanation: Spread is the range of launch directions; launch speed comes from the initial velocity.

questions.source: Emission rate, burst, one-shot and looping
questions.stem: A coding agent is asked for the right emission term for each behaviour. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Emission rate is the number of particles born per unit time, such as 40 per second.
statements.explanation: Rate is a count per unit time, so it spreads births over time.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A looping system plays one cycle and then stops until it is triggered again.
statements.explanation: A looping system starts its cycle again when it ends.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A burst is a stated count of particles born at one instant.
statements.explanation: A burst delivers its whole count at one moment.

statements.label: D
statements.text: One-shot (non-looping) means the system keeps cycling until it is stopped.
statements.explanation: One-shot controls how many cycles play; it plays one and stops.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A burst puts its particles at one instant, unlike a high continuous rate.
statements.explanation: A high rate spreads births over time, whereas a burst delivers them at one moment.

questions.source: Rate, lifetime and live particle count
questions.stem: A smoke emitter runs continuously. Check each statement that is true about the terms that fix how many particles are alive.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The steady-state live count is roughly emission rate times lifetime.
statements.explanation: Births per second times seconds of life gives the number alive once the effect has settled.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Doubling the emission rate at the same lifetime leaves the live count unchanged.
statements.explanation: Live count scales with the rate, so doubling the rate doubles the count.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Lifetime is the time a particle stays alive after it is born, before the system removes it.
statements.explanation: Lifetime is the length of a particle's life in seconds.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Doubling the lifetime at the same rate leaves the live count unchanged.
statements.explanation: A longer life means particles pile up for longer before removal, so the count grows.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Lifetime is the number of particles the emitter makes per second.
statements.explanation: That describes emission rate, not lifetime.

questions.stem: A newly started smoke effect looks thin for its first seconds. Check each statement that is true about the term for fixing this.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Burst mode is a separate emission setting from prewarm.
statements.explanation: Prewarm changes the starting state; burst mode changes how particles are emitted.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Prewarm lets the effect start with its steady-state population instead of ramping up from nothing.
statements.explanation: Skipping the ramp-up is the whole purpose.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Prewarm raises the emission rate for the whole run of the effect.
statements.explanation: Prewarm changes the starting state, not the rate.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Prewarm simulates the system for some time before the first visible frame.
statements.explanation: Prewarm runs the simulation ahead of the first drawn frame.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Prewarm needs to cover less than one particle lifetime to reach a full population.
statements.explanation: Particles reach full population only after one lifetime has passed, so the prewarm has to be at least that long.

questions.stem: A developer sends two prompts for a 2D grenade explosion. Prompt 1: "add an explosion effect". Prompt 2: "add a one-shot burst of 40 particles at the grenade's position, lifetime 0.6 seconds, initial speed 150 to 300 pixels per second in all directions, no gravity, scale curve to zero and alpha ramp to transparent over life". Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: "One-shot burst of 40" leaves the number of particles for the agent to guess.
statements.explanation: One-shot sets the cycle count and burst with a number fixes the particles born at one instant.

statements.label: B
statements.text: "Explosion" in Prompt 1 names no count, lifetime, speed, direction or loop behaviour, so the agent has to guess them.
statements.explanation: A scene word like explosion fixes none of the properties that define the effect.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Prompt 1 leaves the agent free to build a looping emitter that keeps spraying after the grenade has gone off.
statements.explanation: Without one-shot, looping versus playing once is the agent's choice.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Adding "and make it look cool" to Prompt 2 adds a constraint the agent can measure.
statements.explanation: An adjective that cannot be measured adds no constraint and no check.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Prompt 1 is precise because explosion is a standard term with one settled meaning across engines.
statements.explanation: Explosion is a description of a look, not a defined particle setting.

questions.stem: Particles launched in a 2D game are described with physics terms. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Initial velocity is the velocity a particle has at birth.
statements.explanation: Initial velocity is the starting speed and direction.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A particle launched with zero initial velocity stays still while gravity acts on it.
statements.explanation: Velocity grows by the acceleration each second, so it leaves zero and the particle moves.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Gravity is a constant velocity that is added once at birth.
statements.explanation: A velocity added once would be an initial velocity, not gravity.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Gravity on a particle is a constant acceleration, so it keeps changing the particle's velocity.
statements.explanation: Acceleration is a rate of change of velocity, applied continuously.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Acceleration is another word for the speed of a particle.
statements.explanation: Speed is how fast; acceleration is how quickly the velocity changes.

questions.source: Scale curve, colour ramp and normalised age
questions.stem: A particle has a lifetime of 0.6 seconds, a scale curve falling from 1 to 0 and a colour ramp fading alpha from 1 to 0. Check each statement that is true about over-lifetime terms.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A colour ramp sets the colour at birth, and fading needs a script that updates the colour as the particle ages.
statements.explanation: A colour ramp is sampled across the whole life, which is how fades are made without code.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A curve or ramp over lifetime is read by normalised age, which is age divided by lifetime and runs from 0 to 1.
statements.explanation: Normalised age is the fraction of life used so far.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Because curves use normalised age, the same curve works for particles with different lifetimes.
statements.explanation: Reading by fraction of life stretches one curve over any lifetime.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A scale curve changes the colour of a particle over its life.
statements.explanation: A scale curve changes size; a colour ramp changes colour.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A curve read by normalised age ends at the particle's death for lifetimes of 0.6 s and 1.2 s alike.
statements.explanation: Reading by fraction of life puts the end of the curve at death for any lifetime.

questions.stem: Engines let a particle system simulate on the CPU or on the GPU. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: GPU particles lose textures and blend modes, because those belong to the CPU side.
statements.explanation: Textures and blending belong to drawing, which both kinds share.

statements.label: B
statements.text: CPU simulation cost stays flat as the particle count rises.
statements.explanation: CPU simulation is per-particle work, so more particles take more CPU time.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Both CPU particles and GPU particles are drawn by the GPU.
statements.explanation: Both kinds are drawn by the GPU; the setting is about where the simulation runs.

statements.label: D
statements.text: GPU particles update their state in shaders on the graphics card.
statements.explanation: GPU simulation is a data-parallel update on the graphics card.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The setting decides where the per-particle update (the simulation) runs.
statements.explanation: Simulation means the update, and it runs in one place or the other.

questions.stem: A game needs ambient snowfall with 20,000 flakes and, separately, 80 sparks that each damage an enemy on touch. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: GPU particles keep their particle data on the CPU, so scripts read each flake cheaply.
statements.explanation: GPU particle data stays on the graphics card, so scripts cannot cheaply read it.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A cosmetic effect is one whose particles feed back into gameplay logic.
statements.explanation: A cosmetic effect only changes the look; gameplay-affecting particles are the opposite.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Snowfall is a cosmetic effect with a large count, which suits GPU particles.
statements.explanation: Large cosmetic effects are what GPU simulation is built for.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A CPU particle system runs on a wider range of devices because it does not need good GPU compute.
statements.explanation: Older hardware can lack GPU compute, so CPU particles are the safe fallback.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Sparks that apply a gameplay rule need their state read by a script, which is easier with CPU particles or with separate gameplay objects.
statements.explanation: Gameplay logic runs in scripts, which need particle state on the CPU side.

questions.stem: A spaceship flies across the screen. Its exhaust should trail behind it, and its shield shimmer should stay around it. Check each statement that is true about the coordinate-space term for each.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The shield shimmer needs world coordinates so that its particles stay around the ship.
statements.explanation: A shimmer around a ship needs local coordinates, so particles move with it.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The exhaust needs local coordinates so that its particles follow the ship.
statements.explanation: Local space would carry the exhaust along with the ship, so no trail would form.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Local coordinates keep particle positions relative to the emitter, so the particles travel with it.
statements.explanation: Local-space positions are stored relative to the emitter's transform.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The local or world setting changes the result for an emitter that stays still.
statements.explanation: With a stationary emitter both settings give the same positions.

statements.label: E
statements.text: World coordinates leave a particle where it was born while the emitter moves, which forms a trail.
statements.explanation: A world-space particle is no longer tied to the emitter after birth.

questions.stem: Particles are combined with the background by a blend mode. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Additive blending suits fire, sparks and glows.
statements.explanation: Emissive effects accumulate light where they overlap, which suits additive blending.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Additive blending suits dark smoke, because a dark colour darkens the background when it is added.
statements.explanation: Adding a dark colour adds close to nothing, so additive smoke would be nearly invisible.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Additive blending adds the particle's light to the background, so overlap brightens toward white.
statements.explanation: Adding colours can only brighten, and results clamp at white.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Alpha blending mixes the particle colour with the background in proportion to alpha, so drawing order matters.
statements.explanation: Alpha blending is particle times alpha plus background times one minus alpha, which depends on order.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Two additive particles give the same result in either drawing order.
statements.explanation: Addition does not depend on order.

questions.stem: A 3D game draws each smoke particle as a flat textured quad. Check each statement that is true about billboarding.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A billboarded particle can still spin about the view direction, which is how rotation over lifetime works for flat particles.
statements.explanation: Spinning about the view direction leaves the quad facing the camera.

statements.label: B
statements.text: In a 2D game with a flat orthographic camera, billboarding has to be switched on to face the quads to the screen.
statements.explanation: Quads already face the screen with a flat orthographic camera.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Without billboarding, a flat quad seen edge-on shrinks to a thin line.
statements.explanation: A flat quad has no thickness, so from the side it has almost no area.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A billboard is a quad turned each frame to face the camera.
statements.explanation: Turning toward the camera each frame is what billboarding means.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A particle drawn as a mesh keeps its 3D shape instead of being a billboard.
statements.explanation: A mesh particle keeps its 3D shape and orientation; it is the alternative to a billboard.

questions.stem: A smoke effect uses many large transparent quads. Check each statement that is true about the cost terms.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Transparent corners of a quad are still shaded, so they add fragment cost.
statements.explanation: Transparent pixels are still shaded and blended.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Overdraw is the same screen pixel being shaded more than once by overlapping surfaces.
statements.explanation: Overdraw describes layers of overlapping surfaces on one pixel.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Fill rate is how many pixels the GPU can shade and write per second, and overdraw uses it up.
statements.explanation: Fill rate is the throughput limit, and many layers per pixel consume it.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A fragment is one pixel-sized unit of work for the fragment shader.
statements.explanation: Each covered pixel of a quad runs the fragment shader once.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Doubling the width and height of each quad doubles its fragment count.
statements.explanation: Area scales with the square of the side, so the count quadruples.

questions.source: Transparency, depth test and live count
questions.stem: A developer asks why many large transparent particles cost more than opaque ones. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Halving the lifetime at the same emission rate doubles the number of live particles.
statements.explanation: Live count equals rate times lifetime, so halving the lifetime halves the count.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The depth test can reject a hidden opaque fragment when something nearer is already drawn.
statements.explanation: Early rejection by depth skips opaque work that would be hidden.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Lowering alpha everywhere reduces the number of fragments shaded.
statements.explanation: Alpha changes the result colour, not the fragment count.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Overdraw is a cheap cost on mobile GPUs.
statements.explanation: Fill rate is a main constraint on mobile, and overdraw spends it.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Stacked transparent particles are skipped by early rejection, like hidden opaque ones.
statements.explanation: Blended layers are not skipped, because each contributes to the final colour.

questions.stem: A burst effect gives each particle a random speed and direction. Check each statement that is true about random seeds.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A fixed seed makes the effect look different each time it plays.
statements.explanation: The same seed gives the same sequence, so each play looks the same.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A fixed seed makes a burst identical at 30 and at 144 frames per second, because time does not matter.
statements.explanation: Positions also depend on the time step, so frame rates can still differ.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Tests fix the seed so a burst can repeat and a failure can be reproduced.
statements.explanation: Repeatability is the point of seeding in a test.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The same seed with a different draw order gives the same number for each particle.
statements.explanation: A different order of draws changes which number each particle gets, even with the same seed.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A random seed is the starting value of a pseudo-random generator.
statements.explanation: The seed initialises the generator's sequence.

questions.stem: A developer needs a campfire in 3D and writes a prompt: "a looping emitter, 80 particles per second, lifetime 0.8 seconds, world-space coordinates, additive blending, billboarded quads, initial upward velocity, colour ramp from yellow to transparent red, scale shrinking to zero over life". Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: "Billboarded quads" tells the agent to turn each particle toward the camera.
statements.explanation: Billboarding keeps flat particles facing the camera.

statements.label: B
statements.text: "Looping" tells the agent the emitter keeps cycling until it is stopped.
statements.explanation: A looping emitter restarts its cycle again and again.

statements.label: C
statements.text: "World-space" on a carried torch lets the flames trail behind as the player moves.
statements.explanation: World-space particles are left behind when the emitter moves.

statements.label: D
statements.text: "Make the fire look good" would carry the same settings as the prompt.
statements.explanation: A look word fixes no rate, lifetime, space or blend mode.

statements.label: E
statements.text: "Additive blending" is the exact term for flames that cover and darken the background.
statements.explanation: Additive blending adds light, so it brightens; covering and darkening is alpha blending.

questions.stem: An enemy is destroyed the instant it is hit, and a one-shot burst effect is a child of the enemy in the scene hierarchy. A log line says "burst started", yet players never see it. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A child effect can be cut off the moment its parent is destroyed or hidden.
statements.explanation: Children go with their parent when it is destroyed, hidden or deactivated.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A one-shot effect plays again on the next hit without further action.
statements.explanation: A one-shot plays one cycle and stays finished until restarted or spawned again.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Spawning the effect as its own object at the enemy's position lets it outlive the enemy.
statements.explanation: A separate effect object has its own lifetime.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The log line proves the burst was drawn, because starting the effect means drawing it.
statements.explanation: A log line records that the effect started, not that it was visible.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Switching to GPU particles fixes this, because GPU particles are not tied to a parent.
statements.explanation: The cause is the parent-child relationship, not where the simulation runs.

questions.source: State versus visual intent versus cost
questions.stem: A coding agent reports "test passes: the burst is emitting" from a headless run (no window, a dummy renderer that draws nothing). Check each statement that is true about the terms.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Visual intent is what the effect should look like, and a person has to look at the screen to check it.
statements.explanation: Appearance needs a human, or a real render, to judge.

statements.label: B
statements.text: State, visual intent and cost are three names for the same check.
statements.explanation: They are separate kinds of evidence, each reached by a different test.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Emitting is engine state, a flag the engine reports, not proof of appearance.
statements.explanation: State covers what the engine reports, such as emitting, position and finished.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A headless run does not show overdraw or fill rate, since nothing is drawn.
statements.explanation: Drawing costs exist only when a real renderer runs.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A dummy renderer does no GPU work, so its timing says nothing about GPU cost.
statements.explanation: A dummy renderer does no GPU work, so its figure is a property of the instrument.

questions.stem: In Godot, a 2D death burst uses a GPU particle node with a process material (the object that holds speed, direction, spread, gravity and over-life settings). The node reports it is emitting, yet players see almost nothing. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Emitting means the particles are on screen at a visible size.
statements.explanation: Emitting is a state flag and says nothing about size.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The process material holds the motion and over-life settings for the particles.
statements.explanation: The process material is the settings object for how particles move and change.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A node with no texture draws each particle as a tiny square, which is nearly invisible.
statements.explanation: A missing texture leaves a very small default particle.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A texture is a property of the GPU particle node, not of the CPU node alone.
statements.explanation: Both node kinds take a texture as an ordinary property.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A wide spread in a 2D game keeps the motion in the visible plane.
statements.explanation: The material also serves 3D, so velocity can point along the z axis, which a 2D view cannot show.

questions.source: Rewrite of the grenade explosion prompt
questions.stem: An agent rewrites "add an explosion when the grenade hits" into a precise instruction. Check each statement that is true about which wording is exact.

statements.label: A
statements.text: "Spread" is the exact word for the range of launch directions.
statements.explanation: Spread is the width of the cone of launch directions.

statements.label: B
statements.text: "Fade out" is an exact term for a scale curve.
statements.explanation: Fading is a colour or alpha ramp; a scale curve changes size.

statements.label: C
statements.text: "One-shot burst of N particles" is exact wording for a single cycle with a stated count at one instant.
statements.explanation: One-shot gives one cycle and burst gives a count at one instant.

statements.label: D
statements.text: "Spawn at the grenade's position in world coordinates, as its own object" keeps the effect visible after the grenade is hidden.
statements.explanation: World coordinates and a separate object keep the effect independent of the grenade.

statements.label: E
statements.text: "Loop a continuous emission" is the exact wording for a single explosion.
statements.explanation: Looping with a rate keeps spraying; an explosion is a burst.

questions.stem: A smoke effect has a limit on live particles. A burst of 100 particles fires every 0.5 seconds, each living 1.2 seconds. Check each statement that is true about the terms.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A limit on live particles is checked against the average, not the peak.
statements.explanation: A hard cap applies to the peak, because that is when it is exceeded.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The peak live count is the highest number of particles alive at one instant.
statements.explanation: Peak means the maximum over time.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The average live count is emission rate times lifetime, so bursts can have a higher peak than the average.
statements.explanation: A burst pattern is lumpy, so its peak sits above the steady average.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Shortening the lifetime lowers the peak, since fewer bursts overlap.
statements.explanation: A shorter life means older bursts are removed before the next one arrives.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Overlapping bursts raise the peak, because particles from earlier bursts are still alive.
statements.explanation: Burst overlap adds counts.

questions.source: Rewrite of the exhaust and aura prompt
questions.stem: A rocket flies around a 2D screen with an exhaust and a glowing aura. A developer writes: "Attach two particle effects to the rocket." Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: An exhaust set to local coordinates is carried as a rigid plume with no trail.
statements.explanation: Local-space particles travel with the emitter.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Naming rate, lifetime and parent alongside the space makes the instruction more exact.
statements.explanation: Each named setting is one fewer guess for the agent.

statements.label: C
statements.text: An aura set to world coordinates stays around the rocket as it moves.
statements.explanation: A world-space aura is left behind and smears across the screen.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The instruction leaves the coordinate space to the agent's default.
statements.explanation: The word attach does not state the space.

statements.label: E
statements.text: "Exhaust in world coordinates, aura in local coordinates" removes the guess.
statements.explanation: Naming the space for each effect decides trail versus follow.

questions.stem: A 2D developer gets one PNG holding a regular grid of equal-sized drawings of a character in successive poses. Check each statement that is true about the exact names.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The PNG is itself an animation clip, because it records the order and timing of its frames.
statements.explanation: An image holds pixels only; order, timing and looping come from animation data that refers to it.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A tilemap is the same thing as a sprite sheet, because both cut one image into a grid.
statements.explanation: A sprite sheet's cells are poses to play in sequence, whereas a tilemap's tiles build a level.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A texture atlas packs images of different sizes into one texture and keeps a table of their rectangles.
statements.explanation: An atlas is a general packing of many images with a lookup table.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The file is a sprite sheet, and showing its cells in sequence at a chosen rate is frame-by-frame animation.
statements.explanation: A sprite sheet stores the poses of an animation in one image, and playing them in sequence is frame-by-frame animation.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A tilemap holds the poses of one character to play in sequence.
statements.explanation: A tilemap places reusable tiles on a level grid; poses to play in sequence belong to a sprite sheet.

questions.source: What is stored: sprite sheet versus rig
questions.stem: Team 1 animates a hero with a sprite sheet of hand-drawn walk frames. Team 2 animates a 2D cutout character: separate body-part images attached to a skeleton, with a walk clip that rotates and moves the bones. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Team 2's clip stores a table of image rectangles for each pose.
statements.explanation: A rig-based clip stores bone transform keys; a table of rectangles belongs to an atlas.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Team 1's version needs a skeleton, because bones position each drawn frame.
statements.explanation: Frame-by-frame animation has no skeleton, since each frame is a complete picture.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Team 2's animation changes bone transforms, and the attached parts follow.
statements.explanation: Moving a bone carries the parts attached to it.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Team 1's animation changes which image is shown from one frame to the next.
statements.explanation: Frame-by-frame animation swaps whole drawings.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Team 2's walk clip stores a full image for each pose, packed with the bone data.
statements.explanation: A skeletal clip holds transform keys, and the part images are the same in every pose.

questions.stem: A sprite sheet is a regular grid of equal cells with no gaps, numbered from 0, left to right and row by row from the top-left. A developer tells a coding agent to "play the run animation from the sheet". Check each statement that is true about the grid terms.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Frame index is counted from 1 in column-by-column order.
statements.explanation: Frame index names a cell by its position, counted from 0 row by row in this layout.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The agent has to be told the grid layout, as columns and rows or as a cell size, because pixels do not mark frame boundaries.
statements.explanation: Columns, rows or cell size are the grid metadata the image lacks.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Frame rate of a sprite animation is how many drawn cells are shown per second.
statements.explanation: The animation's own rate counts drawn frames per second, apart from the rendering rate.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A wrong guess of columns and rows raises an error.
statements.explanation: A wrong grid divides the image anyway, so nothing fails.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The image file records which cells belong to the run animation.
statements.explanation: A plain image has no record of animation names.

questions.stem: A studio has a 3D walk clip authored for Character X's skeleton. Character Y has a different mesh and different limb lengths but a skeleton whose bones correspond one for one. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Different limb lengths can make retargeted feet slide or float, which IK often corrects.
statements.explanation: Proportions change where feet land, so contact is re-solved with IK.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A sprite-sheet walk drawn for X can be retargeted to Y by mapping bone names to cells.
statements.explanation: A sprite sheet has no bones and shows drawings of one character.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A humanoid clip needs a custom mapping to drive a four-legged skeleton.
statements.explanation: Without corresponding bones there is nothing to pair, so a manual mapping is needed.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Characters that share one skeleton can share clips, since a clip stores bone motion.
statements.explanation: A clip addresses bones by name or path, not pixels.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Retargeting maps a source skeleton's motion onto a target skeleton by pairing bones.
statements.explanation: Retargeting pairs source bones with target bones so motion transfers.

questions.stem: A character has a walk clip and a run clip, and the designer wants a smooth change as speed rises. Check each statement that is true about the exact terms.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A blend space is a way to mix several clips by one or two parameters such as speed.
statements.explanation: A blend space maps parameter values to blends of clips.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Mixing the pixels of two sprite frames gives a ghosted double image, not an in-between pose.
statements.explanation: A cross-fade overlays both drawings and does not draw the pose between them.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A blend weight of 0.5 sets the playback speed to half.
statements.explanation: The blend weight mixes poses; playback speed is a separate setting.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Blending combines two poses by interpolating each bone's transform, weighted by a blend value.
statements.explanation: Skeletal poses are bone transforms, which interpolate per bone.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Cutout rigs have no bones, so their poses are not blended like 3D ones.
statements.explanation: A 2D skeleton is still a skeleton, so its poses blend per bone.

questions.stem: An art lead compares a sprite sheet drawn at a fixed pixel size with a skeletal 3D character drawn from its mesh, on 1080p and 4K screens. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A 3D character is drawn from its mesh at screen resolution, so its sharpness is not locked to a fixed frame size.
statements.explanation: Geometry is rasterised for the current screen each frame.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A cutout rig built from bitmap parts is resolution independent.
statements.explanation: The parts are bitmaps with a fixed pixel size, so enlarging them softens them.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Nearest-neighbour filtering keeps magnified pixels crisp and blocky.
statements.explanation: Nearest-neighbour picks the closest texel, so edges stay hard.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Real detail at 4K for a sprite comes from scaling the frames up with linear filtering.
statements.explanation: Scaling cannot invent detail; frames have to be redrawn or exported larger.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Linear filtering blends neighbouring pixels, so a magnified sprite looks blurry.
statements.explanation: Linear filtering averages neighbours, which softens edges.

questions.stem: An animator wants a cartoon character to squash flat on landing and show a drawn smear on a punch, and a 3D character must bend an elbow without pinching. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Skinning with vertex weights splits one mesh into rigid pieces at a joint.
statements.explanation: Skinning blends bone influence on shared vertices, giving a smooth bend.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Hand-drawn frames can take a squash or smear shape, because each frame is an independent picture.
statements.explanation: Frame-by-frame work is free-form.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Rigid cutout parts rotating about a joint stay joined at the edges.
statements.explanation: Rigid pieces do not stay joined at their edges when they rotate.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A skinned mesh takes the silhouette of a hand-drawn frame because bones move vertices.
statements.explanation: The silhouette is limited by the mesh, weights and bone motion.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A rig changes the pose of one set of art, so an unmodelled shape such as a smear needs extra tools such as blend shapes.
statements.explanation: A rig changes pose, not the underlying shapes.

questions.stem: A producer lists four animation methods: frame-by-frame, cutout, procedural and tweening. Check each statement that is true about the exact names.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Tweening is the name for animation drawn frame by frame.
statements.explanation: A tween computes in-between values of a property between endpoints.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Procedural animation is computed at runtime from rules, physics or targets.
statements.explanation: Procedural motion responds to conditions, so it can differ per playback.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Frame-by-frame animation uses a skeleton with about one bone per drawn piece.
statements.explanation: Frame-by-frame swaps whole drawings and has no skeleton.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Procedural animation is a fixed recording keyed on a timeline.
statements.explanation: Keys on a timeline describe authored animation.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Cutout animation redraws the whole figure for each pose.
statements.explanation: Cutout reuses separate pieces such as limbs and a head.

questions.stem: An animator keys a door's rotation to 0 degrees at 0.0 s and to 90 degrees at 1.0 s and sets nothing else. Check each statement that is true about the terms.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The clip stores one value for each rendered frame.
statements.explanation: The clip stores two keys; the engine computes values for frames.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Interpolation computes the values between keys, so the door shows intermediate angles.
statements.explanation: Interpolation fills in the in-betweens.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Linear interpolation gives 60 degrees at 0.5 s.
statements.explanation: Linear interpolation halfway between 0 and 90 gives 45 degrees.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A keyframe is an authored value at a chosen time.
statements.explanation: A key is a value pinned to a time.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A display with a higher refresh rate needs the clip re-authored with more keys.
statements.explanation: Values are sampled from time, so any display rate works with the same keys.

questions.stem: A menu panel slides from x = 0 to x = 300 over 0.5 s, once linear and once with ease-out. Check each statement that is true about the terms.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Easing shapes the speed profile of the interpolation.
statements.explanation: Easing is the curve that decides how speed varies.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Ease-out starts fast and slows toward the end.
statements.explanation: Ease-out decelerates into the end.

statements.label: C
statements.text: An ease-out finishes sooner than the linear version because it covers more distance early.
statements.explanation: Both versions finish at the same time.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Easing changes the start value, the end value or the duration.
statements.explanation: Easing keeps the endpoints and the duration.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Ease-in starts fast and slows down.
statements.explanation: Ease-in starts slowly and speeds up; ease-out is the one that slows.

questions.source: Clip, track, timeline and animation player
questions.stem: A developer sets up a door with an animation player node and animation clips. Check each statement that is true about the terms.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The animation player plays clips: it advances time, applies values and handles looping and speed.
statements.explanation: The player applies a clip's values to its targets over time.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A clip is data: tracks bound to targets, with keys along time.
statements.explanation: A clip does nothing until something plays it.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A track whose target was renamed or moved reports a loud error that stops the game.
statements.explanation: Tracks refer to targets by path or name, so a changed path can leave a track pointing at nothing without failing loudly.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A timeline is the time axis on which keys sit, and the playhead marks the current time.
statements.explanation: Scrubbing moves the playhead to preview values.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A clip animates one property of one object, so a door needs one clip per property.
statements.explanation: A clip commonly holds many tracks.

questions.stem: A producer says a character "needs a rig". Check each statement that is true about the exact names.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Skinning binds mesh vertices to bones so the mesh follows them.
statements.explanation: Skinning ties vertices to bones with weights.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A skeleton holds structure and pose, and a walk comes from a clip, code or a solver.
statements.explanation: A skeleton holds structure and pose; motion comes from clips, code or solvers.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A rig is the full posable setup: skeleton, skin binding and often controls such as IK handles.
statements.explanation: Rig names the whole setup that makes a character posable.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A skeleton (armature) is a hierarchy of bones where moving a parent bone moves its children.
statements.explanation: Bones are parented so a shoulder rotation carries the arm.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The skeleton is geometry that is drawn as the body in the final game.
statements.explanation: Bones are not drawn by default; the mesh is.

questions.stem: Under linear blend skinning, a vertex near an elbow has weight 0.75 for the upper-arm bone and 0.25 for the forearm bone. Check each statement that is true about the terms.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Vertex weights are one number per bone for the whole mesh.
statements.explanation: Weights vary vertex by vertex.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Vertex weights are normally kept so that they sum to 1.
statements.explanation: Normalised weights keep the blended result on the scale of bone motion.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Vertex weights are stored per vertex, so each vertex has its own mix of bone influences.
statements.explanation: Weight is influence at a vertex.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Painting vertex weights changes the keys stored in the animation clip.
statements.explanation: Weights belong to the skin binding; clip keys are separate.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A weight of 1 for one bone leaves the vertex halfway between two bones.
statements.explanation: With the whole weight on one bone the vertex copies that bone.

questions.stem: A character walks down uneven stairs, and the walk clip keys the hip, knee and ankle rotations of each leg. Check each statement that is true about the terms.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Forward kinematics computes the foot position from the joint rotations down a chain.
statements.explanation: FK goes from rotations to end position.

statements.label: B
statements.text: An IK target beyond the chain's length is reached by lengthening the bones.
statements.explanation: Rotation does not lengthen bones, so a far target is only approached with the chain extended.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Inverse kinematics takes a target for the end of a chain, such as a foot, and solves the joint rotations.
statements.explanation: IK goes from a target position to joint angles.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Forward kinematics starts from the target position and works back to the hip rotation.
statements.explanation: That describes IK; forward kinematics starts from joint rotations.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Adding IK to the legs usually means layering it over the clip, which still drives the rest of the pose.
statements.explanation: IK adjusts the legs on top of the authored animation.

questions.stem: A walk clip's root bone travels 1.2 m forward in each 1.0 s loop. A developer tells a coding agent "make the character walk forward when I press up". Check each statement that is true about the terms.

statements.label: A
statements.text: In-place animation poses the limbs and leaves travel to code or physics.
statements.explanation: An in-place clip has no root translation to extract.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Code can set a different speed with root motion without feet sliding.
statements.explanation: The feet are planted for the distance the clip covers, so another speed slides them.

statements.label: C
