statements.text: Root motion means the clip plays in place so the root bone stays at the origin.
statements.explanation: That is the in-place definition, the opposite of root motion.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Root motion applies the root bone's movement in the clip to the character's position in the world.
statements.explanation: Root motion hands movement authority to the clip.

statements.label: E
statements.text: If root motion moves the character and code also moves the body, the distance is covered twice.
statements.explanation: Two sources of forward movement add up.

questions.stem: A hand-drawn run cycle has 8 frames at 12 frames per second in a looping clip, and frame 8 is an exact copy of frame 1. Check each statement that is true about the loop terms.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The loop seam is the point where the last frame leads back to the first.
statements.explanation: The seam is where one pass ends and the next begins.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A seamless loop needs a last frame that is an exact copy of the first.
statements.explanation: The pose after the last frame has to lead naturally into the first, not duplicate it.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A duplicated end frame shows two different poses in a row.
statements.explanation: A duplicate shows the same pose twice in a row, which reads as a stall.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Removing the duplicate leaves 8 distinct frames in the cycle.
statements.explanation: Removing one of the 8 leaves 7 distinct frames.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Ping-pong mode (forward, then backward) is a good substitute for a run cycle.
statements.explanation: Running played backward steps the wrong way, so ping-pong does not suit a run.

questions.stem: Script 1 turns a fan blade 3 degrees on every drawn frame. Script 2 turns it 180 degrees per second multiplied by delta time. Check each statement that is true about the terms.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Delta time is the time since the previous frame.
statements.explanation: Delta time is the frame-to-frame interval, not the total elapsed time.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Script 2 is frame-rate independent because it scales a per-second rate by elapsed time.
statements.explanation: A rate times delta time gives the same motion per second.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A playback speed scale of 2 makes a clip take twice as long to finish.
statements.explanation: A speed scale of 2 plays twice as fast, so it finishes in half the time.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Frame-rate independence means results do not depend on the number of frames drawn.
statements.explanation: The result depends on time, not frames.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Frame-rate independence is reached by scaling with elapsed time, not by locking the rate.
statements.explanation: Scaling by elapsed time makes results independent of the frame rate.

questions.stem: A sword swing clip lasts 0.6 s. The hitbox is on from 0.20 s to 0.35 s. Option 1 starts a code timer when the swing begins. Option 2 puts animation events (a method-call track) on the clip. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A cancelled clip fires the events that lie past the point where it stopped.
statements.explanation: Keys past the cancel point are never reached, so they do not fire.

statements.label: B
statements.text: An animation event calls a function when playback passes its keyed time.
statements.explanation: A method track is a function call keyed on the timeline.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Events live in clip time, so they stay aligned when playback speed changes.
statements.explanation: Clip time scales with playback speed.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A code timer counts real time, so it drifts from a clip played at 1.5 times speed.
statements.explanation: A timer has its own clock, apart from clip speed.

statements.label: E
statements.text: If the swing is cancelled early, the event turns the hitbox off by itself.
statements.explanation: An event that was never reached does not run, so cleanup also has to happen on cancel.

questions.stem: A project has one file, hero.png. A developer types "animate the character walking" without saying what kind of art it holds. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: An agent that assumes a rig may rotate bone nodes that do not exist.
statements.explanation: Skeletal techniques on flat frames target things that do not exist.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The word "walking" fixes the frame count and the order of the cells.
statements.explanation: Frame count belongs to the art, not the verb.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The word "walking" names neither a sprite sheet nor a rig, so the agent has to guess the method.
statements.explanation: Sprite-sheet and rig animation are built differently, and the sentence names neither.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A precise version says hero.png is a 6 by 1 sprite sheet of 64 by 64 frames played as a looping walk at 10 frames per second.
statements.explanation: It names the art type, grid, frame size, loop and rate.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Loop mode and speed are settings the agent would otherwise choose.
statements.explanation: Looping and speed are not implied by the word walking.

questions.stem: A character must reach for a cup the player can place anywhere on a table. The project has one authored reach clip keyed to reach straight ahead. A developer says "play a reach animation toward the cup". Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Inverse kinematics on the arm chain, with the cup's position as target, is the exact request.
statements.explanation: IK solves joint rotations from a target position.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Forward kinematics makes the hand go to the cup because it starts from the target.
statements.explanation: FK computes the hand position from rotations; it takes no target.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A pole or hint names the elbow direction, since a target alone leaves it open.
statements.explanation: Many joint configurations reach the same point.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The authored clip reaches the place it was keyed for.
statements.explanation: Keyed rotations are fixed data.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A blend space between authored reaches stays inside the range of those clips.
statements.explanation: A blend space interpolates between authored poses, so it stays inside their range.

questions.stem: A pause panel slides in over 0.25 s and a designer wants to scrub and retime it. A health bar eases from its current width to a new width, unknown in advance, on each hit. Check each statement that is true about the terms.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A tween takes a texture and a mesh.
statements.explanation: A tween takes a duration and an easing curve.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The health bar suits a tween created in code, because its end value exists at runtime.
statements.explanation: A tween moves from the current value to a target given when it is created.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A tween has no easing setting and moves at constant speed.
statements.explanation: Tweens normally accept an easing curve.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A tween is authored as keys in the scene so a designer can scrub it.
statements.explanation: A tween is created and run from code.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The panel suits an authored clip, which is stored with the scene and editable on a timeline.
statements.explanation: A clip is made ahead of time.

questions.stem: A studio picks sprite-sheet animation for a pixel-art platformer and rig-based animation for a 3D game with twelve characters on one humanoid body. Check each statement that is true about the terms.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Characters that share a skeleton need separate clips for each body.
statements.explanation: A shared skeleton lets clips be reused and mixed.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A sprite sheet holds drawn images in a grid plus data on which to show and when.
statements.explanation: A sprite sheet is images plus timing data.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A rig-based character holds a skeleton, art bound to it and clips of bone transforms.
statements.explanation: A rig is skeleton, binding and bone-transform clips.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A rig-based clip changes the displayed image from frame to frame.
statements.explanation: Changing the displayed image describes frame-by-frame; a rig changes bone transforms.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Drawn frames transfer between characters by retargeting.
statements.explanation: Drawn frames belong to one character and do not retarget.

questions.stem: A developer tells a coding agent "animate the walk", and the agent has to know the art type. Check each statement that is true about exact rewrites.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A sprite-sheet rewrite names the bones and the skeleton.
statements.explanation: A sheet has grid, cells, rate and loop; a skeleton belongs to a rig.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A sprite-sheet rewrite names the bones to rotate.
statements.explanation: A sheet has no bones.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Slicing a sheet with the wrong grid is one plausible wrong build from a guess.
statements.explanation: A wrong grid cuts the image into the wrong cells.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A rig rewrite names the columns and rows of the sheet.
statements.explanation: Columns and rows belong to a sheet, not a rig.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A rig rewrite names the skeleton or model, the walk clip, its loop mode and whether motion is in place or uses root motion.
statements.explanation: Those are the settings a rig clip needs.

questions.stem: A door rotates from 0 to 90 degrees over 1 second. Check each statement that is true about telling a keyframe, interpolation and easing apart.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Reaching 45 degrees at 0.5 s is interpolation.
statements.explanation: Interpolation computes in-between values.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Keyframe is the name for the computed value between two endpoints.
statements.explanation: That describes interpolation.

statements.label: C
statements.text: 0 degrees at 0.0 s and 90 degrees at 1.0 s are keyframes.
statements.explanation: A keyframe is an authored value at a time.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Easing is the name for the authored value at a chosen time.
statements.explanation: That describes a keyframe.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Slow in, slow out is keyframing.
statements.explanation: Slow in, slow out is easing.

questions.stem: A tester reports that when the character raises an arm, the skin near the shoulder stretches toward the neck and the armpit collapses. Check each statement that is true about the terms.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The animation clip's keys are the likely cause.
statements.explanation: The keys move bones correctly; the skin is the problem.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The symptom points first at vertex weights, which set how much each bone influences a vertex.
statements.explanation: Weights decide how skin follows bones.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Deleting the walk clip is a fitting fix.
statements.explanation: Weight painting corrects influence; the clip is not the cause.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Shoulder vertices following the neck bone point to a clip that was keyed wrongly.
statements.explanation: Wrong or too many bone influences make vertices follow the wrong bone.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A precise report names the bones, the vertex group affected and the pose.
statements.explanation: Naming bone, vertex group and pose lets an artist reproduce it.

questions.stem: A walk clip makes the feet hover above some steps and sink into others on uneven stairs. Check each statement that is true about the terms.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Hip height is adjusted so both feet can reach their targets.
statements.explanation: Hip height lets the legs reach.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A good instruction names the texture of the stairs and the sprite frame rate.
statements.explanation: Chain, pole and blend weight are the terms for an IK setup.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The keyed rotations know nothing about the stair surface, so the foot goes where the keys put it.
statements.explanation: Forward kinematics follows the keys, not the ground.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Finding the ground under a foot with a ray cast and using it as the IK target is a fitting fix.
statements.explanation: A cast finds the surface and IK reaches it.

statements.label: E
statements.text: IK replaces the walk clip for the legs.
statements.explanation: IK is layered on top of the clip.

questions.stem: A developer tells a coding agent "make the character walk forward at 3 metres per second using the walk clip", and the clip's root bone travels 1.2 m per 1.0 s loop. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Ignoring root motion and moving at 3 m/s makes the feet slide, since the clip plants them for 1.2 m per loop.
statements.explanation: The feet were authored for another speed.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Choosing one authority for movement is a fitting rewrite.
statements.explanation: One source of movement keeps the result predictable.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Applying root motion and also moving the body at 3 m/s causes double movement.
statements.explanation: Two sources of forward movement add.

statements.label: D
statements.text: An in-place clip with code-set speed needs no matching of playback speed.
statements.explanation: Matching playback speed to travel speed prevents sliding.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Root motion lets code set the speed freely.
statements.explanation: Root motion gives the clip the authority over speed.

questions.stem: A script moves a platform 2 units each time a frame is drawn, and it is much faster on a 144 frames per second monitor than on a 60 one. Check each statement that is true about the terms.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Defining speed in units per second and multiplying by delta time fixes it.
statements.explanation: Per-second rates scaled by elapsed time are frame-rate independent.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The movement is tied to the number of frames drawn.
statements.explanation: A per-frame increment scales with frames.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A fixed physics step is an engine alternative.
statements.explanation: The fixed step runs at a constant interval.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Per-frame increments are frame-rate independent.
statements.explanation: Per-frame increments depend on frame rate.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A sprite sheet's frame rate is the rendering rate.
statements.explanation: The animation's own rate is separate from the rendering rate.

questions.stem: A designer wants the hitbox on during part of a sword swing and a whoosh at its start. Check each statement that is true about the terms.

statements.label: A
statements.text: An animation event or method track is a function call keyed at a time on the clip.
statements.explanation: Events are keyed calls.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A precise instruction names the clip, the times, the functions and what happens on cancel.
statements.explanation: Those are the details the agent would otherwise guess.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Events keep the timing in code, so retiming the clip leaves them where they were.
statements.explanation: Event timing travels with the clip.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A code timer follows clip playback speed on its own.
statements.explanation: A code timer runs on its own clock, apart from clip playback speed.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A cancelled clip fires the keys that lie past the point where it stopped.
statements.explanation: Keys past the cancel point are not reached, so they do not fire.

questions.stem: Playtesters say a run cycle hitches once per loop, and switching from walk to run pops. Check each statement that is true about the terms.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A rig can cross-fade or blend bone transforms over a short time to hide a pop.
statements.explanation: Skeletal poses interpolate per bone.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A sprite sheet blends frames into a true in-between pose.
statements.explanation: Mixing pixels gives a ghost, not a pose.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A pop on switching is an instant cut between two different poses.
statements.explanation: A pop is a jump between poses.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A sprite-sheet fix switches at a matching point in the cycle or adds transition frames.
statements.explanation: Matching phase or extra frames hide the cut.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A hitch at the loop seam comes from a pop between walk and run.
statements.explanation: A seam hitch comes from a last frame that duplicates the first.

questions.source: State machine: state, transition, condition, parameter
questions.stem: A developer describes a platformer character as an animation state machine with the states Idle, Run, Jump and Fall. Check each statement that is true about the vocabulary.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A transition is the test that compares a value with a threshold.
statements.explanation: That describes a condition; the transition is the route the condition guards.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A transition is an allowed route from one state to another, usually guarded by a condition.
statements.explanation: Transitions are the explicit connections that say which state may follow which.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A state is a named situation of the character, and the machine is in one current state at a time within a layer.
statements.explanation: A state machine has one current state, which separates it from a set of independent flags.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A condition is the allowed route from one state to another.
statements.explanation: That describes a transition; a condition is the test that lets a transition fire.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A parameter is a value supplied by the game, such as speed or on-floor, that conditions read.
statements.explanation: Parameters are the inputs that the game writes and the conditions read.

questions.source: State machine versus flags and nested conditionals
questions.stem: A script tracks animation with four independent boolean flags (is_jumping, is_attacking, is_crouching, is_hurt) inside nested if statements. A teammate proposes a state machine instead. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Four flags describe four situations, one per flag, so the flags stay consistent with each other.
statements.explanation: Independent flags can be set in contradictory ways, which is the weakness of the flag approach.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The number of transitions in a state machine equals the number of states.
statements.explanation: Transitions are the allowed routes between states and their count is independent of the state count.

statements.label: C
statements.text: In a state machine the current state is one named value, so a bug report can name the state the character was in.
statements.explanation: One current state is a single value that can be logged, shown and reported.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A state machine removes the need for conditions, because each state picks its own next state.
statements.explanation: Transitions still need conditions or events that say when a change happens.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Four independent booleans give 16 combinations, and some of them, such as jumping and hurt at once, were not designed.
statements.explanation: Four booleans give 2^4 = 16 combinations, many of them undesigned.

questions.source: Animation tree, state machine, blend tree and blend space
questions.stem: In Godot, an AnimationTree node plays clips stored in an AnimationPlayer. Check each statement that is true about the node types.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The clips live in the AnimationPlayer, and the tree decides how much of each clip enters the final pose.
statements.explanation: The AnimationPlayer stores clips; the tree mixes them into one pose.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A state machine and a blend tree are two names for the same graph.
statements.explanation: A state machine selects among states; a blend tree combines inputs by weight, so they are different nodes.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The AnimationTree keeps its own copy of the clips, separate from the AnimationPlayer.
statements.explanation: The tree references the player's clips and does not hold its own copy.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A blend space picks its output from a position on one or two axes and mixes the clips placed near that position.
statements.explanation: A blend space maps a continuous position to a weighted mix of neighbouring clips.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A blend tree plays one active state at a time and moves between states with transitions.
statements.explanation: That describes a state machine; a blend tree mixes inputs by weight.

questions.stem: A character should walk, jog or sprint according to how far the stick is pushed, and should commit to a jump once it has started. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A jump suits a blend, because a blend gives a committed action its own entry, exit and duration.
statements.explanation: A committed action is a state with defined ways in and out; a blend only mixes clips.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Walk, jog and sprint suit a blend space driven by a speed parameter, because speed varies continuously.
statements.explanation: A blend space maps a continuous number such as speed to a mix of neighbouring clips.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A blend space can prevent a started jump from being interrupted by movement input.
statements.explanation: Interrupt rules belong to states and transitions; a blend only sets clip weights.

statements.label: D
statements.text: One state per tiny speed step, such as walk_1 to walk_20, is a more precise form of blending.
statements.explanation: Many states need many transitions and still jump between steps; a blend changes smoothly with one parameter.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A blend space needs a transition with its own condition between neighbouring clips on its axis.
statements.explanation: Blend spaces mix by position and do not use per-pair transitions.

questions.stem: In Unity, an Animator Controller reads Animator parameters of type float, int, bool and trigger, and a script writes them. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A parameter is an output of the controller, written back to the script to say what to do next.
statements.explanation: Parameters are inputs that the script writes and the controller reads.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A bool holds its value until the script changes it, so a condition on it stays satisfied while it is true.
statements.explanation: A bool is a level: it keeps its value until it is changed.

statements.label: C
statements.text: An int is the parameter type meant for a one-shot event that resets itself.
statements.explanation: That describes a trigger; an int holds a whole number.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A float such as Speed suits a comparison like greater than 0.1 and can also drive a blend tree.
statements.explanation: Floats feed numeric comparisons and blend parameters.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A trigger is meant for a one-time event and is reset once a transition consumes it.
statements.explanation: A trigger is a boolean that the controller clears when a transition uses it.

questions.stem: Physics runs in fixed ticks and the animation graph updates once per rendered frame. A held jump key makes the character land on one tick and jump on the next, and the graph reads on-floor only at its own update. Players see the character stay in its Fall state while it rises. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Running the graph in the physics step is one way to align the two sampling rates.
statements.explanation: Engines offer update or callback modes that run animation in the physics step.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The fault is a physics engine bug, because physics should not let a landing and a take-off share one frame.
statements.explanation: Physics is correct; the graph samples more slowly than the state changes.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A tick is one step of the physics simulation, and an update is one evaluation of the animation graph.
statements.explanation: Ticks belong to the physics clock and updates belong to the animation or render clock.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Polling means the engine calls your code at the moment a value changes.
statements.explanation: That describes a callback or event; polling is checking a value on each update.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A condition read once per graph update can miss a value that changed and changed back between two reads.
statements.explanation: A sampled value can miss a short-lived state, which is a sampling gap.

questions.stem: A developer tells a coding agent: 'when the player presses Space, switch to the jump state'. The character also has a Hurt state that ignores input. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Choosing animation straight from key presses keeps the picture in step with what the movement code does.
statements.explanation: Movement code can ignore or override a press, so picture and movement can disagree.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A guard is an extra condition on a transition, such as the character being on the floor.
statements.explanation: Guards add conditions so a transition fires only in the right situation.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Driving Jump from physical state, such as leaving the floor with upward velocity, stays consistent when a bounce pad causes the launch.
statements.explanation: A condition on what the body is doing agrees with movement whatever caused it.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Interpreting key presses is the job of the animation state machine itself.
statements.explanation: Gameplay code interprets input and then sets state or parameters for animation.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The phrase ties the state change to the key press, so the agent may start a jump during Hurt.
statements.explanation: A press-only condition ignores whether the character can jump now.

questions.stem: A character has the states Idle, Run, Attack, Hurt and Dead. Hit reactions interrupt an attack, Dead overrides the other states, and Run input does not interrupt an attack. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Priority is needed because two states can be active at once.
statements.explanation: A machine has one active state; priority chooses between several valid transitions.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A transition from Any State to Dead expresses that death overrides the other states.
statements.explanation: Any State is a special source that stands for the states in the machine.

statements.label: C
statements.text: An interrupt is a transition taken out of the current state before its clip ends.
statements.explanation: An interrupt leaves a state early, through a transition that does not wait for the clip to finish.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Leaving out an Attack-to-Run transition forbids that interruption, and Attack still needs some exit.
statements.explanation: A missing transition is how a machine forbids a change, but a state without an exit sticks.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Priority or order decides which transition is taken when more than one is valid at the same moment.
statements.explanation: Equal-looking choices are settled by an order, which should be stated.

questions.stem: After the player is hit, the character plays the Hurt animation and then freezes in its last pose. The only transition out of Hurt has the condition 'hurt_finished is true', and nothing in the code sets it. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: An unconditional transition from Hurt to Dead is a clean fix without side effects.
statements.explanation: An unconditional route would send every hurt character to Dead, which is a new fault.

statements.label: B
statements.text: This is a stuck state: the machine sits in a state whose exit condition stays false.
statements.explanation: A state whose exit condition is never met cannot be left.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A stuck state is hard to detect because a machine has no single current state to look at.
statements.explanation: The current state is one visible value, so logging it shows the machine sitting in Hurt.

statements.label: D
statements.text: An exit-time transition, which leaves when the clip ends, removes the dependence on a flag nobody sets.
statements.explanation: Leaving at the end of the clip needs no extra flag.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The cause is a fault in the animation clip, because clips decide transitions.
statements.explanation: Conditions and parameters decide transitions; a clip supplies the pose over time.

questions.stem: The animation state machine has the states Idle, Run, Attack and Dodge, and no transition from Attack to Dodge is defined. A developer tells an agent: 'when the player presses Dodge, play the dodge animation'. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A state is reachable when a path of defined transitions leads to it from the current state.
statements.explanation: Reachability comes from transitions that were defined.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A clip played directly, outside the machine, leaves the machine's recorded state unchanged, so the machine and the screen disagree.
statements.explanation: A clip played outside the machine does not update the machine's current state.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The engine adds the missing Attack-to-Dodge transition the first time Dodge is pressed.
statements.explanation: Engines do not invent transitions; missing ones are authored.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The sentence leaves open whether Dodge may cancel an attack, so the agent has to choose.
statements.explanation: Whether an attack can be cancelled is a rule the sentence does not state.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A trigger or condition request for a state needs a defined transition, while a direct play call that forces a state skips transitions.
statements.explanation: Forcing a state skips transitions, as with Animator.Play in Unity.

questions.stem: An attack clip lasts 0.5 s and the player presses Attack five times in quick succession. Three input policies are named: an input lock (ignore presses while attacking), a restart (begin the attack again on each press) and an input buffer (remember one press and use it when the attack ends). Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: An input lock is the policy that remembers a press for later.
statements.explanation: Remembering a press is buffering, not locking.

statements.label: B
statements.text: An input lock discards presses that arrive while the attack is playing.
statements.explanation: A lock ignores input while the action runs.

statements.label: C
statements.text: An input buffer remembers a press made during the attack and starts the next attack when the first one ends.
statements.explanation: A buffer keeps a press and uses it when the action becomes available.

statements.label: D
statements.text: An input buffer discards the presses that arrive during the attack.
statements.explanation: A buffer keeps the press instead of discarding it.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A restart cuts off the swing in progress each time a new press arrives.
statements.explanation: A restart replaces the running attack with a new one.

questions.stem: A game uses an input buffer for Attack. The next attack becomes available at t = 0.50 s when recovery ends, and a press is remembered for 0.15 s. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A press whose window expires before the attack becomes available is dropped.
statements.explanation: A press that expires early is lost.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Lengthening the buffer improves precision with no downside.
statements.explanation: A long buffer queues presses the player did not mean and makes controls feel loose.

statements.label: C
statements.text: An input buffer is the delay between the button press and the start of the animation.
statements.explanation: That delay is input latency, a different idea.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A press that arrives when the attack is already available is remembered until the window ends and then used.
statements.explanation: When the action is available the press is used at once; the buffer matters for early presses.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A press at 0.40 s is still remembered when the attack becomes available, so the next attack starts at 0.50 s.
statements.explanation: The press at 0.40 s lasts until 0.55 s, past 0.50 s, so it is used then.

questions.source: Cooldown versus animation lock versus buffer
questions.stem: A dash lasts 0.2 s and cannot be used again until 1.5 s after it starts. Check each statement that is true about the terms cooldown, animation lock and input buffer.

statements.label: A
statements.text: An animation lock blocks actions for a time that outlasts the animation.
statements.explanation: A lock blocks action while the animation plays, so it ends with the animation.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A cooldown is a minimum time between uses of an action and can last longer than the animation.
statements.explanation: A cooldown is measured between uses and can run past the end of the clip.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A cooldown and an animation lock are the same thing.
statements.explanation: A cooldown restricts repeated use; a lock restricts action during playback.

statements.label: D
statements.text: An input buffer can hold a press made shortly before the cooldown ends and use it when the dash is allowed again.
statements.explanation: A buffer remembers an early press and uses it when the action is available.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A cooldown is the grace period after leaving the ground in which a jump is still accepted.
statements.explanation: That describes coyote time.

questions.stem: Players complain that jumping 'does not work' when they press Jump a few milliseconds after running off a ledge, and when they press it just before landing. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Jump buffering remembers a press made shortly before landing and performs the jump on landing.
statements.explanation: Jump buffering forgives an early press before landing.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Jump buffering is another name for coyote time.
statements.explanation: The two forgive opposite timing errors.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Coyote time is a brief grace period after leaving the ground in which a jump is still accepted.
statements.explanation: Coyote time forgives a late press after the edge.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Coyote time is the delay between the button press and the jump animation.
statements.explanation: Press-to-animation delay is input latency.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Both are input tolerance windows and leave the physics of the jump unchanged.
statements.explanation: They adjust when input is accepted and not how high or far the jump goes.

questions.source: Animation event, property track, finished signal
questions.stem: A sword swing clip is 0.6 s long. The designer needs the hitbox on from 0.20 s to 0.35 s, a sound at 0.20 s, and a return to Idle when the clip ends. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: An animation event is a call keyed at a time on the clip's timeline, which suits the hitbox and sound moments.
statements.explanation: Events run code at keyed times inside the clip.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Events are evaluated when the playhead passes their time during an update, so a frame at the exact time is not needed.
statements.explanation: Events fire when the playhead passes them.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A finished signal reports that a clip or state has ended, which suits the return to Idle.
statements.explanation: Completion is signalled by a finished signal or an end-of-state transition.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A code timer set to 0.20 s stays in step with the clip's events when playback speed is doubled.
statements.explanation: At double speed the clip reaches its 0.20 s mark early and a seconds timer fires late.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A property track in the clip can switch the hitbox's enabled property on and off.
statements.explanation: A property track stores the timing inside the clip.

questions.stem: In a melee game the player's sword and an enemy both need collision shapes. A developer asks an agent for 'a collider on the sword and one on the enemy'. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A hitbox is the attacker's damaging region, and a hurtbox is the defender's region that can receive damage.
statements.explanation: Hitbox is the dealing region and hurtbox is the receiving region.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A hurtbox is a solid collider that physically stops the blade.
statements.explanation: Both are normally detection shapes, such as areas, that report overlap without blocking.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The word 'collider' names neither which shape deals damage nor which receives it.
statements.explanation: 'Collider' states neither role nor behaviour.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Layers and masks make a body's own hitbox able to detect its own hurtbox.
statements.explanation: Layers and masks are used to stop a body detecting its own boxes.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A hurtbox is the attacker's region that deals damage.
statements.explanation: That describes a hitbox.

questions.stem: An attack clip has three phases named startup, active and recovery. Its hitbox is on only in one of them. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Startup is the part of the attack before the hitbox turns on.
statements.explanation: Startup is the lead-in before damage can happen.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Recovery is the part after the hitbox turns off, before the character is free to act.
statements.explanation: Recovery is the wind-down after the active window.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A hit list records the enemies already hit, so an overlap lasting several updates damages one enemy once per swing.
statements.explanation: Without a hit list, an overlap on several updates damages again on each update.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Active is the phase in which the weapon is drawn back before the swing.
statements.explanation: That describes startup; active is when the hitbox is on.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Recording already-hit enemies means the hitbox switches off after its first overlap.
statements.explanation: The hitbox can stay on for other enemies; the record only blocks repeat hits on the same one.

questions.stem: A developer tells a coding agent: 'make the character animate when it moves'. The project has idle, walk, run and jump clips. Check each statement that is true about what the instruction leaves open.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The word 'moves' fixes an exact condition, so two agents would build the same machine.
statements.explanation: 'Moves' leaves thresholds, directions and priorities open.

statements.label: B
statements.text: It leaves open the speed threshold at which walk gives way to run.
statements.explanation: The walk-to-run threshold is a number the sentence does not give.

statements.label: C
statements.text: It names the transitions between the clips.
statements.explanation: The sentence lists no transitions at all.

statements.label: D
statements.text: It leaves open whether each clip loops or plays once.
statements.explanation: Loop mode against one-shot playback is a per-clip choice not stated.

statements.label: E
statements.text: It leaves open whether clips cross-fade or cut, and how long a cross-fade lasts.
statements.explanation: Blend behaviour and its length are not mentioned.

questions.stem: A developer must tell a coding agent how four states (Idle, Run, Jump, Fall) connect. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A loop setting is a per-clip choice that needs its own line in the instruction.
statements.explanation: Looping belongs to the clip, not the transition, and needs its own statement.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Naming the four states without conditions is enough, because the conditions follow from the names.
statements.explanation: A name such as Fall does not say whether the condition is velocity or floor contact.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A table with one row per transition (from state, to state, condition, cross-fade time) leaves the agent little to guess about which routes exist and when they fire.
statements.explanation: Each row fixes both ends, the trigger and the blend.

statements.label: D
statements.text: An arrow diagram shows which routes exist but not when they fire.
statements.explanation: Arrows show routes, not conditions or blend times.

statements.label: E
statements.text: An interrupt rule says which state may be cut short and by what.
statements.explanation: Interrupt rules are design decisions to state.

questions.stem: A designer says: 'the attack can be cancelled into a dodge, but not into another attack, until its recovery phase starts'. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Markers in clip time keep the window aligned with the visuals when playback speed changes.
statements.explanation: Clip-time markers scale with playback.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A timer in code measured in seconds keeps the window aligned when playback speed changes.
statements.explanation: Fixed seconds drift away from the visuals when speed changes.

statements.label: C
statements.text: An animation event can set a flag such as can_cancel that a transition condition reads.
statements.explanation: Events can set flags that conditions use to allow transitions.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Recovery is the phase before the hitbox turns on.
statements.explanation: Recovery comes after the active phase.

statements.label: E
statements.text: This describes a cancel window: a span of an action during which another action may interrupt it.
statements.explanation: A cancel window is the portion of an action in which interruption is allowed.

questions.stem: A project has a gameplay state machine in code. An agent asked to 'add an animation state machine' builds a second machine that tracks its own Idle, Move, Attack and Hurt states from the player's input. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A single source of truth means one machine, usually gameplay, is the authority and the other reads it.
statements.explanation: One authority keeps picture and gameplay in agreement.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The animation machine should decide whether damage is dealt.
statements.explanation: Damage is a gameplay decision; animation presents state.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Two machines fed the same input agree, because identical input gives identical states.
statements.explanation: Different rules and sampling give different states from the same input.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The two machines can disagree, for example when gameplay says Hurt while animation is still in Attack.
statements.explanation: Separate rules and timing let the two fall out of step.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The animation machine should keep its own copy of gameplay state rather than read a parameter.
statements.explanation: A copy can drift; reading a parameter keeps one source.

questions.source: Testing state machines: dead end, enumerable transitions
questions.stem: A team wants automated tests for a character's animation state machine. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A test that writes the state variable straight to the target tests the transitions.
statements.explanation: Writing the state skips the transition logic being tested.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A test can check for dead ends, meaning states with no exit other than a deliberate end state.
statements.explanation: A dead end is a property of the graph that a check can find without playing.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A passing state test shows that the motion looks and feels right to players.
statements.explanation: Looks and feel need a person to watch and play.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Because states and transitions can be listed, a test can try each listed transition and check that unlisted ones do not occur.
statements.explanation: Enumerable transitions can be exercised one by one.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A test can drive the real jump action and then read the current state.
statements.explanation: Real input exercises the conditions that link input to state.

questions.source: Undesigned flag combinations versus designed states
questions.stem: A teammate says a nested-if flag approach and a state machine are the same thing written differently. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: One boolean per state is the same thing as a state machine.
statements.explanation: Several booleans can be true at once, which a single current state excludes.

statements.label: B
statements.text: In a state machine, transitions are decided by deeply nested if checks on flags.
statements.explanation: Transitions are explicit routes guarded by conditions, not nested flag checks.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Nested conditionals make the current state one explicit named value.
statements.explanation: With nested conditionals the state is implied by flag combinations, not named.

statements.label: D
statements.text: In a state machine, jumping, crouching and hurt can be active together by default.
statements.explanation: A machine has one current state within a layer.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Independent flags can combine into undesigned situations, and a state machine lists the situations that were designed.
statements.explanation: Designed states are listed; flags allow combinations nobody designed.

questions.source: Rewrite a vague animation prompt with exact terms
questions.stem: Four rewrites of a vague animation prompt are being compared. Check each statement that is true about whether the wording uses exact terms.

statements.label: A
statements.text: 'Go from Idle to Walk when speed is above 0.1, with a 0.1 s cross-fade' names a transition, a condition with a threshold and a blend time.
statements.explanation: It gives source, destination, a numeric condition and a blend duration.

statements.label: B
statements.text: 'Animate sensibly' specifies the states and their conditions.
statements.explanation: It names no states or conditions.

statements.label: C
statements.text: 'Loop walk and run, and play jump once' uses loop and one-shot correctly.
statements.explanation: Looping repeats a clip; one-shot plays it once.

statements.label: D
statements.text: 'Transitions not in this table do not exist' states that the table is the complete set of routes.
statements.explanation: It closes the list of routes, so none are invented.

statements.label: E
statements.text: 'Blend nicely between the clips' names a cross-fade time.
statements.explanation: 'Nicely' gives no number or duration.

questions.source: Animation tree nesting and engine names
questions.stem: A character has an animation tree: a ground state that holds a speed-driven blend space, plus Jump and Fall states. Check each statement that is true about the vocabulary.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A state machine is one possible part of the animation tree.
statements.explanation: State machines, blend trees and blend spaces can all appear in a tree.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The animation tree is the whole graph that plays clips through nodes such as state machines and blends.
statements.explanation: The tree is the whole graph; nodes are parts of it.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A ground state that contains a speed blend space is an example of nesting.
statements.explanation: One kind of node can sit inside another.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Unity's Animator Controller plays a similar role to the animation tree in Godot.
statements.explanation: Animator Controller, like Unreal's Animation Blueprint, holds the graph that drives clips.

statements.label: E
statements.text: 'State machine' is a synonym for the whole animation tree.
statements.explanation: A state machine is one kind of node, not the whole tree.

questions.stem: A jump animation intermittently stays in Fall after a quick land-and-jump, only on some runs. Check each statement that is true about the vocabulary of this fault.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A good test runs the sequence at both tick offsets within an update, with real input.
statements.explanation: Running both offsets catches the unlucky timing.

statements.label: B
statements.text: If the landing and take-off ticks share one graph update, the graph does not see on-floor, and the landing is missed.
statements.explanation: A sampled condition misses a state that comes and goes between reads.

statements.label: C
statements.text: An intermittent fault depends on certain timing and is absent on some runs.
statements.explanation: Intermittent means timing dependent.

statements.label: D
statements.text: An event-driven fix has the movement code push the state change at the moment it happens, instead of waiting for the graph to poll.
statements.explanation: Pushing an event avoids reading the value late.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Intermittent means the fault lies in the clip data.
statements.explanation: The cause is sampling, not the clip.

questions.stem: A tester reports three bugs. Match each symptom to its name. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A character frozen in a pose is an impossible transition.
statements.explanation: A freeze points to a stuck state; an impossible transition concerns a missing route.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Rapid input needs no policy, because the engine picks the right behaviour.
statements.explanation: A chosen policy such as lock, restart or buffer is needed.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Repeated presses that restart, stack up or get lost show a rapid-input problem.
statements.explanation: With no rule for presses during an action, the behaviour is accidental.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A character frozen in a pose because its exit condition stays false is a stuck state.
statements.explanation: A state with an unmet exit condition cannot be left.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A requested change with no defined route between the states is an impossible (missing) transition.
statements.explanation: Reachability needs a defined route.

questions.stem: Players say the game 'eats' their jump presses just before landing. Check each statement that is true about the fix.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A jump buffer is the fix for presses made shortly before landing.
statements.explanation: A buffer remembers the early press and uses it on landing.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A longer animation lock is the fix for presses made shortly before landing.
statements.explanation: A lock blocks action and does not remember presses.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Coyote time is the fix for presses made shortly before landing.
statements.explanation: Coyote time covers late presses after leaving ground.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The length of the buffer window is a design value to state in the instruction.
statements.explanation: The window length changes the feel, so it should be stated.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A cooldown is the fix for presses made shortly before landing.
statements.explanation: A cooldown limits repeated use and does not remember presses.

questions.stem: A sword attack has a hitbox switched on and off by animation events. The attack can be interrupted partway. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Hitbox timing is best set by a fixed seconds timer in code.
statements.explanation: Seconds in code drift from the animation when speed changes.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The instruction should give the active window in frames or clip time.
statements.explanation: The active window should be stated in the clip's own time.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Leaving or interrupting the attack state should also switch the hitbox off.
statements.explanation: Cleanup on exit keeps the hitbox from lingering.

statements.label: D
statements.text: If the attack is interrupted before the off event, the event may not fire and the hitbox stays on.
statements.explanation: Events keyed after the interruption point do not run.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A hit list is a record kept for each swing of the targets already damaged.
statements.explanation: A hit list stops repeat damage in one swing.

questions.source: Rewrite for single source of truth
questions.stem: A developer writes: 'add an animation state machine that tracks its own states from the player's input'. Check each statement that is true about the wording.

statements.label: A
statements.text: 'Tracks its own states' creates a second authority that can disagree with gameplay.
statements.explanation: Two machines can fall out of step.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A better wording also says which transitions the animation machine has.
statements.explanation: Naming the transitions removes guesses.

statements.label: C
statements.text: 'Reads raw input' is the intended way for the animation machine to learn the state.
statements.explanation: Raw input is for gameplay code to interpret.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Letting the animation machine decide whether damage is dealt is fine.
statements.explanation: Damage belongs to gameplay.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A better wording says the animation machine reads gameplay state through a parameter.
statements.explanation: A parameter carries state from the authority.

questions.stem: A Godot game has background music, a menu click and the footsteps of an enemy walking around a 3D world. The developer chooses between a plain AudioStreamPlayer and a positional AudioStreamPlayer3D for each. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Attenuation is the drop in loudness as the distance between a positional source and the listener grows.
statements.explanation: Attenuation, also called falloff, is the distance-dependent loss of level.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The menu click suits a positional player, so that it pans and fades like the rest of the 3D world.
statements.explanation: A menu click has no place in the world, and a positional player would change its level and pan with the camera.

statements.label: C
statements.text: For a positional player, the listener is the point whose position and orientation define what is heard, and in Godot 3D it defaults to the active camera.
statements.explanation: A positional sound is heard relative to a listener, which Godot takes from the current camera unless told otherwise.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The listener is the object that emits a positional sound, so each positional sound needs its own listener at its source.
statements.explanation: The listener is the receiver (the ears), and one is active at a time.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A plain AudioStreamPlayer is non-positional, so its loudness does not depend on where the camera is.
statements.explanation: A non-positional player ignores listener position, which suits music and interface sounds.

questions.source: Wiring an event to a sound: signal, handler, bus
questions.stem: A developer tells a coding agent: 'Play a click when the button is pressed.' Check each statement that is true about what the wording leaves out.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A signal is connected to a handler that calls play() on a stream player holding a stream.
statements.explanation: Game logic wires an event to a handler that starts a player.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The instruction already fixes the bus, the loudness and the behaviour on rapid presses.
statements.explanation: The sentence names an event and a sound; bus, level and overlap behaviour are left to guesswork.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The player's playing flag reading true after play() shows that the click reached the output and is audible.
statements.explanation: The flag shows a voice was started and says nothing about routing, level or mute.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A muted bus on the route to Master silences the click even though the player reports that it is playing.
statements.explanation: Mute and level apply along the bus chain.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A sound can be audible and still be routed to a different bus than intended.
statements.explanation: A misrouted sound can still be heard, so audibility does not verify routing.

questions.stem: A stream player is set to -6 dB and routed to an SFX bus whose fader is -6 dB, and that bus sends to Master at 0 dB. Check each statement that is true about the decibel vocabulary.

statements.label: A
statements.text: dBFS states a level relative to digital full scale, where 0 dBFS is the loudest value a digital signal can hold.
statements.explanation: dBFS counts down from digital full scale.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A linear slider value from 0.0 to 1.0 passed straight to a bus as dB behaves like a linear volume knob.
statements.explanation: Decibels are logarithmic, so a linear slider needs converting to dB.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Gain staging means one -6 dB stage is enough to reach the level of the whole chain, so the later stages are ignored.
statements.explanation: Gain staging is the set of level changes along the chain, and each stage contributes.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Decibels are a logarithmic scale, so gains in series add and the two -6 dB stages give about -12 dB.
statements.explanation: Decibel gains in series add.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A change of about -6 dB roughly halves the amplitude.
statements.explanation: A factor of 10^(-6/20) is about 0.5.

questions.stem: A game has Music, SFX and Voice buses that each send to Master, with a settings slider per bus. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A reverb on the SFX bus also processes the Music bus.
statements.explanation: A bus effect processes the sounds routed through that bus.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Separate buses let the player change the music level without changing the effects level.
statements.explanation: Each bus is an independent control point for level, mute and effects.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Master is the final bus, so muting it silences the sounds routed to it directly or through child buses.
statements.explanation: Master ends the chain.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Muting Master silences just the sounds played straight onto Master.
statements.explanation: Child buses feed Master, so muting it silences them too.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Muting the SFX bus also silences the Music bus, because both feed Master.
statements.explanation: Buses with a shared parent do not affect each other.

questions.stem: A designer says: 'When a character speaks, the music should get quieter, then come back up when the speech ends.' The developer passes it to an agent as 'pause the music during dialogue'. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Calling stop() on the music and later play() resumes from where it stopped.
statements.explanation: Stop discards position, so play() restarts from the beginning.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Ducking needs the music and the voice to share one stream player.
statements.explanation: Music and voice normally sit on separate players and buses.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Ducking is the automatic, temporary lowering of one group of sounds while another is active.
statements.explanation: Ducking lowers and then restores the level on its own.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A paused track and a ducked track sound the same to the player.
statements.explanation: A paused track is silent and frozen; a ducked track plays on quietly.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Ducking can be driven by a side-chain, where an effect on the music bus reacts to the level of the voice.
statements.explanation: Side-chain compression makes one bus's level follow another's signal.

questions.stem: A designer wants a chime when the player walks into a glowing zone, while the player keeps walking through the zone. A developer asks for 'a zone collider that plays a chime'. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Collision layers or filtering keep enemies and projectiles from playing the chime.
statements.explanation: Layers and masks decide which objects count.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Placing a chime player inside the zone makes the audio system detect the overlap and play it with no code.
statements.explanation: Game logic detects the overlap and calls the player.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A trigger (Area in Godot, trigger collider in Unity, overlap volume in Unreal) reports overlap as an event and does not block.
statements.explanation: A trigger observes and raises events.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A solid collider is the right choice, because it reports contact and lets the player pass.
statements.explanation: A solid collider blocks; passing through is what a trigger does.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The chime should start from the enter event, which marks the start of the overlap.
statements.explanation: The enter event fires at the start of the overlap, the moment for the chime.

questions.stem: A pressure plate click is wired to a callback that runs on each physics step while an overlap persists (Unity's OnTriggerStay). At 50 steps per second, players hear a buzzing, machine-gun click while they stand on the plate. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A trigger has no event for the start of an overlap.
statements.explanation: Triggers report enter, stay and exit.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A stay callback fires on each physics step during the overlap, restarting the click about once per 20 ms.
statements.explanation: 50 steps per second gives a callback every 20 ms.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Raising polyphony removes the cause of the buzzing.
statements.explanation: More voices let the retriggers overlap and make it noisier.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Starting the click from the enter event plays it once at the start of the overlap, and an exit event marks leaving.
statements.explanation: Enter and exit mark the transitions of an overlap.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A longer click file fixes the buzzing, because a longer sound is restarted less often.
statements.explanation: The callback still fires on each step.

questions.stem: A developer asks an agent: 'Make the engine hum loop while the car drives, and make the horn honk once per press.' The project is Godot. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A one-shot is a sound that is triggered once per session and then disabled.
statements.explanation: A one-shot plays through once per trigger and can be triggered again.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A hum recorded with a fade-out at the end makes a good loop, since the fade hides the join.
statements.explanation: A fade-out dips the volume at each pass, so the loop pulses.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Restarting with play() from the finished handler is as seamless as the stream's built-in loop.
statements.explanation: Restarting after finished can leave a gap.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A seamless loop ends at the same level and phase at which it begins.
statements.explanation: The loop point should match in level and phase.

statements.label: E
statements.text: In Godot, whether a sound loops is set on the stream resource.
statements.explanation: Loop settings live on the stream, while the player plays what it is given.

questions.stem: A stream player cuts off its oldest voice when play() is called beyond its maximum polyphony. A 60 ms click is triggered at 0 ms, 40 ms and 80 ms on the same player. Check each statement that is true about the vocabulary.

statements.label: A
statements.text: With a polyphony of 2, the three clicks need three voices at one instant.
statements.explanation: At most two clicks overlap at an instant, so two voices suffice.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Polyphony is the number of voices a player can sound at once.
statements.explanation: Polyphony counts simultaneous voices.

statements.label: C
statements.text: With a polyphony of 1, the click at 40 ms cuts off the click that started at 0 ms.
statements.explanation: A single voice is replaced by the newest trigger.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A voice is one playing instance of a sound.
statements.explanation: A voice is one instance in progress.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Polyphony is the length of a sound.
statements.explanation: Length is duration, not polyphony.

questions.source: Audio clock, mixing block, output latency
questions.stem: A rhythm game judges a tap within 50 ms of a beat. One version sums frame delta into a song-time variable; another reads the music player's playback position. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Calling play() in the same frame as the tap makes the hit sound start exactly on the beat.
statements.explanation: Playback starts at the next mix boundary, then output latency adds delay.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The reported playback position includes device latency and is exact to the sample.
statements.explanation: The position ignores output latency and updates by block.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Judging taps against the audio clock, corrected for latency, tracks what the player hears.
statements.explanation: The audio clock is the reference the music follows.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Summed frame delta can drift away from the audio actually playing, since frame time and audio run on different clocks.
statements.explanation: Game loop and audio hardware are separate clocks.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Audio is mixed in blocks, so the reported position advances in coarse steps.
statements.explanation: Mixing happens in chunks.

questions.stem: An inverse-distance falloff lowers a sound by about 6 dB for each doubling of distance from the listener. Check each statement that is true about the terms.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Reverb is a kind of attenuation.
statements.explanation: Reverb adds reflections; attenuation lowers level.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The listener is the sound source whose level is being reduced.
statements.explanation: The listener is the receiver.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Attenuation raises a sound's level as the source moves away.
statements.explanation: Attenuation lowers the level.

statements.label: D
statements.text: An inverse law reaches zero at a finite distance, so no maximum distance setting is needed.
statements.explanation: An inverse law keeps getting smaller without reaching zero, so engines add a maximum distance.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Attenuation and falloff are two words for the loss of level with distance.
statements.explanation: Both describe distance-dependent level loss.

questions.stem: A game plays an explosion when an enemy dies. The agent made the stream player a child of the enemy, called play() and freed the enemy. Players hear nothing or a clipped pop. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Checking 'health <= 0' on each frame is the same as a death signal, since both start the sound when the enemy dies.
statements.explanation: Polling is true on each frame the condition holds and restarts the sound repeatedly.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Raising the volume fixes the problem.
statements.explanation: The sound is being destroyed, not quiet.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Freeing a node frees its children, including the stream player.
statements.explanation: Children live and die with their parent.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Playing from a node that outlives the enemy avoids the cut-off.
statements.explanation: The player needs an owner that survives the sound.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A died signal emitted once, with an audio handler responding, separates the enemy's lifetime from the sound's.
statements.explanation: A signal fires once and decouples emitter and listener.

questions.stem: Audio designers want to change footstep sounds without code edits. Gameplay code asks for a cue named 'footstep_stone', and the audio data decides which recordings play. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A cue is a bus that other sounds are routed through.
statements.explanation: A bus is a routing channel; a cue is a named sound event.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Unreal's Sound Cue is a node graph that combines and modifies sounds and is played by reference.
statements.explanation: Sound Cue fits the cue idea.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The same gameplay event can request different cues, such as stone or grass, so the cue name carries the situation.
statements.explanation: Choosing the cue name from state gives varied sounds.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A cue can choose among recordings and vary pitch or volume slightly.
statements.explanation: Variation reduces repetition.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A cue is a named request for a sound event, and its mapping to recordings can change without gameplay code changes.
statements.explanation: A cue separates what happened from which files play.

questions.source: Process mode, autoload, pause versus stop
questions.stem: In Godot, a pause menu pauses the scene tree. A developer asks an agent: 'The menu click should still sound while paused, the music should resume where it left off, and restart should reload the level.' Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A sound that survives a reload is attached to the scene being reloaded.
statements.explanation: Surviving a reload means living outside the scene, such as in an autoload.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A menu-click player plays normally while the tree is paused without a change to its process mode.
statements.explanation: A paused player needs a process mode that keeps it running.

statements.label: C
statements.text: stop() then play() resumes from where it stopped.
statements.explanation: Stop discards position; pausing the stream keeps it.

statements.label: D
statements.text: After a scene reload, music players from the old scene keep playing from their position.
statements.explanation: Reloading frees the old players and creates new ones.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A stream player in its default process mode pauses with the tree and resumes after.
statements.explanation: Audio nodes follow the tree's pause.

questions.source: Bus effect versus attenuation; enter and exit
questions.stem: A cave region adds reverb to the SFX bus from the cave trigger's enter event and removes it on the exit event. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The reverb also colours the Music bus.
statements.explanation: Only sounds routed through SFX are processed.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Enter and exit events are paired, and a missed exit can leave the reverb on.
statements.explanation: A toggle driven by two events is correct only if both arrive.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Reverb on a bus is the same as positional attenuation.
statements.explanation: Reverb adds reflections; attenuation lowers level with distance.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The reverb applies to sound effects routed through the SFX bus, including ones from far outside the cave.
statements.explanation: A bus effect is not positional.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The cave trigger blocks the player, or its exit event will not fire.
statements.explanation: A trigger reports enter and exit without blocking.

questions.stem: A developer moves between engines and gives an agent the engine's term for each audio idea. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: In Unity, an AudioClip is the imported sound and an AudioSource is the component that plays it.
statements.explanation: Unity separates the asset from the playing component.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Unity's AudioListener acts like a microphone, and a scene works with one.
statements.explanation: The listener is the receiver.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Unity's Audio Mixer groups play the role that buses play in Godot.
statements.explanation: Mixer groups route, set level and add effects like buses.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Unreal's Play Sound at Location does not follow an actor, so a moving enemy needs an attached audio component.
statements.explanation: An attached component travels with the actor.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Unreal's Play Sound 2D applies distance attenuation, so it suits sounds that belong in the world.
statements.explanation: Play Sound 2D plays without attenuation, for interface sounds.

questions.source: Rewriting an audio prompt with exact terms
questions.stem: A developer rewrites 'Add a click sound when the button is pressed' as a precise instruction. Check each statement that is true about wording that fits.

statements.label: A
statements.text: 'Play a short non-looping stream on a non-positional player' names the sound type and player.
statements.explanation: A one-shot on a non-positional player suits an interface sound.

statements.label: B
statements.text: 'The playing flag is true' proves the click is audible.
statements.explanation: The flag does not show routing or audibility.

statements.label: C
statements.text: 'Set the level in dB relative to the music and say what happens on rapid presses' fills gaps in the original.
statements.explanation: Level and overlap behaviour are left open by the original.

statements.label: D
statements.text: 'Connect the pressed signal to a handler that calls play()' names the trigger.
statements.explanation: Signal, handler and play() describe the wiring.

statements.label: E
statements.text: 'Route it to the SFX bus, which sends to Master' names the bus.
statements.explanation: The bus decides level, mute and effects.

questions.stem: A coin should chime and vanish when touched while the player passes through, and a closed door should thud and stop the player. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The coin is a trigger and its chime starts from the enter event.
statements.explanation: A trigger reports overlap without blocking.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Game logic receives the event and calls the audio player.
statements.explanation: Audio does not decide when to play.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A stay callback restarts the sound on each physics step while the player stands in the zone.
statements.explanation: Stay fires continuously, so the retrigger buzzes.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The chime player should be a child of the coin.
statements.explanation: Freeing the coin would cut the chime off.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The door should be a trigger, so the player passes through while the thud plays.
statements.explanation: A door that stops the player is a solid collider, with the thud on a contact event.

questions.stem: A game has music, effects and voice buses. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A bus is a channel with its own level, mute and effects whose output goes to a parent bus.
statements.explanation: Buses are mixing and routing channels.

statements.label: B
statements.text: On a single bus, music and effects are hard to balance independently.
statements.explanation: Separate control needs separate buses.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The master bus is the bus for music.
statements.explanation: Master receives the whole mix.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A linear slider value is converted to dB before being applied.
statements.explanation: Decibels are logarithmic.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Ducking lowers the music level for good.
statements.explanation: Ducking is temporary and restores itself.

questions.stem: A developer tells an agent: 'Make the robot's footsteps 3D.' Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Music and the menu click suit positional players too.
statements.explanation: They have no place in the world.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The positional player should be attached to the robot so it moves with it.
statements.explanation: A positional source follows its node.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The listener stands in for the player's ears and is typically the active camera.
statements.explanation: Level and pan are computed relative to the listener.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Attenuation lowers the level with distance, optionally to a maximum distance.
statements.explanation: Distance sets loudness, and a maximum distance cuts the sound off.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The listener should be attached to the robot.
statements.explanation: The listener belongs to the player's view.

questions.stem: A rhythm game compares taps with the music. Check each statement that is true.
