statements.label: A
statements.text: Frame time and audio hardware run on the same clock.
statements.explanation: They are separate clocks.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A test with no sound device proves the sound lines up with the beat as heard.
statements.explanation: Lining up as heard needs a person with speakers.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A sound begins the instant play() is called.
statements.explanation: Playback begins at the next mix boundary.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Output latency is the delay between a sample being mixed and being heard.
statements.explanation: That delay is output latency.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Latency should be compensated or made adjustable.
statements.explanation: Judgment should match what the player hears.

questions.stem: A test asserts that a stream player's playing property is true right after the hit event and prints PASS. A reviewer says it proves little. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Measuring the signal on the bus is stronger than reading a flag.
statements.explanation: A measurement shows signal and level.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A negative case, where a miss stays silent, strengthens the test.
statements.explanation: A miss that stays silent shows the trigger discriminates.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The flag shows that the event reached the handler and play() was called.
statements.explanation: The trigger path is wired.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Audibility and balance against the music are judged by a person on real hardware.
statements.explanation: Audibility needs a listener.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The flag shows which bus the sound reached.
statements.explanation: The flag says nothing about routing.

questions.stem: A shooter needs a rapid gunshot (10 per second, 0.5 s tail), a rain ambience for the whole level and a horn that honks while a key is held. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A polyphony limit needs no rule about which voice to drop.
statements.explanation: When the voices are full, a policy such as dropping the oldest or quietest is chosen.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The gunshot is a looping sound because it repeats ten times a second.
statements.explanation: Each gunshot is a one-shot; repetition comes from triggers.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The horn can be a loop that starts on key down and stops on key up.
statements.explanation: A held honk fits a loop gated by the key.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A single-voice player cuts off the oldest sound when triggered again, chopping gunshot tails.
statements.explanation: Retriggering a single voice cuts the tail.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The rain is a looping ambience whose loop points are seamless.
statements.explanation: A seam click or gap is audible if the loop points do not match.

questions.source: Frame time, frame budget, FPS, refresh rate
questions.stem: A team talks about speed using the terms frame time, frame budget, FPS and refresh rate. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A larger frame budget goes with a higher target frame rate.
statements.explanation: A higher target rate leaves less time per frame, so the budget gets smaller.

statements.label: B
statements.text: FPS and frame time are reciprocals, so losing the same number of FPS costs more milliseconds at a low frame rate than at a high one.
statements.explanation: Because FPS is the reciprocal of frame time, equal FPS drops are not equal millisecond costs.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Frame time is the duration of one frame, measured in milliseconds.
statements.explanation: Frame time is the time one frame takes, usually given in milliseconds.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Refresh rate is the number of frames the GPU renders each second.
statements.explanation: Refresh rate is how often the display updates, not how often the GPU renders.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A frame budget is the longest frame time that still meets the target frame rate, about 16.7 ms at 60 Hz.
statements.explanation: The budget is 1000 divided by the target rate, so 60 Hz gives about 16.7 ms.

questions.source: Hitch, stutter, mean versus percentile frame time
questions.stem: A capture shows most frames finishing quickly but a few frames taking much longer. Check each statement that is true about the terms used to describe it.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Stutter is the name for a high average frame rate.
statements.explanation: Stutter is uneven frame delivery that the player can see, not a high frame rate.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A hitch is a single frame that takes much longer than the frames around it.
statements.explanation: A hitch is one long frame among shorter ones.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A frame-time graph shows a hitch as a spike above the budget line.
statements.explanation: Plotting frame time per frame makes a hitch appear as a spike.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The mean frame time is the best number for exposing hitches, because slow frames dominate it.
statements.explanation: A mean is pulled very little by a few slow frames, so it hides hitches.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The 99th percentile frame time is the value that 99 percent of frames stay at or below, so it exposes rare slow frames.
statements.explanation: A high percentile reports the slow end of the distribution that an average hides.

questions.stem: A game takes 22 ms per frame on the target phone. Lowering the render resolution does not change frame time. Check each statement that is true about the terms involved.

statements.label: A
statements.text: An unchanged frame time after lowering resolution suggests the frame is not fill-rate bound.
statements.explanation: If fewer pixels did not help, pixel shading was not the limit.

statements.label: B
statements.text: GPU-bound means GPU work such as shading sets the length of the frame.
statements.explanation: A GPU-bound frame waits on rendering work.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Lowering resolution reduces pixel work, so it helps a frame that is limited by fill rate.
statements.explanation: Fewer pixels means less fragment work, which helps when fill rate is the limit.

statements.label: D
statements.text: CPU-bound means CPU-side work such as game logic, physics or draw-call submission sets the length of the frame.
statements.explanation: A CPU-bound frame waits on CPU work.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Fill rate is the number of draw calls the CPU can submit each second.
statements.explanation: Fill rate is how many pixels the GPU can write per second, not a CPU submission rate.

questions.source: Bottleneck, main thread, render thread, pipeline
questions.stem: A renderer runs the main thread, the render thread and the GPU as a pipeline. Check each statement that is true about bottlenecks.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Game script logic runs on the render thread.
statements.explanation: Game logic runs on the main thread; the render thread prepares and submits drawing work.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Speeding up a stage that is not the bottleneck leaves the frame time unchanged.
statements.explanation: Only improving the bottleneck shortens the frame.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The bottleneck is the stage with the longest time per frame, and it sets the pace.
statements.explanation: The slowest stage limits throughput.

statements.label: D
statements.text: In a pipeline, frame time is the sum of the times of the stages.
statements.explanation: Pipeline stages overlap in time, so the slowest one sets frame time rather than the sum.

statements.label: E
statements.text: After a bottleneck is removed, another stage can become the new bottleneck.
statements.explanation: Once the slowest stage speeds up, the next slowest becomes the limit.

questions.stem: A scene has 1,000 small props, each with its own draw call, and it is slow on the CPU. Check each statement that is true about the terms.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Draw call and triangle are two names for the same measurement.
statements.explanation: A draw call is a command; a triangle is a piece of geometry.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Triangle count and draw-call count are separate costs that can be tuned apart.
statements.explanation: A scene can have few triangles and many calls, or the reverse.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A draw call is a command from the CPU asking the GPU to draw geometry with a given mesh, material and state.
statements.explanation: A draw call submits a batch of geometry plus the state to draw it.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Draw-call cost is mostly GPU shading work.
statements.explanation: Each call costs CPU submission and validation time, not mainly shading.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A frame with many small draw calls can be CPU-bound even when the triangle count is low.
statements.explanation: Per-call overhead can dominate with many small objects.

questions.stem: A developer is choosing between batching, instancing and a texture atlas to cut draw calls. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Instancing draws many copies of one mesh and one material in a single call, with per-instance data such as transform.
statements.explanation: Per-instance data such as transform is supplied alongside the shared mesh.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Batching merges geometry that shares a material into fewer draw calls.
statements.explanation: Shared material is the condition for merging into fewer calls.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A texture atlas packs many images into one texture, so objects that show different images can share a material.
statements.explanation: An atlas lets different pictures live in one texture and one material.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Instancing draws many copies of different meshes with different materials in one call.
statements.explanation: Instances share one mesh and one material.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Giving each object its own unique material makes batching easier.
statements.explanation: Unique materials split the groups and defeat batching.

questions.stem: A developer tells a coding agent: "The grass is slow. Use instancing." The grass is 50,000 blades, each a separate scene node with its own mesh and material. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Instancing needs one shared blade mesh, one shared material and a per-instance list of transforms.
statements.explanation: Instancing needs a shared mesh and material plus per-copy data.

statements.label: B
statements.text: If the grass is slow because of overdraw, fewer draw calls will fix it.
statements.explanation: Overdraw is shading cost on the GPU, which draw-call count does not touch.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Instancing reduces the number of triangles the GPU processes for the grass.
statements.explanation: Each copy still has its triangles processed; only submission overhead falls.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The saving from instancing comes from fewer pixels being shaded.
statements.explanation: Instancing cuts draw calls, not shaded pixels.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The word instancing in the prompt also asks the agent to add level of detail and culling.
statements.explanation: Level of detail and culling are separate terms and would have to be requested.

questions.stem: A scene is slow because eight full-screen semi-transparent smoke layers are shaded for each pixel. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Overdraw is a cost on the CPU.
statements.explanation: Overdraw is shading work on the GPU.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A fragment is a candidate pixel produced by rasterization that the fragment shader processes.
statements.explanation: Each fragment is a potential pixel that gets shaded.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Merging the overlapping planes into one mesh removes the overdraw.
statements.explanation: A merged mesh still covers the same pixels the same number of times.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Fill rate is how many pixels the GPU can write per second, and stacked transparent layers strain it.
statements.explanation: Fill rate limits pixel output, and each layer adds more of it.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Overdraw is the same screen pixel being shaded more than once in a frame.
statements.explanation: Eight layers over one pixel give an overdraw factor of eight.

questions.stem: A 3D game draws a city, and the developer wants fewer objects submitted. Check each statement that is true about culling terms.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Frustum culling removes a building hidden behind a wall when the building is inside the view volume.
statements.explanation: Being inside the frustum is not the same as being visible, which is the gap occlusion culling fills.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Occlusion culling skips objects that are inside the view volume but hidden behind other geometry.
statements.explanation: Occlusion culling tests visibility against other geometry.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A culled object is not submitted, which saves the draw calls and shading work it would have caused.
statements.explanation: Culling decides what not to draw, so the culled cost disappears.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Frustum culling skips objects that lie outside the camera's view volume.
statements.explanation: The frustum is the volume the camera can see.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Backface culling discards individual triangles that face away from the camera.
statements.explanation: Backface culling works on triangles, not whole objects.

questions.stem: A character has three meshes: a detailed one for close-ups, a medium one and a simple one for the distance. Check each statement that is true about level of detail (LOD).

statements.label: A
statements.text: LOD replaces the need for culling, since distant objects cost nothing to draw.
statements.explanation: Cheap objects still cost something, so culling is a separate tool.

statements.label: B
statements.text: LOD swaps in a simpler version as the object gets farther away or smaller on screen.
statements.explanation: LOD chooses a representation by distance or screen size.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Cross-fading or tuning the switch distances can reduce popping.
statements.explanation: Blending or better thresholds hides the swap.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Popping is the visible jump when the engine switches from one LOD version to another.
statements.explanation: Popping is the visible swap between versions.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Keeping three LOD versions uses less memory than keeping the detailed mesh alone.
statements.explanation: Extra versions are extra mesh data held in memory.

questions.stem: A developer tells a coding agent: "Pool the bullets." Each shot currently creates a new bullet and destroys it on impact. Check each statement that is true about object pooling.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Acquire takes an object from the pool and release returns it.
statements.explanation: Acquire and release are the two basic pool operations.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Pooling creates objects in advance and reuses them instead of creating and destroying them.
statements.explanation: A pool trades creation and destruction for reuse.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Pool exhaustion is the situation where no free object is left when one is requested, and the code needs a policy for it.
statements.explanation: Exhaustion needs a policy such as growing, skipping the shot or recycling the oldest.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Idle pooled objects are free, taking up no memory.
statements.explanation: Pooled objects still occupy memory while they wait.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A reused pooled object needs no reset, because it was cleaned when it was created.
statements.explanation: A reused object keeps its old state, so it needs a reset such as position, velocity and timers.

questions.stem: A game written in a language with a tracing garbage collector allocates a small temporary list each frame, and players see short freezes. Check each statement that is true about the terms.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Garbage is allocated memory that is no longer referenced and waits to be reclaimed by the collector.
statements.explanation: Garbage is unreachable memory awaiting reclamation.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Pooling reduces allocation, which means less garbage for the collector.
statements.explanation: Reusing objects avoids creating short-lived garbage.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Lowering the refresh rate removes the freezes by giving the collector more time.
statements.explanation: Refresh rate does not change allocation, which is the cause.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Garbage collection manages GPU memory, so a faster GPU shortens the pauses.
statements.explanation: The collector manages CPU-side memory.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A collection pause is time the collector takes out of a frame, which shows as a hitch.
statements.explanation: The collector's work lands inside a frame as a spike.

questions.stem: A team wants to cut texture memory on a phone. Check each statement that is true about the terms.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The size of a PNG file on disk is the same as the texture's footprint in VRAM.
statements.explanation: VRAM size follows resolution and format, not the file.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A mipmap chain is a series of smaller copies of a texture used when the texture appears small on screen.
statements.explanation: Mip levels are pre-shrunk copies for distant or small use.

statements.label: C
statements.text: GPU texture compression is the same thing as saving the image as a smaller PNG.
statements.explanation: GPU compression formats stay compressed in memory; PNG is decoded before use.

statements.label: D
statements.text: VRAM is the memory of the GPU, where textures are held for sampling.
statements.explanation: VRAM is video memory.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Texture streaming loads textures or mip levels into memory as they are needed.
statements.explanation: Streaming brings in data on demand.

questions.stem: A developer compares two builds of a system with several timed runs each. Check each statement that is true about benchmarking terms.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A warm-up period is the start of a run that is discarded because shader compilation and cache filling are not steady-state cost.
statements.explanation: Start-up work is not representative, so it is dropped before measuring.

statements.label: B
statements.text: One run is enough to show a real difference between two versions.
statements.explanation: A single run cannot separate a real effect from noise.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Variance is how much results differ from run to run for the same code.
statements.explanation: Variance measures run-to-run spread.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A difference smaller than the run-to-run spread is within noise.
statements.explanation: A gap smaller than the normal spread does not show a real change.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The median is the middle value of the sorted samples.
statements.explanation: Median is the middle of the sorted values.

questions.source: Vertical sync, build type, target hardware, headroom
questions.stem: A developer reports: "A steady 60 FPS, so plenty of headroom." The display runs at 60 Hz with vertical sync on, in the editor, on a fast development PC. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A development PC counts as the target hardware if it is faster than the phone.
statements.explanation: Target hardware is the device the game ships to.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Vertical sync caps the frame rate at the refresh rate, which can hide spare time in the frame.
statements.explanation: A frame that finishes early waits for the next refresh, so FPS stays at 60.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Vertical sync makes the game's work run faster.
statements.explanation: Vertical sync waits on the display and does not speed the work.

statements.label: D
statements.text: An editor session or debug build adds overhead that a release build does not have.
statements.explanation: Tool overhead and extra checks change timings.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Headroom is the part of the frame budget that is already used.
statements.explanation: Headroom is the unused part of the budget.

questions.stem: A developer tells a coding agent: "Make the game faster." Check each statement that is a precise rewrite fragment using correct performance terms.

statements.label: A
statements.text: "Optimize the parts of the code that look slow."
statements.explanation: Looks slow is a guess, not a profiled hot spot.

statements.label: B
statements.text: "Boost FPS as much as you can."
statements.explanation: It names no target, device or measurement.

statements.label: C
statements.text: "Profile first to find whether the frame is CPU-bound or GPU-bound, then change one thing and re-measure."
statements.explanation: Naming the bottleneck type and one change at a time is exact use of the terms.

statements.label: D
statements.text: "Bring frame time to the 16.7 ms budget at 60 Hz on the target phone, measured in a release build."
statements.explanation: It gives a measurable frame-time budget, target device and build type.

statements.label: E
statements.text: "Report the 99th percentile frame time as well as the mean, after discarding a warm-up period."
statements.explanation: It names a percentile and a warm-up period.

questions.stem: A scene has 5,000 small separate objects, each with its own draw call, and the frame is CPU-bound. Check each statement that is a sensible instruction to the coding agent.

statements.label: A
statements.text: "Use instancing for the 5,000 props, each with its own mesh and material."
statements.explanation: Instancing needs one shared mesh and material.

statements.label: B
statements.text: "Batch the props that share a material to reduce draw calls."
statements.explanation: Batching merges geometry that shares a material.

statements.label: C
statements.text: "Use GPU texture compression to lower the draw-call count."
statements.explanation: Compression lowers memory, not calls.

statements.label: D
statements.text: "Add LOD meshes to lower the draw-call count."
statements.explanation: LOD cuts triangles at a distance and does not reduce calls.

statements.label: E
statements.text: "Pack the prop images into a texture atlas so the props can share one material."
statements.explanation: An atlas makes different images share a material, enabling batching.

questions.source: Premature optimization, hot spot, profiler overhead
questions.stem: A team discusses premature optimization and hot spots. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A profiler reports the fix as well as the slow part.
statements.explanation: A profiler shows data; choosing the change is the developer's work.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A detailed profiling run adds overhead, so its absolute times are inflated.
statements.explanation: Instrumentation slows the program.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A hot spot is a function or frame stage that takes a large share of the frame time.
statements.explanation: Hot spots are where time concentrates.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Premature optimization is optimizing before measurement shows a need.
statements.explanation: Optimizing without evidence may miss the real bottleneck.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Headroom is the amount by which the frame exceeds its budget.
statements.explanation: Headroom is spare budget; exceeding the budget is a miss.

questions.stem: A developer is learning to use a profiler. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A profiler records where time or memory goes during a run.
statements.explanation: Recording time and memory by function or stage is the purpose of a profiler.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A profiler reports CPU time and GPU time as the same number.
statements.explanation: CPU and GPU timings are separate readings.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A capture of one frame at a busy moment is enough for a game whose load changes during play.
statements.explanation: One frame can be unrepresentative.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A hot spot is the function that uses the least time.
statements.explanation: A hot spot is a large cost, not the smallest.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A capture should span a representative stretch of play.
statements.explanation: A representative capture avoids mistaking an outlier for the norm.

questions.stem: A game runs out of GPU memory. Check each statement that is true about the options.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Removing the mipmap chain reduces draw calls.
statements.explanation: Mipmaps affect memory and sampling, not draw calls.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A texture atlas is a lower-resolution copy used for distant objects.
statements.explanation: That describes a mip level; an atlas packs several images into one texture.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Lowering texture resolution reduces memory but loses detail.
statements.explanation: Fewer pixels means less memory and less detail.

statements.label: D
statements.text: GPU texture compression reduces bytes per pixel at some risk of visible artifacts.
statements.explanation: Compressed formats store fewer bytes per pixel and can add artifacts.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Texture streaming keeps the full set of textures resident in memory at the same time.
statements.explanation: Streaming loads data on demand rather than keeping everything resident.

questions.stem: A shooter pools its bullets. Check each statement that is true about sizing and operating the pool.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Pool size is set from peak simultaneous demand plus a margin.
statements.explanation: Peak demand sets the needed count, with margin for spikes.

statements.label: B
statements.text: An inactive pooled bullet stays visible and colliding so it is ready to use.
statements.explanation: Inactive objects are hidden with processing and collision disabled.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Pool size is set from the average number of bullets alive, with no margin.
statements.explanation: Average demand would run out at peaks.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Releasing an object back to the pool twice is harmless.
statements.explanation: A double release can put the same object in the pool twice and cause bugs.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Pooling helps little when objects are few and long-lived.
statements.explanation: Pooling saves creation cost, which is small for few long-lived objects.

questions.stem: Classify fixes by the bottleneck they address. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Reducing overdraw is a fix for a GPU-bound frame.
statements.explanation: Overdraw is GPU pixel work.

statements.label: B
statements.text: GPU texture compression is a fix for a CPU-bound frame.
statements.explanation: Compression saves memory, not CPU time.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Simplifying a pixel shader is a fix for a GPU-bound frame.
statements.explanation: A cheaper shader reduces GPU work per pixel.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Batching is a fix for CPU-side draw-call submission cost.
statements.explanation: Fewer calls means less CPU submission time.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Updating AI less often is a fix for CPU-side work.
statements.explanation: Less frequent AI updates cut CPU logic cost.

questions.stem: A developer says: "I ran it once and version B was faster, so we are switching." Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Reporting FPS alone is enough, because an average shows hitches.
statements.explanation: Averages hide hitches; percentiles reveal them.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Repeated runs let the developer report the spread.
statements.explanation: Repetition shows variance.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Comparing a release build of A with a debug build of B is a fair test.
statements.explanation: Build type changes timing, so conditions must match.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Run-to-run noise comes from things such as other processes and thermal effects.
statements.explanation: Noise sources vary between runs.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Frames from the warm-up period are representative of steady-state cost.
statements.explanation: Warm-up frames include start-up work and are discarded.

questions.stem: A game targets 60 Hz and takes 12 ms per frame. A teammate wants a complex rewrite to save an estimated 0.2 ms. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The game is over budget.
statements.explanation: 12 ms is under 16.7 ms.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A game that is within budget is GPU-bound by definition.
statements.explanation: Being within budget says nothing about CPU or GPU limits.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The estimated saving should be confirmed by measurement before counting.
statements.explanation: An estimate is not a measurement.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The headroom is the unused part of the 16.7 ms budget, about 4.7 ms.
statements.explanation: Headroom is budget minus frame time.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The rewrite targets a confirmed hot spot.
statements.explanation: A hot spot needs profile evidence.

questions.stem: A developer asks a coding agent to build a guard non-player character (NPC) as a finite state machine (FSM) instead of nested if statements. Check each statement that is true about the terms.

statements.label: A
statements.text: An FSM has a defined set of states, one of which is the current state.
statements.explanation: A finite state machine has states and one current state at a time.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A transition is a rule for moving from one state to another.
statements.explanation: Transitions are the rules that connect states.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Ordered child nodes that are re-evaluated from a root describe an FSM.
statements.explanation: Ordered children ticked from a root describe a behavior tree.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A guard stuck in Search is often missing a transition out of that state.
statements.explanation: A missing or unreachable exit leaves the NPC stuck in that state.

statements.label: E
statements.text: An FSM lets the guard be in the Chase state and the Patrol state at the same time.
statements.explanation: An FSM has one current state, so blending needs a different design.

questions.source: FSM transitions versus behavior tree priority
questions.stem: A designer wants to add a Flee state that the guard can enter when hurt. Check each statement that is true about where the logic lives.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A transition table is a list of nodes that are ticked from the root.
statements.explanation: A transition table lists which states lead to which, with conditions.

statements.label: B
statements.text: In an FSM, transitions are edges between states, and their number can grow quickly as states are added.
statements.explanation: Each state that can lead to another needs its own edge.

statements.label: C
statements.text: In an FSM, adding Flee needs edits to the new state alone, because existing states need no way of reaching it.
statements.explanation: Existing states need a new exit edge into Flee.

statements.label: D
statements.text: In a behavior tree, "flee when hurt" can be one new high-priority branch.
statements.explanation: A priority branch checked first avoids adding edges to the other behaviors.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A behavior tree stores its logic as edges between states.
statements.explanation: A behavior tree has no state-to-state edges; its logic is in node order and type.

questions.source: Behavior tree: tick, selector, sequence, status
questions.stem: A guard's behavior tree has a root selector with children: a sequence of CanSeePlayer then Chase, a sequence of HasLastKnownPosition then Search, and Patrol. Check each statement that is true about the terms.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A tick is one evaluation pass of the tree starting at the root.
statements.explanation: Each tick walks the tree from the root.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A selector tries its children in order and stops at the first child that does not fail.
statements.explanation: A selector looks for the first child that works or is still in progress.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Nodes report one of success, failure or running.
statements.explanation: Success, failure and running are the three results.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A sequence returns success as soon as its first child succeeds.
statements.explanation: A sequence needs its children to succeed in turn; it stops at the first child that does not succeed.

statements.label: E
statements.text: RUNNING means the node has failed.
statements.explanation: RUNNING means the node is still in progress and has not finished.

questions.source: FSM, behavior tree, utility AI, GOAP
questions.stem: A studio is choosing a decision architecture for its NPCs. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: In GOAP the designer writes the fixed order of actions for each goal.
statements.explanation: GOAP's planner finds the sequence; the designer supplies actions and goals.

statements.label: B
statements.text: In a behavior tree, priority comes from the order of child nodes.
statements.explanation: Earlier children are tried first.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A finite state machine is ticked from a root node so higher-priority behaviors pre-empt lower ones.
statements.explanation: Root ticking with ordered priority describes a behavior tree.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Utility AI scores candidate actions from numeric considerations and picks the highest score.
statements.explanation: Utility AI chooses by score.

statements.label: E
statements.text: GOAP describes actions by preconditions and effects, and a planner searches for a sequence that reaches a goal.
statements.explanation: Preconditions, effects and a search are what define GOAP.

questions.stem: A developer wants to tell a coding agent how a guard patrols, chases and searches. Check each statement that is a precise instruction using the correct terms.

statements.label: A
statements.text: "Go from Chase to Search when the player is lost for a while."
statements.explanation: Lost and a while are undefined, so no test can check them.

statements.label: B
statements.text: "Use machine learning so the guard learns to catch the player and will not get stuck."
statements.explanation: It names no states or conditions and promises an outcome that cannot be checked.

statements.label: C
statements.text: "Make the guard intelligent and believable."
statements.explanation: It names no structure, states or conditions.

statements.label: D
statements.text: "Build a finite state machine with states Patrol, Chase and Search, and a table of transitions with their conditions."
statements.explanation: It names the architecture, the states and the transition conditions.

statements.label: E
statements.text: "Expose the current state name as a readable property so a test can read it."
statements.explanation: A readable state name gives a test hook.

questions.stem: A guard enters Chase when the player is within a radius, and leaves Chase at a larger radius. Check each statement that is true about the terms.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Hysteresis is meant to make the guard move faster.
statements.explanation: Its purpose is to stop flicker, not to change speed.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Flicker is rapid switching between two states near a boundary.
statements.explanation: Flicker is the unwanted rapid state change.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Using one radius for both entering and leaving Chase invites flicker when the player stays near the edge.
statements.explanation: A player hovering at the boundary toggles the state each decision.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Hysteresis means the NPC remembers the last known position of the player.
statements.explanation: Remembering a position is memory, often held in a blackboard.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Hysteresis uses different thresholds for entering and leaving a state.
statements.explanation: Separate enter and exit thresholds define hysteresis.

questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about steering behaviors and pathfinding.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Pursue steers toward where a moving target will be, not where it is now.
statements.explanation: Pursue predicts the target's position.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Arrive is seek that slows down near the target so the NPC stops on it.
statements.explanation: Arrive reduces speed inside a slowing radius.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Flee steers toward the target.
statements.explanation: Flee steers away from the target.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Pathfinding computes a route as a list of points, and steering turns it into per-frame motion by adjusting velocity.
statements.explanation: Pathfinding is global planning; steering is local, per-frame motion.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Seek knows the level layout, so it routes around walls.
statements.explanation: Seek heads straight at the target and has no knowledge of walls.

questions.stem: A flock of birds follows three local rules with no code describing the flock's shape. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Emergent behavior means the AI is defective.
statements.explanation: Emergence is often the goal, as with flocks and crowds.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Separation steers a bird away from very close neighbors.
statements.explanation: Separation avoids crowding.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Emergent behavior is a global pattern that arises from local rules and is not coded directly.
statements.explanation: The flock shape emerges from simple interactions.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Alignment steers a bird toward the average position of nearby neighbors.
statements.explanation: Alignment matches heading, not position.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Cohesion steers a bird toward the average position of nearby neighbors.
statements.explanation: Cohesion pulls birds toward the local center.

questions.source: Grid, A*, navigation mesh, baking, agent radius
questions.stem: A developer needs enemies to navigate a level with walls and furniture. Check each statement that is true about grids, A* and navigation meshes.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A grid and a navigation mesh are two ways to represent walkable space, and A* is a search algorithm that can run on either.
statements.explanation: Grid and navmesh describe space; A* searches over a graph built from either.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A larger agent radius widens the walkable area of the navigation mesh.
statements.explanation: A larger radius shrinks the walkable area.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A* is a representation of walkable space, like a grid.
statements.explanation: A* is an algorithm, not a data structure for the world.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A navigation mesh covers walkable surface with polygons, so open floor needs fewer nodes than a grid.
statements.explanation: A grid stores one node per cell, while polygons cover open floor cheaply.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A navigation mesh is baked from level geometry and agent size, so it goes stale when static geometry changes.
statements.explanation: Baking happens from geometry, so changes need a rebake.

questions.source: A*, f, g, h, admissible heuristic
questions.stem: A* picks nodes by f = g + h. Check each statement that is true about the terms.

statements.label: A
statements.text: An admissible heuristic lets A* return a shortest path.
statements.explanation: With no overestimate, A* cannot skip the best route.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Manhattan distance is admissible on a grid with 4-direction movement.
statements.explanation: With 4-direction moves, Manhattan distance equals the true cost without obstacles.

statements.label: C
statements.text: An admissible heuristic overestimates the true remaining cost.
statements.explanation: Admissible means the heuristic does not overestimate.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Setting h to zero makes A* order nodes by cost so far, like Dijkstra's algorithm.
statements.explanation: With h = 0, f equals g.

statements.label: E
statements.text: g is the cost so far and h is the heuristic estimate of the remaining cost.
statements.explanation: f combines the cost so far and the estimate.

questions.stem: In Godot, a developer tells a coding agent: "Use a NavigationAgent2D so the enemy walks to the player." Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The navigation agent moves its parent body along the path by itself.
statements.explanation: The agent does not move the body.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The next path position is queried once when the target is set and needs no update afterward.
statements.explanation: The next path position changes as the body moves, so it is queried each physics frame.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Navigation data is synchronised a step after it is added, so a path requested in the same frame the level is built can be empty.
statements.explanation: The navigation system applies changes after a physics step.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Having a computed path means the enemy has arrived.
statements.explanation: A path is a plan; arrival depends on the body reaching the target.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The navigation agent computes the path, and the body's movement code follows the next path position.
statements.explanation: The agent supplies the path; the body does the moving.

questions.source: Perception: range, cone, line of sight
questions.stem: A guard's sight uses a range, a field-of-view cone and a line-of-sight test. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A line-of-sight test, such as a raycast, checks whether obstacles block the view.
statements.explanation: A raycast tests for blockers.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Field of view is the distance at which the guard can see.
statements.explanation: Field of view is an angle, not a distance.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A cone check can compare the dot product of facing and direction-to-target with the cosine of the half-angle.
statements.explanation: A larger dot product means the target is within the half-angle.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Range and cone checks also handle walls.
statements.explanation: Range and angle ignore obstacles.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Sight range limits how far the guard can see.
statements.explanation: Range is the distance limit.

questions.stem: A guard hears a bottle break out of sight and goes to the sound's position, stored in a blackboard entry. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A blackboard is shared memory that nodes read and write.
statements.explanation: A blackboard shares facts between nodes.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Hearing is usually modelled as an event with a position and loudness.
statements.explanation: A noise event carries a location and loudness.

statements.label: C
statements.text: An NPC that reads the player's position directly is omniscient.
statements.explanation: Omniscient means knowing the player's position without perceiving it.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A stored noise position should expire or be cleared once it has been checked.
statements.explanation: Knowledge goes stale, so it should be cleared.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The blackboard is the logic that decides whether the guard searches or patrols.
statements.explanation: The blackboard stores data; states or the tree hold the logic.

questions.stem: A developer asks an agent for "random terrain" and gets static-looking heights. Check each statement that is true about noise.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Adding octaves smooths the terrain by removing detail.
statements.explanation: More octaves add detail rather than smoothing.

statements.label: B
statements.text: White noise returns similar values for nearby coordinates.
statements.explanation: White noise has no relation between neighbors, which is why it looks like static.

statements.label: C
statements.text: An octave is a layer of noise at higher frequency and lower amplitude that adds finer detail.
statements.explanation: Octaves layer finer detail over broad shapes.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Coherent noise gives a different value each time the same coordinate is sampled.
statements.explanation: Noise is a deterministic function of coordinate and seed.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Coherent noise needs a separate seed for each coordinate.
statements.explanation: One seed defines the whole noise field.

questions.stem: A level generator should produce the same level whenever it is given seed 7. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Adding a random call for decorations before the layout code leaves the layout unchanged.
statements.explanation: An extra draw shifts the later values.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A seed makes the output unpredictable.
statements.explanation: A seed makes output repeatable.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A seed fixes a pseudo-random sequence, so the same seed and algorithm give the same level.
statements.explanation: Pseudo-random output is deterministic given its seed.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A seed gives the same level across engine updates even if the engine changes its generator.
statements.explanation: A changed generator algorithm changes the sequence.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Seeding from the clock keeps levels reproducible.
statements.explanation: A clock-based seed differs each run.

questions.source: Validator, generate-and-test, constructive generation, safety margin
questions.stem: A platform generator sometimes makes gaps wider than the player's jump. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Constructive generation builds within the player's limits, so an impossible gap is not representable.
statements.explanation: Limits applied during building prevent bad gaps.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A validator proves that a level is fun.
statements.explanation: A validator only checks rules in a model of the game.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A safety margin keeps gaps below the exact measured jump limit.
statements.explanation: A margin guards against frame-perfect jumps.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Generate-and-test rejects failing levels and re-rolls them.
statements.explanation: Generate-and-test discards failures.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A validator checks reachability against the measured jump limits.
statements.explanation: Reachability is a playability rule.

questions.stem: A team trains an NPC with reinforcement learning (RL) to cross a grid and reach a goal. Check each statement that is true about the terms.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The environment is the NPC that acts.
statements.explanation: The agent is the NPC that acts.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Reward is the agent's current location.
statements.explanation: Reward is a numeric feedback signal; location is state.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Training uses a labeled dataset of correct moves.
statements.explanation: RL learns from reward by trial and error.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The agent is the grid world and its rules.
statements.explanation: The grid world and rules are the environment.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The policy maps what the agent observes to the action it takes.
statements.explanation: A policy is the decision rule.

questions.source: Return, discount factor, learning rate, Q-learning
questions.stem: An RL agent collects rewards over several steps. Check each statement that is true about return and Q-learning.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The learning rate sets how far Q moves toward the target in an update.
statements.explanation: The learning rate scales the step toward the target.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A Q-learning update needs labeled correct moves.
statements.explanation: Q-learning learns from reward and next-state values, not labels.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Return is the sum of the rewards over steps, each weighted by a discount.
statements.explanation: Return is the discounted sum of rewards.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A discount factor below 1 values a distant reward less than an immediate one.
statements.explanation: Discounting shrinks later rewards.

statements.label: E
statements.text: With a discount factor of 0, the agent values a distant reward as much as an immediate one.
statements.explanation: With a discount of 0, only the immediate reward counts.

questions.source: Sparse reward, reward hacking, reward shaping, training versus deployment
questions.stem: A designer discusses reward design and deployment of an RL NPC. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A sparse reward is feedback that arrives rarely, which makes learning hard.
statements.explanation: Rare reward gives little signal.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A trained policy is expected to keep learning during play by default.
statements.explanation: A trained policy typically runs as a fixed decision function.

statements.label: C
statements.text: RL lets designers directly author each behavior.
statements.explanation: Behavior is learned, so it is hard to author or debug directly.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Reward shaping removes the need to inspect the trained behavior.
statements.explanation: Shaping adds guiding rewards; the result still has to be inspected.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Reward hacking is an agent exploiting a loophole that scores well without doing what the designer meant.
statements.explanation: The agent optimizes the score, not the intent.

questions.stem: A developer tells a coding agent: "Add enemy AI." Check each statement that is a precise rewrite using the correct terms.

statements.label: A
statements.text: "Use a sight range and a line-of-sight raycast that walls can block."
statements.explanation: It names the range and an obstacle-aware check.

statements.label: B
statements.text: "Make the AI smart."
statements.explanation: Smart names no mechanism.

statements.label: C
statements.text: "Use pathfinding on a navigation mesh with steering, so the guard goes around walls."
statements.explanation: It names pathfinding, the representation and steering.

statements.label: D
statements.text: "Leave Chase at a larger radius than the radius used to enter it, so the guard does not flicker."
statements.explanation: It names hysteresis in effect.

statements.label: E
statements.text: "Move the guard toward the player each frame."
statements.explanation: Moving straight at the target ignores walls.

questions.stem: A game has a door guard, a boss with several interruptible phases and attacks, and a villager balancing hunger, tiredness and work. Check each statement that is a sound match of architecture to NPC.

statements.label: A
statements.text: An FSM suits the door guard, which has a few distinct modes.
statements.explanation: A few distinct modes fit states.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Utility AI suits the villager, whose competing needs are continuous.
statements.explanation: Scoring suits continuous needs.

statements.label: C
statements.text: An FSM is best for choosing among continuous competing needs.
statements.explanation: FSMs switch between discrete modes, not weighted needs.

statements.label: D
statements.text: GOAP picks the action with the highest numeric score.
statements.explanation: That describes utility AI; GOAP plans a sequence.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A behavior tree suits the boss, with priority branches that interrupt one another.
statements.explanation: Ordered priority supports interruption.

questions.source: Waypoint, local avoidance, unreachable target, stale navmesh
questions.stem: An enemy walks into the first wall when told to move toward the player each frame. Check each statement that is true about pathfinding terms.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Local avoidance is steering that reacts to nearby moving objects.
statements.explanation: Steering handles local, moving things.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A larger agent radius lets the agent through narrower passages.
statements.explanation: A larger radius blocks narrow passages.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A waypoint is a check of whether the player is visible.
statements.explanation: A waypoint is a point along a path.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A stale navigation mesh still gives correct paths after geometry changes.
statements.explanation: A stale mesh no longer matches the level.

statements.label: E
statements.text: An unreachable target is a case where pathfinding returns no path and the code has to handle it.
statements.explanation: A missing path is a case to handle.

questions.stem: A designer wants a crowd of 100 pedestrians that walk to destinations and avoid bumping into each other. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Emergent crowd results can be guaranteed without simulation.
statements.explanation: Emergent results depend on conditions and need testing.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Weights are tuned to balance the combined behaviors.
statements.explanation: Weights set the balance.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Pathfinding handles the reaction to other moving pedestrians.
statements.explanation: Pathfinding gives the global route; steering reacts locally.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Obstacle avoidance steers toward the nearest obstacle.
statements.explanation: Obstacle avoidance steers away from obstacles.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Several steering outputs can be combined as a weighted sum.
statements.explanation: Weighted sums combine steering outputs.

questions.stem: A developer says: "Our level generator is random, so we cannot test it." Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A random generator is untestable by definition.
statements.explanation: Fixed seeds and validators make it testable.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Fixing the seed makes the generated output reproducible for tests.
statements.explanation: A fixed seed repeats the output.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A validator passing means the level fits a model of the rules, not that it is fun.
statements.explanation: The validator checks rules only.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Playtests are still needed alongside a validator.
statements.explanation: Human play checks what the model misses.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A pseudo-random generator is deterministic given its seed.
statements.explanation: Determinism follows from the seed.

questions.stem: A director describes camera moves to a coding agent, and the agent builds exactly the move that the word names. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A roll spins the camera around the direction it is looking, which tips the horizon.
statements.explanation: A roll rotates about the viewing direction, so the horizon line tilts.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A tilt turns the camera left or right on the spot, without changing where the camera is.
statements.explanation: Left and right rotation is a pan; a tilt is up and down.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A pan turns the camera up or down on the spot, without changing where the camera is.
statements.explanation: Up and down rotation is a tilt; a pan is left and right.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A tilt lifts the camera straight up on a crane while it keeps facing the same way.
statements.explanation: Moving the camera body straight up or down is a pedestal (or crane move); a tilt is only a rotation.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A pan moves the camera sideways through the scene while it keeps facing the same way.
statements.explanation: Sideways movement of the camera body is a truck, not a pan.

questions.stem: A level designer wants the camera to change position, not just direction. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A dolly moves the camera forward or backward along the direction it is facing.
statements.explanation: Dolly in and dolly out are movements along the view direction.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A dolly turns the camera to the left or right without moving its position.
statements.explanation: Turning on the spot is a pan.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A truck is a change of lens focal length that makes the subject look closer.
statements.explanation: A change of focal length is a zoom, and nothing about it moves the camera body.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A truck moves the camera left or right while it keeps facing the same way.
statements.explanation: Truck left and truck right are sideways movements of the camera body.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A pedestal moves the camera left or right while it keeps facing the same way.
statements.explanation: Left and right movement of the camera body is a truck; a pedestal is up or down.

questions.stem: A developer asks for a "zoom" on a boss reveal and gets a different feel than expected. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A zoom changes the field of view or focal length while the camera stays where it is.
statements.explanation: A zoom is a lens change, so the camera body does not move.

statements.label: B
statements.text: When the camera dollies toward a subject, nearby and distant objects shift against each other (parallax); a zoom does not produce that shift.
statements.explanation: A dolly changes the camera's position, so objects at different depths move differently on screen; a zoom just magnifies the same view.

statements.label: C
statements.text: In an engine, changing the camera's field-of-view value is a dolly, not a zoom.
statements.explanation: Field of view is the lens angle, so editing it is a zoom; a dolly moves the camera body.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A zoom in and a dolly in give the same perspective because both make the subject larger on screen.
statements.explanation: The subject grows in both cases, but the relationship between near and far objects differs.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Moving the camera node closer to the subject changes its field of view.
statements.explanation: Position and field of view are separate camera properties.

questions.stem: A game prompt says "make the camera follow the player". Check each statement that is true about the terms involved.

statements.label: A
statements.text: An orbit moves the camera around a subject along a curved path while the subject stays framed.
statements.explanation: In an orbit the camera body travels around the subject.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Smoothing (damping) on a follow camera makes it jump straight onto the target in a single frame.
statements.explanation: Smoothing spreads the catch-up over time, so the camera trails slightly instead of jumping.

statements.label: C
statements.text: An orbit and a pan are the same move, because both rotate the camera.
statements.explanation: A pan turns the camera in place; an orbit changes the camera position.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A follow camera and a camera that stays in one place and only turns to face the target are the same thing.
statements.explanation: A camera that only turns toward a target is a look-at (or fixed tracking) camera; a follow camera also changes position.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A follow camera keeps tracking a moving target, usually with some smoothing.
statements.explanation: A follow camera moves with its target; smoothing softens the motion.

questions.stem: A 2D platformer camera needs tuning words an agent can act on. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Screen shake is a constant sideways offset that leaves the camera shifted after the impact.
statements.explanation: Shake is brief and fades back to zero, so the camera returns to its normal framing.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A deadzone is the screen area where the engine skips drawing objects.
statements.explanation: A deadzone concerns camera movement, not drawing.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Look-ahead shifts the framing behind the player so more of the ground already crossed is visible.
statements.explanation: That would be the opposite of look-ahead.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A deadzone is a region around the screen centre where the target can move without the camera moving.
statements.explanation: Inside the deadzone the camera holds still; leaving it makes the camera move.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Look-ahead shifts the framing in the direction of travel so the player sees more of what is coming.
statements.explanation: Look-ahead leads the target in its direction of travel.

questions.stem: A designer describes a camera behaviour in plain words and a student must name it. Check each statement in which the name fits the description.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Calling it a pan fits "the camera moves closer to the hero through the crowd".
statements.explanation: Moving closer is a dolly in.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Calling it an orbit fits "the camera swings around the hero while the hero stays in the centre of the frame".
statements.explanation: Travelling around a subject while keeping it framed is an orbit.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Calling it a dolly fits "the lens narrows so the hero fills the frame while the camera stays still".
statements.explanation: A lens change with no camera movement is a zoom.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Calling it a truck fits "the camera glides sideways along the street while still facing the same way".
statements.explanation: Sideways camera movement is a truck.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Calling it a tilt fits "the camera swings up from the hero's boots to her face without changing position".
statements.explanation: Up or down rotation without moving is a tilt.

questions.source: Spot the wrong word in a camera prompt
questions.stem: A student types this to a coding agent: "Pan the camera 5 metres closer to the player, then zoom out by moving the camera back." Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: "Zoom out by moving the camera back" mixes terms; moving the camera backward is a dolly out.
statements.explanation: A true zoom out widens the lens and leaves the camera where it is.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The prompt is precise because it states a distance.
statements.explanation: A distance does not repair wrong move names, so the agent could build the wrong move.

statements.label: C
statements.text: "Pan" is correct because the camera changes position.
statements.explanation: A pan does not change position.

statements.label: D
statements.text: "Pan" is the wrong word for moving 5 metres closer; the move is a dolly in.
statements.explanation: A pan is a rotation; moving along the view direction is a dolly.

statements.label: E
statements.text: "Zoom out" is correct whenever the camera node's position changes.
statements.explanation: Position changes are dollies, trucks or pedestals; a zoom is a lens change.

questions.stem: A vague prompt reads "make the camera feel more alive when the player gets hit". Check each rewrite that uses the exact camera jargon correctly to ask for a sensible hit effect.

statements.label: A
statements.text: "Add a deadzone around the player when hit so the camera freezes in place."
statements.explanation: A deadzone is a framing region for following; it does not freeze the camera on an event.

statements.label: B
statements.text: "Truck the camera up and down on hit so it looks up at the player."
statements.explanation: Up and down movement is a pedestal, and looking up is a tilt; a truck is sideways.

statements.label: C
statements.text: "On hit, briefly reduce the field of view by a few degrees (a quick zoom in), then ease it back."
statements.explanation: A field-of-view punch is a valid zoom effect and is described with exact terms.

statements.label: D
statements.text: "Add screen shake on hit: 0.2 seconds, small random offset of the camera position, with the amplitude decaying to zero."
statements.explanation: This names the effect, its duration, what moves and how it fades.

statements.label: E
statements.text: "Dolly the lens narrower when hit."
statements.explanation: A dolly moves the camera body; a narrower lens is a zoom.

questions.stem: An agent is asked to make a follow camera "less jerky". Check each statement that is true about the settings it may adjust.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A wider deadzone makes the camera react to small movements sooner.
statements.explanation: A wider deadzone makes the camera ignore more small movement.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A higher smoothing (damping) speed makes the camera catch up to the target more slowly.
statements.explanation: A higher smoothing speed closes the gap faster.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A larger look-ahead distance shifts the framing farther in the direction of travel.
statements.explanation: Look-ahead distance is the size of that forward shift.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A camera that follows a physics body is not affected by whether the camera and the body update on the same tick.
statements.explanation: Mismatched update rates between the body and the camera are a common cause of visible jitter.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Turning smoothing on makes the camera snap onto the target instantly.
statements.explanation: Smoothing spreads the move over time; instant snapping is the absence of smoothing.

questions.source: Projection, field of view and camera limits
questions.stem: A student must tell an agent which projection and lens words apply. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Field of view is the distance between the camera and its subject.
statements.explanation: Field of view is an angle, not a distance.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A wider field of view shows more of the scene and exaggerates perspective.
statements.explanation: A wide lens fits more in view and makes depth differences look stronger.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Camera limits (bounds) keep the camera from showing space outside the level.
statements.explanation: Limits clamp the camera position so the level edge stays off screen.

statements.label: D
statements.text: In a perspective camera, objects farther away look smaller.
statements.explanation: Perspective projection shrinks distant objects.

statements.label: E
statements.text: In an orthographic camera, an object's size on screen does not depend on its distance.
statements.explanation: Orthographic projection has no foreshortening with distance.

questions.stem: A student describes how a door should open to a coding agent. Check each statement that is true about the terms.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Easing changes the final value that the animation ends on.
statements.explanation: Easing leaves the start and end values alone.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A keyframe is a stored value (such as a rotation) at a specific moment on the timeline.
statements.explanation: Keyframes are the authored anchor values.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Interpolation is the calculation of the in-between values between two keyframes.
statements.explanation: The engine fills the gaps between keyframes by interpolating.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A keyframe is the computed in-between frame that the engine draws between two poses.
statements.explanation: In-betweens are produced by interpolation; they are not keyframes.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Easing changes the frame rate at which the engine draws the scene.
statements.explanation: Easing shapes the speed curve of one animated value; it does not change how often frames are drawn.

questions.stem: A designer asks for a button that "eases in" or "eases out" when it appears. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Ease-in starts slowly and speeds up.
statements.explanation: Ease-in accelerates from rest.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Linear interpolation changes the value at a constant rate.
statements.explanation: Linear means a straight line from start to end.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Ease-out starts quickly and slows down toward the end.
statements.explanation: Ease-out decelerates into the final value.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Ease-in-out is slow at both the start and the end, and quicker in the middle.
statements.explanation: Ease-in-out combines both.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Ease-out means the animation plays backward after it finishes.
statements.explanation: Direction of playback is a separate setting from easing.

questions.stem: A developer wants a UI panel to slide in using code instead of an authored clip. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A tween is the better tool for a short one-off effect, such as a pop-up scaling in.
statements.explanation: Quick procedural effects are a good fit for tweens.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A tween needs a rig before it can move a node.
statements.explanation: A tween can animate any property, such as position or scale, with no skeleton involved.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A tween is a code-driven interpolation of a property from a start value to an end value over a set time.
statements.explanation: Tweens are created in code and animate a property over time.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A tween usually takes an easing type and a duration as settings.
statements.explanation: Duration and easing are the usual parameters.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A tween is another name for a keyframe stored in an animation clip.
statements.explanation: Keyframes are authored data in a clip; a tween is a runtime process.

questions.stem: A rigged character needs to blend and switch motions. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A blend tree decides when the character is allowed to die.
statements.explanation: Life and death are game logic; the animation system only shows the result.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A state machine holds states and the transitions that move between them when conditions are met.
statements.explanation: States such as idle and jump are linked by transitions with conditions.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A state machine blends clips by weight and has no concept of transitions.
statements.explanation: Transitions are the core idea of a state machine.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A blend tree is the right tool to switch from the idle clip to a death clip when health reaches zero.
statements.explanation: A one-time switch on a condition is a state machine transition; a blend tree mixes clips by a parameter.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A blend tree mixes several clips together according to one or more parameters, such as speed.
statements.explanation: A blend tree outputs a weighted mix of clips driven by parameters.

questions.stem: An artist hands over a 3D character. Check each statement that is true about the skeleton terms.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Skinning weights say which texture is applied to each bone.
statements.explanation: Skinning weights say how strongly each vertex follows each bone.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A bone is a vertex that is hidden from the renderer.
statements.explanation: A bone is not a vertex; it is a joint transform.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A rig is a skeleton of bones together with the setup that lets the mesh follow them.
statements.explanation: A rig is the skeleton plus the binding of mesh to skeleton.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A rig is a texture that stores the colour of the character's skin.
statements.explanation: Skin colour comes from textures; the rig is structural.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A bone is a transform in the skeleton hierarchy that can be rotated to pose the character.
statements.explanation: Bones form a parent-child hierarchy and are posed by transforms.

questions.stem: A walking character slides across the ground in the game, and a student must name the cause and the fix. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: If a clip uses root motion and the script also moves the body, the character travels half the distance.
statements.explanation: Two sources of motion add together, so the character travels the distance twice.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Root motion uses the movement baked into the animation to move the character's root in the game.
statements.explanation: With root motion the animation drives the character's travel.

statements.label: C
statements.text: An in-place clip is unsuitable for a character that moves through the world.
statements.explanation: In-place clips are the usual choice for code-driven movement.

statements.label: D
statements.text: An in-place animation moves the character's root through the world by itself.
statements.explanation: An in-place clip runs on the spot; game code supplies the movement.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Root motion means the camera is attached to the character's root bone.
statements.explanation: Root motion concerns who moves the character, not the camera.

questions.stem: A character's foot must land on uneven stairs and a hand must grip a rail. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: FK starts from a target position and solves backward for the joint angles.
statements.explanation: That description is IK.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Forward kinematics (FK) sets the rotation of each joint from the parent down and the end position results from those rotations.
statements.explanation: FK poses by rotating each joint in order along the chain.

statements.label: C
statements.text: IK and FK are two names for the same technique.
statements.explanation: They solve in opposite directions.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Inverse kinematics (IK) works out the joint angles needed to put the end of a chain, such as a foot, at a target position.
statements.explanation: IK solves from the goal back to the joint angles.

statements.label: E
statements.text: IK is a good fit for planting a foot on a step whose height is only known at run time.
statements.explanation: Foot placement on varied ground is a classic IK use.

questions.stem: A 2D game uses a sprite sheet for its hero. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Frame rate for a sprite animation is how many frames are shown per second.
statements.explanation: Frame rate is frames per second.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A sprite sheet is one image holding many frames laid out in a grid.
statements.explanation: Many frames share one texture.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Halving the frame rate makes the same animation play at twice the speed.
statements.explanation: Fewer frames per second makes the animation slower.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Slicing a sprite sheet needs the number of bones in the skeleton.
statements.explanation: Slicing needs the grid layout (cell size or columns and rows); sprite sheets have no bones.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A sprite sheet stores bones and skinning weights.
statements.explanation: Bones belong to rigs, not to sprite sheets.

questions.stem: A student rewrites the vague prompt "animate the character walking". Check each rewrite that uses the exact terms for a 3D rigged character correctly.

statements.label: A
statements.text: "Play the walk clip from the rig, looping, in place, and move the body in script at the speed value."
statements.explanation: This names the clip, loop mode, root handling and who moves the body.

statements.label: B
statements.text: "Cut the walk clip into a 4 by 2 grid and show each cell for 100 ms."
statements.explanation: Cutting into a grid describes a sprite sheet, not a rigged clip.

statements.label: C
statements.text: "Give the walk clip a frame rate of 12 and a sprite sheet of 8 bones."
statements.explanation: A sprite sheet has frames, not bones; the terms are mixed up.

statements.label: D
statements.text: "Rotate the walk of the rig by tweening its UV."
statements.explanation: UV is a texture coordinate and is not a thing to rotate to make a walk.

statements.label: E
statements.text: "Add a blend tree on the speed parameter that mixes the idle, walk and run clips."
statements.explanation: Blending clips by a parameter is the tool for idle, walk and run.

questions.source: Spot the wrong word in an animation prompt
questions.stem: A prompt says: "Animate the rig with a sprite sheet and key the bones every frame at 24 bones per second." Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: "Bones per second" is a standard unit of animation speed.
statements.explanation: There is no such unit.

statements.label: B
statements.text: "24 bones per second" is the wrong unit; speed of playback is frames per second.
statements.explanation: Playback speed is frames per second.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The prompt is correct because a sprite sheet and a rig mean the same thing.
statements.explanation: They are different animation methods.

statements.label: D
statements.text: "Sprite sheet" is the wrong word for a rig; a rig is animated with clips of bone transforms.
statements.explanation: Sprite sheets are flat image frames; rigs use bone transforms.

statements.label: E
