statements.text: "Key the bones" is acceptable, since a keyframe stores a bone's transform at a time.
statements.explanation: Keying a bone means storing its transform at a given time.

questions.stem: A student asks an agent for "faster movement" and gets the wrong change. Check each statement that is true about the movement terms.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Acceleration is the rate at which velocity changes.
statements.explanation: Acceleration changes velocity over time.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Acceleration is another word for speed.
statements.explanation: Speed is how fast; acceleration is how quickly the speed changes.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Speed is the direction of the velocity, with no size.
statements.explanation: Speed is the size of the velocity; direction is the other part of velocity.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Velocity is speed together with a direction, so it is a vector.
statements.explanation: Velocity has magnitude and direction.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Velocity is the distance travelled so far.
statements.explanation: Distance travelled is a different quantity.

questions.stem: A game runs at 30 frames per second on one laptop and 144 on another, and the character moves at different speeds. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Delta time is the total time since the game started.
statements.explanation: That is elapsed time, not delta time.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Multiplying a per-second speed by delta time makes movement per frame match real time.
statements.explanation: Scaling by delta time gives frame-rate independent movement.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Movement code that adds a fixed amount each frame gives the same real-time speed on both laptops.
statements.explanation: A fixed amount per frame covers more distance per second when more frames are drawn per second.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Delta time is the time that passed since the previous frame.
statements.explanation: Delta time is the length of the last frame.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Delta time is a setting that raises the frame rate.
statements.explanation: Delta time measures frames; it does not change them.

questions.stem: A platformer feels unfair because jumps fail by a hair. Check each statement that is true about the forgiveness terms.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A jump buffer helps a player who presses jump a moment early.
statements.explanation: Early presses are held until landing.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Coyote time helps a player who presses jump a moment late.
statements.explanation: Late presses still count inside the window.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Coyote time makes the character fall more slowly after leaving a ledge.
statements.explanation: It changes when a jump is allowed, not the fall speed.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Coyote time is a short grace window after leaving a ledge in which a jump is still allowed.
statements.explanation: Coyote time extends the ground check after the feet leave.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A jump buffer remembers a jump press made just before landing and performs the jump on landing.
statements.explanation: The input is stored for a few frames and used when the character lands.

questions.stem: A student types: "Make the jump forgiving." Check each rewrite that uses exact terms correctly.

statements.label: A
statements.text: "Add a jump buffer of 0.12 seconds so a press just before landing still jumps."
statements.explanation: This is a jump buffer, named with its window.

statements.label: B
statements.text: "Add coyote time so the jump input is remembered until landing."
statements.explanation: Remembering a press until landing is the jump buffer.

statements.label: C
statements.text: "Add a jump buffer so the character can jump again after leaving the ground."
statements.explanation: A mid-air extra jump is a double jump, not a buffer.

statements.label: D
statements.text: "Add coyote time of 0.1 seconds after the character leaves a platform."
statements.explanation: This is coyote time, named with its window.

statements.label: E
statements.text: "Set delta time to 0.1 so the jump lasts longer."
statements.explanation: Delta time is measured, not a tuning value for jump length.

questions.stem: A designer must choose between collision shapes and areas. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A collider shape is a copy of the visible mesh, triangle for triangle.
statements.explanation: Colliders are usually simple shapes that approximate the mesh.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A trigger detects that something overlapped it but does not block movement.
statements.explanation: Triggers report overlaps (often through an area or signal) without pushing back.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A trigger stops a character the same way a wall collider does.
statements.explanation: A solid collider blocks; a trigger does not.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A pickup coin is better made as a solid collider than as a trigger.
statements.explanation: Collecting needs detection without blocking, which is what a trigger does.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A collider is a shape that the physics system uses to detect contact.
statements.explanation: Colliders define the shape used for collision tests.

questions.stem: A game has a moving platform, a crate that tumbles, and a player character. Check each statement that is true about body types.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A static body is moved around by applying impulses.
statements.explanation: A static body does not move.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A crate that should tumble under physics is a good fit for a static body.
statements.explanation: A static body does not move; a tumbling crate needs a rigid body.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A rigid body is moved by the physics simulation using forces, mass and collisions.
statements.explanation: Rigid bodies are simulated.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A kinematic body falls under gravity by itself without any code.
statements.explanation: A kinematic body only moves when code moves it.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A kinematic body is moved by code (or animation) and is not pushed around by forces.
statements.explanation: Kinematic bodies obey the script, and can still push other bodies.

questions.stem: An agent is told to "make the character slide to a stop instead of stopping dead". Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Acceleration also describes the speed-up from standing still when input starts.
statements.explanation: Acceleration applies both for speeding up and slowing down.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Gravity is a force that gives a steady downward acceleration.
statements.explanation: Gravity accelerates things downward.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Deceleration changes the direction of the velocity but not its size.
statements.explanation: Deceleration reduces the size of velocity.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Setting velocity to zero when input stops gives an instant stop.
statements.explanation: An assignment to zero stops at once.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Friction or deceleration reduces velocity over time when no input is held.
statements.explanation: Friction removes speed gradually.

questions.source: Spot the wrong word in a movement prompt
questions.stem: A prompt reads: "Use delta time to make the kinematic body fall, and give it a trigger so it blocks the player." Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The prompt is correct, since a trigger and a solid collider are the same.
statements.explanation: They differ in blocking behaviour.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A kinematic body falls without code because physics owns it.
statements.explanation: That is true of rigid bodies only.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A trigger does not block, so "trigger so it blocks the player" uses the wrong word; a collider blocks.
statements.explanation: Blocking is done by a collider; a trigger only detects.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A kinematic body does not fall by itself, so code has to add gravity to its velocity.
statements.explanation: Kinematic bodies rely on code for their motion.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Multiplying the gravity change by delta time keeps the fall the same at any frame rate.
statements.explanation: Scaling by delta time makes the result independent of frame rate.

questions.stem: A student must write the exact words for platformer jump feel. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Terminal velocity is the speed at the start of a jump.
statements.explanation: Terminal velocity is a cap on falling speed.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Coyote time and a double jump are the same feature.
statements.explanation: One is a grace window on the ground edge, the other an additional jump.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Terminal velocity is the highest fall speed the character is allowed to reach.
statements.explanation: The fall speed is capped.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Variable jump height lets a short press give a low jump and a long press give a high jump.
statements.explanation: The jump is cut short when the button is released early.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A double jump is an extra jump allowed while in the air.
statements.explanation: A double jump spends an extra mid-air jump.

questions.stem: A student asks for "smooth physics" and must say which update loop to use. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Tunnelling is when a fast object passes through a thin collider without a hit being detected.
statements.explanation: Tunnelling happens when an object moves farther than a collider's thickness in one step.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A fixed timestep removes the need for colliders.
statements.explanation: Colliders are still needed for contact tests.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A fixed timestep runs physics at a steady interval regardless of how fast frames are drawn.
statements.explanation: Fixed steps give stable simulation.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Movement of physics bodies belongs in the fixed-timestep step in most engines.
statements.explanation: Physics calls such as moving bodies are made in the physics step.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A per-frame update runs once per drawn frame, so its interval varies.
statements.explanation: Frame time varies, so per-frame steps vary.

questions.stem: A student must tell an agent which shader stage to edit. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A vertex shader runs once per vertex and decides where that vertex ends up on screen.
statements.explanation: The vertex stage outputs the position of each vertex.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Tinting every pixel of a surface by distance to the player is a job for the fragment shader.
statements.explanation: Per-pixel colour is fragment work.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Making a flag wave by moving its mesh points is a job for the vertex shader.
statements.explanation: Displacing vertices changes the shape, which is vertex work.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A fragment shader runs once per covered pixel (fragment) and decides its colour.
statements.explanation: The fragment stage outputs colour per fragment.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A fragment shader runs once per vertex of the mesh.
statements.explanation: Per-vertex execution describes the vertex shader.

questions.stem: A student asks for a pulsing glow driven from a script. Check each statement that is true about shader inputs.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A varying is set once from the script for the whole mesh.
statements.explanation: That describes a uniform.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A varying is a value passed from the vertex stage to the fragment stage, interpolated across the surface.
statements.explanation: Varyings carry per-vertex data to the fragment stage with interpolation.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A uniform is calculated separately for each fragment.
statements.explanation: Per-fragment values are computed in the shader, not set as uniforms.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A script changes a shader's glow strength by setting a uniform each frame.
statements.explanation: Script-driven parameters are uniforms.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A uniform is a value set from game code that is the same for every vertex and fragment in a draw.
statements.explanation: Uniforms are constant across a draw call.

questions.stem: A texture looks stretched on a model. Check each statement that is true about UVs.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A stretched texture means the image file is too small to use.
statements.explanation: Stretching usually comes from an uneven UV layout, not from the image.

statements.label: B
statements.text: UV coordinates store the direction in which the surface faces.
statements.explanation: Surface direction is stored by the normal.

statements.label: C
statements.text: UV stands for the ultraviolet value of a pixel.
statements.explanation: U and V are the names of the two texture axes.

statements.label: D
statements.text: UV coordinates store a colour for each point on a surface.
statements.explanation: UVs are 2D lookup coordinates; colour comes from the texture they look up.

statements.label: E
statements.text: UV unwrapping flattens a 3D mesh into 2D so it can be painted.
statements.explanation: Unwrapping produces the UV layout.

questions.stem: An artist says a flat wall should look like rough brick without adding polygons. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A normal map stores a surface direction per pixel so lighting reacts as if there were bumps.
statements.explanation: The colours in a normal map encode directions.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A normal map moves the vertices outward to add real geometry.
statements.explanation: Moving vertices is displacement, which a normal map does not do.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A normal map changes the colour of the surface.
statements.explanation: Colour belongs to albedo.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A normal map is a good way to make a flat wall light up as if it had brick grooves.
statements.explanation: Face-on detail is a typical use.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A normal map fakes surface detail in lighting without changing the mesh's shape or silhouette.
statements.explanation: The silhouette stays flat because no geometry moves.

questions.stem: A material has parameters an agent can set. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Emission is light that the surface gives off by itself.
statements.explanation: An emissive surface appears to glow.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Metallic says how much the surface behaves like a metal.
statements.explanation: Metallic switches between non-metal and metal reflection behaviour.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Roughness controls how sharp or blurry reflections and highlights are.
statements.explanation: A low roughness gives a mirror-like highlight; a high roughness spreads it out.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Roughness controls how bright the surface is lit.
statements.explanation: Brightness comes from lights and emission; roughness shapes the highlight.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Albedo is the base colour of the surface, before lighting.
statements.explanation: Albedo is colour without light or shadow.

questions.stem: A student must pick the exact material word for a described look. Check each statement in which the term fits the description.

statements.label: A
statements.text: "A matte red plastic ball" suggests setting its albedo to a red colour.
statements.explanation: Albedo supplies the base colour.

statements.label: B
statements.text: "Polished steel with sharp reflections" suggests high metallic and low roughness.
statements.explanation: Metals with sharp reflections have high metallic and low roughness.

statements.label: C
statements.text: "A mirror" suggests high roughness.
statements.explanation: A mirror has very low roughness.

statements.label: D
statements.text: "A neon sign that lights its own surface" suggests an emission value above zero.
statements.explanation: Self-lit surfaces use emission.

statements.label: E
statements.text: "Dry chalk with no visible shine" suggests low metallic and high roughness.
statements.explanation: Chalk is a rough non-metal.

questions.stem: A student wants a more realistic material set-up. Check each statement that is true about PBR.

statements.label: A
statements.text: PBR is a file format for animated meshes.
statements.explanation: PBR is a shading approach, not a file format.

statements.label: B
statements.text: PBR materials respond consistently across different lighting conditions.
statements.explanation: One set-up looks plausible under varied lights.

statements.label: C
statements.text: PBR stands for physically based rendering and describes materials with measured-style parameters.
statements.explanation: PBR models how light interacts with surfaces.

statements.label: D
statements.text: PBR stands for per-bone rendering.
statements.explanation: The letters do not stand for that.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A PBR material usually combines albedo, roughness, metallic and normal inputs.
statements.explanation: These are the common PBR inputs.

questions.stem: A particle effect and a window need different transparency settings. Check each statement that is true about blend modes.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Alpha blending mixes by opacity, so a half-transparent window shows the scene behind it.
statements.explanation: Alpha is opacity.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Multiply blending darkens what is behind it, which suits shadows and tints.
statements.explanation: Multiplying by a value of 1 or less keeps or darkens.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Additive blending can make a surface darker than the background.
statements.explanation: Adding non-negative colour cannot darken.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A blend mode sets how a surface's output colour is combined with the colour already on screen.
statements.explanation: The blend mode is the combining rule.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Additive blending adds colour to what is behind it, so fire and glows look brighter.
statements.explanation: Adding light brightens, so overlapping glows brighten.

questions.source: Spot the wrong word in a material prompt
questions.stem: A student writes the prompt: "Add a normal map to change the colour of the wall and a fragment shader to move its vertices." Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A normal map is the standard way to set a wall's colour.
statements.explanation: A normal map does not store colour.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A normal map does not set colour; albedo (base colour) is the right word.
statements.explanation: Colour is albedo; a normal map changes lighting direction.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The prompt is accurate because both stages move vertices.
statements.explanation: The fragment stage works on pixels.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The prompt would be accurate if the words "normal map" were replaced with "albedo" and "fragment" with "vertex".
statements.explanation: With those two changes the sentence uses the terms correctly.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Moving vertices is vertex shader work, so "fragment shader" is the wrong stage.
statements.explanation: Vertex positions are handled in the vertex stage.

questions.stem: A vague prompt reads "make the sword look cool". Check each rewrite that uses exact shader and material terms correctly.

statements.label: A
statements.text: "Use additive blend mode on the whole opaque blade so it looks like steel."
statements.explanation: Additive blending makes a surface glow like light; it is not how steel is shaded.

statements.label: B
statements.text: "Add a fragment shader that scrolls the UV over time to make a glint pass along the blade."
statements.explanation: Scrolling UVs in the fragment stage animates a glint across the texture.

statements.label: C
statements.text: "Give the blade a vertex roughness of 0.2 and a UV metallic of 1."
statements.explanation: Roughness and metallic are material parameters, not vertex or UV properties.

statements.label: D
statements.text: "Add an emission colour of pale blue to the blade's fuller, at low strength."
statements.explanation: Emission supplies self-lit colour.

statements.label: E
statements.text: "Set the blade's metallic to 1 and roughness to 0.2, and add a normal map for the engraving."
statements.explanation: Metallic, roughness and a normal map are used for their meanings.

questions.stem: A student confuses related texture maps. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A roughness map stores a roughness value per pixel instead of one value for the whole material.
statements.explanation: Maps vary a parameter across the surface.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A height map stores how high each point is, and displacement can use it to move geometry.
statements.explanation: Height maps can drive displacement or parallax.

statements.label: C
statements.text: An emission map stores the metal grade of each pixel.
statements.explanation: Emission maps store self-lit colour, and metal grade is the metallic map.

statements.label: D
statements.text: An albedo map stores the lighting direction at each pixel.
statements.explanation: Albedo stores colour; direction is in the normal map.

statements.label: E
statements.text: An ambient occlusion map darkens creases where ambient light would be blocked.
statements.explanation: Ambient occlusion adds contact shading.

questions.stem: A student wants a shader to respond to a value that changes while the game runs. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Several materials can share one shader with different parameter values.
statements.explanation: This is why one shader can serve many looks.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Passing time into a shader as a uniform lets it animate a pattern.
statements.explanation: A time uniform is the standard way to animate.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Changing a material parameter requires rewriting the shader code.
statements.explanation: Parameters are exposed so they can change without editing code.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A material is a shader together with the parameter values and textures it uses.
statements.explanation: A material packages a shader and its settings.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A shader is a texture file that stores a painted colour.
statements.explanation: A shader is a program, not an image.

questions.section: Jargon test: sprite sheets, rigs, colliders and state machines
questions.stem: A team debates the method for each character. Check each statement that is true about sprite-sheet and rig-based animation.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A sprite sheet holds drawn frames, and the animation shows them one after another.
statements.explanation: Sprite animation is a flipbook of images.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Characters that share a skeleton can share clips, which separate drawn sprite-sheet frames do not.
statements.explanation: Clips apply to any character with a matching skeleton.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A rig-based clip stores a separate picture for each frame.
statements.explanation: Rig clips store transforms over time, not images.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A rig-based animation changes bone transforms, and the mesh follows the bones.
statements.explanation: Skeletal animation poses bones.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A sprite sheet stores a skeleton and skinning weights.
statements.explanation: Skeleton data belongs to rigs.

questions.section: Jargon test: sprite sheets, rigs, colliders and state machines
questions.stem: An agent must slice and play a sprite sheet. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A frame is one image cell in the sheet.
statements.explanation: Each cell is a frame.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Frame order matters, so a prompt should say which cells make the walk and in what order.
statements.explanation: The order is part of the animation.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Setting an animation to loop makes it restart after the last frame.
statements.explanation: Looping repeats the sequence.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Frame rate and playback loop are the same setting.
statements.explanation: Frame rate is speed; looping is repeat behaviour.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A sheet of 6 columns and 2 rows holds 12 frames if every cell is used.
statements.explanation: Six times two is twelve.

questions.section: Jargon test: sprite sheets, rigs, colliders and state machines
questions.stem: Two designers argue about blocking and detecting. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A trigger zone around a door blocks the player until the door opens.
statements.explanation: A trigger detects overlap and does not block; blocking is a solid collider's job.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A trigger zone moves the player back out when the player enters it.
statements.explanation: Triggers do not push.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A collision shape on a wall lets characters walk through it while the engine reports an overlap.
statements.explanation: A solid collider blocks; reporting an overlap without blocking is a trigger.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Collision layers and masks choose which kinds of objects can touch each other.
statements.explanation: Layers say what an object is; masks say what it looks for.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Collision layers change the colour of the objects.
statements.explanation: Layers have nothing to do with colour.

questions.section: Jargon test: sprite sheets, rigs, colliders and state machines
questions.stem: A student says "enemy hits" and the agent builds the wrong thing. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A hitbox is normally a trigger, since it needs to detect an overlap and not block.
statements.explanation: Detection is enough, so triggers fit.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A hitbox is an area on an attacker that deals damage when it overlaps a target.
statements.explanation: A hitbox is the attack volume.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A hurtbox is an area on a character that can receive damage.
statements.explanation: A hurtbox is the vulnerable volume.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A hurtbox is the weapon area that deals the damage.
statements.explanation: The weapon area is the hitbox.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A hitbox and a hurtbox are the same area with two names.
statements.explanation: They play opposite roles.

questions.section: Jargon test: sprite sheets, rigs, colliders and state machines
questions.stem: A character needs states for idle, run, jump and fall. Check each statement that is true about state machines.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A state machine is in exactly one current state at a time.
statements.explanation: One state is active at once.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A transition is the animation clip played inside a state.
statements.explanation: A clip belongs to a state; a transition is the link between states.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A transition is a rule that moves the machine from one state to another when a condition becomes true.
statements.explanation: Transitions carry conditions.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A state machine runs its states in parallel.
statements.explanation: Only the current state is active.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A state machine replaces a pile of nested if checks with named states and transitions.
statements.explanation: Named states make behaviour easier to read and extend.

questions.section: Jargon test: sprite sheets, rigs, colliders and state machines
questions.stem: An agent is asked to code enemy behaviour. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Chase and attack are transitions, not states.
statements.explanation: They are states; the arrows between them are transitions.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A transition from patrol to chase could fire when the player enters the enemy's sight range.
statements.explanation: Sight is a typical transition condition.

statements.label: C
statements.text: An enter or exit action runs once when the machine enters or leaves a state.
statements.explanation: Entry and exit actions mark the edges of a state.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A state machine for an enemy needs a separate script per frame.
statements.explanation: The machine runs on updates; no per-frame script is needed.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A finite state machine for an enemy might have patrol, chase and attack states.
statements.explanation: These are typical states.

questions.section: Jargon test: sprite sheets, rigs, colliders and state machines
questions.stem: A student must rewrite "make the player move and animate properly". Check each rewrite that uses exact terms correctly.

statements.label: A
statements.text: "Slice the rig into a 4 by 4 grid and set its bones to loop."
statements.explanation: Grids belong to sprite sheets and loops belong to clips.

statements.label: B
statements.text: "Make the player a kinematic body that reads input, applies acceleration and gravity scaled by delta time, and moves with collision."
statements.explanation: This names the body type, forces, delta time and collision.

statements.label: C
statements.text: "Use a state machine with idle, run, jump and fall states, each playing its clip."
statements.explanation: States and clips map cleanly to the player's modes.

statements.label: D
statements.text: "Make the player a trigger so walls block it."
statements.explanation: A trigger does not get blocked by walls.

statements.label: E
statements.text: "Add a trigger area as the player's hurtbox so enemy hitboxes can detect it."
statements.explanation: A hurtbox area that is a trigger detects overlapping hitboxes.

questions.section: Jargon test: sprite sheets, rigs, colliders and state machines
questions.stem: A student reads an agent's plan and must spot imprecise words. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: "Blend the idle and run clips with a blend tree on speed" uses the terms correctly.
statements.explanation: This is the right use of blend tree and parameter.

statements.label: B
statements.text: "The tween stores a keyframe in a rig" describes how a tween works.
statements.explanation: A tween is a code interpolation; keyframes live in clips.

statements.label: C
statements.text: "The camera pans toward the boss by moving closer" mixes up pan and dolly.
statements.explanation: Moving closer is a dolly.

statements.label: D
statements.text: "The fragment shader displaces each vertex" gives the wrong stage.
statements.explanation: Vertices belong to the vertex stage.

statements.label: E
statements.text: "The coin is a solid collider so it detects pickups" should say the coin is a trigger.
statements.explanation: Detecting pickups is trigger behaviour.

questions.section: Jargon test: from the essay prompts
questions.stem: A producer types "Make the camera swoop in on the boss, then pan back out to show the arena." Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A zoom out widens the field of view while the camera stays where it is.
statements.explanation: Zoom is a lens change, not a position change.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A pan is a rotation of the camera on the spot, so it does not move the camera back out.
statements.explanation: A pan turns the camera left or right without changing its position.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A dolly out moves the camera body backward along its view direction.
statements.explanation: Dolly names a move of the camera body toward or away from the subject.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A dolly changes the lens angle and leaves the camera position unchanged.
statements.explanation: That describes a zoom; a dolly changes position.

statements.label: E
statements.text: "Pan back out" is the correct term for moving the camera body away from the subject.
statements.explanation: Moving the body away is a dolly out; pan is a rotation.

questions.section: Jargon test: from the essay prompts
questions.stem: A producer wants the boss reveal written as two exact readings: one where the camera body moves and one where only the lens changes. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: For the camera-body reading, ask for the focal length to change.
statements.explanation: Focal length is a lens property, so it belongs to the zoom reading.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A dolly in changes the parallax between near and far objects.
statements.explanation: Moving the viewpoint shifts near objects more than far ones.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A zoom in shifts near objects relative to far objects, which is parallax.
statements.explanation: Parallax needs the viewpoint to move, and a zoom does not move it.

statements.label: D
statements.text: For the lens reading, ask for the field of view to narrow and then widen with the camera position fixed.
statements.explanation: Field of view is the lens angle, the quantity a zoom changes.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A zoom in keeps the viewpoint and magnifies the same view.
statements.explanation: Only the lens angle changes, so relative positions of objects stay put.

questions.section: Jargon test: from the essay prompts
questions.stem: A designer asks an agent to "stabilise the camera" and needs the framing words defined. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Screen shake is a smoothing setting that makes the camera trail its target.
statements.explanation: Smoothing (damping) does that; screen shake is a brief decaying random offset.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A deadzone is a brief decaying random offset used to sell an impact.
statements.explanation: That describes screen shake.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Look-ahead shifts the framing toward the direction of travel.
statements.explanation: It shows more of the space the target is heading into.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Camera limits clamp the camera so it does not show space outside the level.
statements.explanation: Limits, also called bounds, restrict where the camera can go.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A deadzone is a screen region where the target can move without the camera moving.
statements.explanation: It stops the camera reacting to small movements.

questions.section: Jargon test: from the essay prompts
questions.source: Pick the camera term for a behaviour
questions.stem: Match each described behaviour to its camera term. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: An explosion rattles the view for a moment, so the term is camera limits.
statements.explanation: A brief rattle is screen shake.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Small twitches of the player should not move the view, so the term is deadzone.
statements.explanation: A deadzone ignores movement inside a region.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The camera stops scrolling at the left edge of the level, so the term is look-ahead.
statements.explanation: Stopping at the edge is camera limits (bounds).

statements.label: D
statements.text: The camera gently trails the player and catches up, so the term is look-ahead.
statements.explanation: Trailing and catching up is smoothing (damping).

statements.label: E
statements.text: A fast runner needs to see more of the level ahead, so the term is look-ahead.
statements.explanation: Look-ahead offsets the framing in the direction of travel.

questions.section: Jargon test: from the essay prompts
questions.stem: A student says, "A zoom and a dolly are the same: both make the subject bigger." Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A zoom and a dolly produce the same parallax because both enlarge the subject.
statements.explanation: Only the dolly changes perspective and parallax.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A zoom changes the field of view or focal length while the camera stays put.
statements.explanation: The lens changes, the viewpoint does not.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A dolly suits moving through a space so that depth is felt.
statements.explanation: The changing viewpoint produces parallax.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A dolly changes the field of view as it moves the camera.
statements.explanation: A dolly moves the body and leaves the lens angle alone.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A sniper scope view is a typical use of a zoom.
statements.explanation: A scope magnifies the same view without moving the viewpoint.

questions.section: Jargon test: from the essay prompts
questions.source: Field of view and focal length
questions.stem: An artist asks an agent for a "tighter, more dramatic lens". Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A narrow field of view gives a magnified look.
statements.explanation: The same part of the scene fills the screen more.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Widening the field of view is called a dolly out.
statements.explanation: Widening the lens angle is a zoom out; a dolly out moves the body.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A dolly in is done by lowering the field of view.
statements.explanation: A dolly in moves the camera body forward.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Field of view is the angle of the scene that the lens covers.
statements.explanation: A wide angle shows more of the scene.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A longer focal length widens the field of view.
statements.explanation: A longer focal length narrows the field of view.

questions.section: Jargon test: from the essay prompts
questions.stem: A prompt asks for "a 2D platformer follow camera that feels smooth." Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Look-ahead gives an offset in the direction the player faces or travels.
statements.explanation: It frames the space the player is moving into.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A follow camera tracks a named target such as the player.
statements.explanation: The target is the thing the camera follows.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The deadzone size sets how far the camera runs ahead of the player.
statements.explanation: That is look-ahead; a deadzone is a region where the target moves without the camera.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Screen shake is the setting to raise when the view looks jittery while following.
statements.explanation: Screen shake adds motion; jitter is reduced by smoothing and a deadzone.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Smoothing (damping) makes the camera trail slightly and catch up over a fraction of a second.
statements.explanation: It softens the camera motion toward the target.

questions.section: Jargon test: from the essay prompts
questions.stem: After the follow camera is built, a tester describes what to watch for. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A camera offset that fades out after a hit tests the deadzone.
statements.explanation: A decaying offset after a hit is screen shake.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Standing still near the centre and seeing no camera twitch tests the deadzone.
statements.explanation: A deadzone keeps small movements from moving the camera.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The view staying inside the level at the left edge tests look-ahead.
statements.explanation: Staying inside the level tests camera limits.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The camera settling to rest in a fraction of a second after the player stops tests smoothing (damping).
statements.explanation: Damping controls how quickly the camera catches up.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The camera showing more space to the right while running right tests camera limits.
statements.explanation: That is look-ahead.

questions.section: Jargon test: from the essay prompts
questions.stem: A door opens from 0 to 90 degrees in one second. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A keyframe is a stored value at a specific time, such as 90 degrees at 1 second.
statements.explanation: Keyframes mark the values that the motion passes through.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A tween is a stored value at a given time.
statements.explanation: That is a keyframe; a tween is a code-driven interpolation.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Easing changes the end values of the door angle.
statements.explanation: Easing changes the pacing and leaves the end values alone.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Interpolation is the shape of the speed over time, such as a slow start and fast finish.
statements.explanation: That describes easing; interpolation computes the in-between values.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A tween is authored by placing keyframes on a timeline in an animation editor.
statements.explanation: A tween is set up in code with a property, a duration and an easing.

questions.section: Jargon test: from the essay prompts
questions.stem: A team chooses between an authored clip and a tween for different jobs. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: An authored clip suits designed, reusable motion on a rig or sprite.
statements.explanation: Clips hold hand-made motion that can be played repeatedly.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Interpolation computes the values between keyframes in an authored clip.
statements.explanation: The engine fills in the in-between frames.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A quick UI pop-up scale is better suited to an authored clip on a rig than to a tween.
statements.explanation: Short procedural effects suit tweens.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A tween is a code-driven interpolation of a property over a duration.
statements.explanation: It is usually given an easing setting.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A tween has no use for an easing setting.
statements.explanation: Easing shapes the speed of a tween over its duration.

questions.section: Jargon test: from the essay prompts
questions.source: Spot the wrong word in an animation prompt
questions.stem: A student writes: "Animate the sprite sheet with bones and use IK to cut it into frames." Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Slicing is done by assigning bone weights to each cell.
statements.explanation: Bone weights belong to skinning of a mesh.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A sprite sheet is a grid of image frames, so it has no bones.
statements.explanation: Bones belong to a rig or skeleton, not to a grid of images.

statements.label: C
statements.text: IK is a method of cutting a sprite sheet into frames.
statements.explanation: Inverse kinematics solves joint angles so a limb reaches a target.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A sprite sheet is animated by a skeleton of bones.
statements.explanation: A skeleton belongs to a rig; a sprite sheet plays image frames.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A rig is the grid of columns and rows in a sprite sheet.
statements.explanation: A rig is a skeleton of bones with a mesh bound to it.

questions.section: Jargon test: from the essay prompts
questions.source: Sprite sheet instruction versus rig instruction
questions.stem: An agent is asked for two characters: one from a sprite sheet and one rigged in 3D. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The rigged instruction should name the cell size of the sheet.
statements.explanation: Cell size is a sprite sheet term.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The rigged instruction names the skeleton, the clip, the loop mode, and in-place versus root motion.
statements.explanation: These terms define a bone-driven animation.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The sprite-sheet instruction names the grid, which frames play in what order, the frame rate and loop.
statements.explanation: Those terms define a flipbook animation.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Stating the method (sprite sheet or rig) up front removes a guess for the agent.
statements.explanation: The two methods use different vocabulary and different tools.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The sprite-sheet instruction should name bone weights.
statements.explanation: Bone weights apply to skinned meshes, not image grids.

questions.section: Jargon test: from the essay prompts
questions.stem: A walking character slides over the floor and also travels twice as far as expected. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: An in-place clip keeps the root still and lets the script supply the travel.
statements.explanation: In-place is the choice for script-driven movement.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Sliding feet are fixed by raising delta time.
statements.explanation: Sliding is a mismatch between travel speed and the foot speed in the clip.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Double distance can come from a root motion clip while the script also moves the body.
statements.explanation: Two sources of travel are added together.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The fix for double movement is to keep root motion and keep the script moving at walking speed.
statements.explanation: That keeps both sources of travel; one should be removed.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Root motion is movement baked into the clip that drives the character's root through the world.
statements.explanation: The animation, not the script, supplies the travel.

questions.section: Jargon test: from the essay prompts
questions.stem: A bug report describes feet that slide while walking and a character that travels too far. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Root motion is the name for a clip that loops.
statements.explanation: Looping is the loop mode; root motion is movement carried by the clip.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Raising the script travel speed beyond the clip's foot speed reduces sliding.
statements.explanation: Sliding grows when travel speed and foot speed differ.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Using root motion and removing the script movement also fixes double movement.
statements.explanation: Only the clip supplies travel.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Using an in-place clip and letting the script move the body fixes double movement.
statements.explanation: Only the script supplies travel.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Sliding is called tunnelling.
statements.explanation: Tunnelling is a fast body passing through a thin collider.

questions.section: Jargon test: from the essay prompts
questions.stem: A 3D character idles, walks, runs, jumps and lands. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A blend tree is a weighted mix of clips driven by a parameter such as speed.
statements.explanation: It produces a smooth mix of motions.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A transition is a named value that the logic reads.
statements.explanation: That is a parameter; a transition is a rule that moves between states.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The gradual mix of idle, walk and run on speed suits a blend tree.
statements.explanation: A continuous parameter drives a continuous mix.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Jump and land are best handled by a blend tree on speed.
statements.explanation: They are separate states reached by transitions.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A state machine has named states with transitions, and one state is active at a time.
statements.explanation: It models discrete modes such as jump and land.

questions.section: Jargon test: from the essay prompts
questions.stem: An agent is told to build the locomotion and jump logic. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A parameter is the rule that decides when to switch states.
statements.explanation: That is a transition.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A blend tree has one active state and moves between states by transitions.
statements.explanation: That describes a state machine.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A transition is a rule with a condition, such as "on the ground" changing to false.
statements.explanation: It decides when the active state changes.

statements.label: D
statements.text: An instruction naming the parameter, the clips and the transition conditions removes guessing.
statements.explanation: Each missing name would otherwise be a guess.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A parameter is a named value, such as speed, that the logic reads.
statements.explanation: Parameters feed transition conditions and blend trees.

questions.section: Jargon test: from the essay prompts
questions.stem: A designer says, "The jump feels unfair." Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Coyote time forgives a jump press that came too early.
statements.explanation: Early presses are forgiven by the jump buffer.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Coyote time is a short grace window after leaving a ledge in which a jump is still allowed.
statements.explanation: It forgives a press that came a little late.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A jump buffer remembers a jump press made just before landing and performs the jump on landing.
statements.explanation: It forgives a press that came a little early.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Both are measured as short durations in seconds or frames.
statements.explanation: They are time windows.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A jump buffer forgives a press made after walking off a ledge.
statements.explanation: That is coyote time.

questions.section: Jargon test: from the essay prompts
questions.stem: A prompt adds coyote time and a jump buffer to a platformer. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The coyote window starts again when the player lands on the ground.
statements.explanation: Landing restores the grace window for the next ledge.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Coyote time is measured in pixels.
statements.explanation: It is a duration.

statements.label: C
statements.text: "Make the jump feel less unfair" is as precise as naming both features with durations.
statements.explanation: The vague phrase leaves features and values to a guess.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A buffered jump press is cleared once the jump has been performed.
statements.explanation: Otherwise it would trigger a second jump.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The jump buffer is the window used after leaving a ledge.
statements.explanation: That is coyote time.

questions.section: Jargon test: from the essay prompts
questions.source: Velocity, speed, acceleration and delta time
questions.stem: Two players report that movement code works on one machine and not another. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Delta time is the time since the previous frame.
statements.explanation: It is the length of the last frame.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Delta time is the number of frames drawn each second.
statements.explanation: That is frame rate.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Speed is the size of the velocity.
statements.explanation: It is the magnitude without direction.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Velocity is speed together with a direction, so it is a vector.
statements.explanation: Velocity carries a magnitude and a direction.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Acceleration is the rate at which velocity changes.
statements.explanation: It acts on velocity over time.

questions.section: Jargon test: from the essay prompts
questions.stem: A character runs faster on a 144 frames per second monitor than on a 30 frames per second laptop. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The fix is to scale per-second speed by delta time.
statements.explanation: Distance then follows real time.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Running physics in a fixed timestep keeps physics updates at a constant rate.
statements.explanation: Physics steps no longer depend on the frame rate.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Frame-rate independent movement gives the same distance per second on both machines.
statements.explanation: That is what the term means.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The cause is that velocity was stored as a scalar.
statements.explanation: Storing velocity as a scalar does not tie movement to frames.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The cause is movement that adds a fixed amount each frame, so more frames give more distance per second.
statements.explanation: The step is tied to frames, not to time.

questions.section: Jargon test: from the essay prompts
questions.stem: Choose the body or area type for each object in a level. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The player character moved by script is a static body.
statements.explanation: A script-controlled mover is kinematic, not static.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A tumbling crate pushed around by physics is a rigid body.
statements.explanation: A rigid body is simulated by the physics engine.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A platform moved by a script or animation is a rigid body.
statements.explanation: A body moved by code or animation is kinematic.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A coin that detects overlap without blocking is a trigger.
statements.explanation: A trigger is a volume that reports overlap and does not block.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A wall that does not move is a static body.
statements.explanation: Static bodies are fixed in place.

questions.section: Jargon test: from the essay prompts
questions.stem: A student mixes up the physics vocabulary. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A trigger is a volume that detects overlap without blocking.
statements.explanation: It reports entering and leaving.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A trigger blocks movement like a wall.
statements.explanation: Blocking is the job of a solid collider.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A collider is the shape used for contact tests.
statements.explanation: It describes where an object touches others.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A static body falls under gravity when nothing supports it.
statements.explanation: A static body does not move.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A kinematic body is moved by physics forces and gravity.
statements.explanation: A kinematic body is moved by code or animation.

questions.section: Jargon test: from the essay prompts
questions.stem: A vague prompt says: "Make the player move nicely and the platforms work." Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: "Nicely" is an exact term for tuning movement.
statements.explanation: It does not name a quantity that can be set or checked.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The player can be named as a kinematic character body that is controlled by script.
statements.explanation: Script-driven movement uses a kinematic body.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The rewrite says movement changes are scaled by delta time.
statements.explanation: This keeps movement independent of frame rate.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The moving platform can be named as a static body.
statements.explanation: A static body does not move; a moving platform is kinematic.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Velocity, acceleration, friction and gravity are movement-rule terms.
statements.explanation: They describe how motion is built up and slowed.

questions.section: Jargon test: from the essay prompts
questions.stem: After a movement rewrite, a tester lists checks and shapes. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A pickup zone is a trigger area.
statements.explanation: It detects the player without blocking.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Standing on the moving platform and riding along tests that the platform carries the player.
statements.explanation: It checks the body type and contact.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Measuring speed at 30 and 144 frames per second tests frame-rate independence.
statements.explanation: Equal speeds show delta time is applied.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A capsule is a common collider shape for a character and a box for a simple platform.
statements.explanation: Shapes are chosen to match the object.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A pickup zone should be a rigid body that blocks the player.
statements.explanation: A pickup should detect overlap, not block.

questions.section: Jargon test: from the essay prompts
questions.stem: A shader tutorial compares the pipeline stages and inputs. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A uniform is a value that changes for each vertex and is chosen by the vertex stage.
statements.explanation: A uniform comes from game code and is the same across a draw call.

statements.label: B
statements.text: UV is the 3D world position of a vertex.
statements.explanation: UV is a 2D coordinate that maps a surface to a texture.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A vertex shader runs per vertex and sets positions.
statements.explanation: It can move the vertices of a mesh.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A fragment shader runs per vertex and sets positions.
statements.explanation: A fragment shader runs per pixel and sets colour.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A varying is a value that the fragment stage sends back to the vertex stage.
statements.explanation: A varying passes from the vertex stage to the fragment stage and is interpolated.

questions.section: Jargon test: from the essay prompts
questions.stem: An artist wants a water wave and a surface glint, and a script to change them while the game runs. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A tint or glint on the surface is a fragment stage effect.
statements.explanation: It changes pixel colour.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A script sets a varying directly from game code each frame.
statements.explanation: Varyings come from the vertex stage.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A wave that displaces the mesh is a vertex stage effect.
statements.explanation: It changes positions.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A script changes the effect while the game runs by setting a uniform each frame.
statements.explanation: A uniform is the input from game code.

statements.label: E
statements.text: UV coordinates are 2D values that map a surface to a texture.
statements.explanation: They say which texture point goes where.

questions.section: Jargon test: from the essay prompts
questions.stem: An artist who has never written a shader asks what the material words mean. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Emission is the blur of the reflections.
statements.explanation: Emission is self-lit colour.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Albedo is the base colour without lighting.
statements.explanation: It is the colour before lights act on it.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Roughness controls whether highlights are sharp or blurry.
statements.explanation: Low roughness gives sharp highlights.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Metallic describes how much the surface behaves like a metal.
statements.explanation: It switches reflection behaviour between non-metal and metal.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A normal map stores a per-pixel surface direction that fakes small bumps in lighting without moving geometry.
statements.explanation: It changes shading and not the mesh.

questions.section: Jargon test: from the essay prompts
questions.source: Describe a material with exact terms
questions.stem: Describe a worn metal door with glowing warning lights in material terms. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A normal map can supply the dents.
statements.explanation: It changes shading and not the mesh.

statements.label: B
statements.text: An emission colour can supply the glow of the lights.
statements.explanation: Emission is self-lit colour.

statements.label: C
statements.text: PBR means the material behaves consistently under different lights.
statements.explanation: It is a physically based set-up.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Paint the dents by raising the metallic value.
statements.explanation: Dents are faked with a normal map.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Bare metal parts use a high metallic value.
statements.explanation: Metallic marks metal-like surfaces.

questions.section: Jargon test: from the essay prompts
questions.source: Spot the wrong word in a shader prompt
questions.stem: A student writes: "Use a normal map to make the lava glow and the fragment shader to move the vertices." Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A normal map is the setting that makes a surface glow.
statements.explanation: It fakes small bumps in lighting.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Moving vertices is vertex shader work.
statements.explanation: Vertex shaders set positions.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A corrected instruction asks for emission on the lava and a vertex shader for the movement.
statements.explanation: Each effect is assigned to its proper term.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Glow is emission, not a normal map.
statements.explanation: Emission is self-lit colour.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The fragment shader is the stage that moves vertices.
statements.explanation: It sets pixel colour.

questions.section: Jargon test: from the essay prompts
questions.stem: An artist chooses a blend mode for rising smoke and for a glow. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Additive blending adds light to what is behind it, which suits a glow.
statements.explanation: Glows brighten the background.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Additive blending is the better choice for dark smoke.
statements.explanation: Dark smoke needs to cover what is behind it, which is alpha blending.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Alpha blending mixes by opacity, which suits smoke.
statements.explanation: Semi-transparent smoke mixes with what is behind it.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Alpha blending adds light and brightens the overlap of layers.
statements.explanation: That describes additive blending.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Additive blending darkens the area where layers overlap.
statements.explanation: Additive blending brightens where layers overlap.

questions.section: Jargon test: from the essay prompts
questions.stem: An agent is asked for an enemy that patrols, chases and attacks. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A hurtbox is the area that deals the attack.
statements.explanation: A hurtbox is where a character can be damaged.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A sight range is best made a solid collider that blocks the player.
statements.explanation: Sight detection is a trigger area, which does not block.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A hitbox is the area where an attack deals damage.
statements.explanation: It belongs to the attacker.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A sight trigger area and an attack range can be the conditions for transitions.
statements.explanation: They tell the machine when to change states.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A state machine names patrol, chase and attack as states and defines the transitions between them.
statements.explanation: Each behaviour is one state at a time.

questions.section: Jargon test: from the essay prompts
questions.source: Say it to the agent: enemy behaviour
questions.stem: A "say it to the agent" paragraph for the enemy uses exact terms. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: An animation state and the enemy's health are the same thing.
statements.explanation: An animation state is a mode of playback, and health is a value.

statements.label: B
statements.text: "Make the enemy smart" gives the same detail as naming states and conditions.
statements.explanation: It names no state or condition.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Without a named transition condition the agent has to guess when chase becomes attack.
statements.explanation: The condition is what triggers the change.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A hurtbox is where the enemy deals damage.
statements.explanation: The hurtbox takes damage; the hitbox deals it.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Naming one animation clip per state, with a blend or transition between them, tells the agent how motion changes.
statements.explanation: Clips are assigned to states.

questions.stem: A coin is an Area2D on collision layer 4. The player body is on layer 1. The coin must fire body_entered when the player touches it. A reviewer unpacks the layer and mask settings into checkable constraints. Check each statement that is a correct unpacking.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The player's collision mask must include layer 4 for the coin's body_entered signal to fire.
statements.explanation: The signal depends on the area's mask, not the player's mask, so changing the player's mask does not fix detection.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The coin's collision mask must include layer 1, because the area scans for bodies on the layers in its mask.
statements.explanation: An area detects a body when the body's layer is in the area's own mask, so the mask must name layer 1.

statements.label: C
statements.text: If the coin's mask is empty, body_entered does not fire even while the player overlaps the coin.
statements.explanation: With no layer in its mask the area scans for nothing, so overlapping bodies are never reported.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Moving the coin from layer 4 to layer 1 does not make it detect the player, because detection comes from the mask.
statements.explanation: Changing the coin's layer changes what the coin is, not what it looks for, so detection stays broken.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The coin's collision layer must include layer 1 so that it can see the player.
statements.explanation: The coin's layer declares what the coin is, not what it sees, so adding layer 1 there would not make it detect the player.

questions.stem: A platformer has walls (StaticBody2D, layer 2), enemies (layer 3) and a player CharacterBody2D (layer 1). The player must be stopped by walls and must not be blocked by enemies. Ignore the enemies' own settings. Check each statement that is a correct unpacking.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The wall's collision mask must include layer 1 for the wall to stop the player.
statements.explanation: A static body does not move or scan, so its mask does not decide whether the player is stopped.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The player's collision mask includes layer 2.
statements.explanation: A moving body is stopped by the layers listed in its own mask, so layer 2 must be there for walls to block it.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The player's collision mask leaves out layer 3.
statements.explanation: A layer missing from the mask is passed through by this body, so enemies on layer 3 do not block the player.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The player's own layer must be set to 2 so that it can hit walls.
statements.explanation: The player's layer says what the player is; the walls are found through the player's mask, so changing the layer is wrong.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Moving the player from layer 1 to layer 5 does not change whether walls stop it, as long as its mask still includes layer 2.
statements.explanation: Blocking is decided by the moving body's mask, not by its own layer.

questions.stem: Layers: player 1, walls 2, enemies 3, bullets 4. Spec: "A bullet hits walls and enemies, passes through the player, and passes through other bullets." Check each statement that is a correct unpacking or compression of that spec.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Clearing the bullet's collision layer does not change what the bullet hits, because hits come from its mask.
statements.explanation: The mask still contains the same layers, so the bullet keeps hitting the same things as before.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Set the bullet's mask to include layers 2 and 3 and exclude layers 1 and 4.
statements.explanation: The mask lists what the bullet checks for, so walls and enemies are in it while the player and bullets are left out.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Putting the bullet on layer 4 labels it as a bullet but does not by itself decide what it hits.
statements.explanation: The layer states what the bullet is; what it hits is chosen by its mask.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Leaving layer 4 out of the bullet's mask is what stops bullets from hitting one another.
statements.explanation: A bullet reports only bodies on layers in its mask, so omitting layer 4 lets bullets pass through each other.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Set the bullet's mask to layers 1 and 4.
statements.explanation: That makes the bullet hit the player and other bullets, which is the opposite of the spec and misses walls and enemies.

questions.stem: A programmer pastes the term pair "_physics_process versus _process" into a spec and asks for unpackings that can be checked in code. Check each statement that is a correct unpacking.

statements.label: A
statements.text: _physics_process is called on the fixed physics tick, so its delta is the same each call.
statements.explanation: The physics tick runs at a fixed step, so the delta passed in stays constant from call to call.

statements.label: B
statements.text: _process is called once per rendered frame, so its delta changes when the frame rate changes.
statements.explanation: Rendered frames take varying time, so the delta passed to _process varies with the frame rate.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Defining both functions on one node makes Godot ignore _process.
statements.explanation: Godot calls both functions on the node each in its own cycle, so neither one disables the other.

statements.label: D
statements.text: _physics_process is called once per rendered frame, so it runs less often on a slow computer.
statements.explanation: It follows the physics tick instead; on a slow computer it can run more than once per rendered frame to catch up.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A health bar that only needs to animate smoothly on screen fits _process, because it does not touch physics.
statements.explanation: Visual updates tied to the display belong in the per-frame callback, since no physics step is involved.

questions.stem: A spec says: "Make the movement frame-rate independent." An agent proposes the changes below. Check each statement that correctly unpacks "frame-rate independent" for a character that moves by changing its position in _process.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Multiplying a per-second speed by delta gives the same distance per second at 30 and 144 frames per second.
statements.explanation: Delta shrinks as the frame rate rises, so more frames each cover a proportionally smaller step.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Raise the maximum frame rate until the movement looks the same on the developer's machine and a slow laptop.
statements.explanation: Frame rate is not guaranteed on other hardware, so the movement would still differ between machines.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Store the speed in units per second and add speed multiplied by delta to the position each frame.
statements.explanation: Scaling by delta converts a per-second rate into a per-frame step, so distance per second is the same at any frame rate.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Add gravity multiplied by delta to the vertical velocity each frame.
statements.explanation: Gravity is an acceleration in units per second squared, so it is scaled by delta when it changes velocity.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Multiply the velocity by delta before assigning it to the velocity that move_and_slide uses.
statements.explanation: move_and_slide applies the time step itself, so the velocity is scaled twice and the character moves far too slowly.

questions.stem: A level designer writes "coyote time 0.1 s" in the spec. Check each statement that is a correct unpacking into a checkable constraint.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The timer starts when the player presses the jump button.
statements.explanation: Starting at the press would build a buffer, not a grace window that opens after leaving the ground.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A jump press 0.08 s after walking off a ledge still jumps.
statements.explanation: The press arrives inside the 0.1 s grace window, so the jump is accepted.

statements.label: C
statements.text: After a real jump the window is cleared, so a second press during the same fall does not give a second jump.
statements.explanation: Clearing it prevents coyote time from turning into a free double jump.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A jump press 0.08 s before landing still jumps when the character lands.
statements.explanation: That behaviour is a jump buffer, a separate feature that remembers early presses, not coyote time.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The timer starts at the moment the character leaves the floor without jumping.
statements.explanation: That moment opens the short grace window in which a jump is still allowed after walking off an edge.

questions.stem: A level designer writes "jump buffer 0.1 s" in the spec. Check each statement that is a correct unpacking into a checkable constraint.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A jump press 0.05 s after walking off a ledge results in a jump.
statements.explanation: That is coyote time, a different feature that allows jumping after leaving the floor.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The press is stored when the character is standing on the floor, and ignored while it is in the air.
statements.explanation: The press must be stored while airborne, since remembering an early press before landing is the whole purpose.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A jump press 0.05 s before landing results in a jump on the landing frame.
statements.explanation: The early press is remembered for the buffer duration, and the jump fires when the character lands inside that time.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The buffer makes the jump reach a higher apex.
statements.explanation: It changes when the jump starts, not how high it goes, so apex height is unaffected.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The remembered press expires after 0.1 s, so a press 0.3 s before landing does not jump on landing.
statements.explanation: The buffer is a timer, so presses older than its duration are forgotten.

questions.source: Coyote time, jump buffer, variable jump height
questions.stem: A producer pairs a described behaviour with a one-line instruction for the agent. Check each pair in which the instruction correctly compresses the behaviour.

statements.label: A
statements.text: "A short tap makes a small hop and holding makes a full jump" is compressed by "add a jump buffer".
statements.explanation: A buffer changes when a jump starts, not how high it goes, so the tap and hold behaviour would be missing.

statements.label: B
statements.text: "A short tap makes a small hop and holding makes a full jump" is compressed by "add variable jump height".
statements.explanation: Variable jump height makes the apex depend on how long the button is held.

statements.label: C
statements.text: "Players who walk off a ledge can still jump for a split second" is compressed by "add coyote time of 0.1 s".
statements.explanation: Coyote time is the grace window that allows a jump just after leaving the floor.

statements.label: D
statements.text: "A jump pressed just before landing still happens on landing" is compressed by "add a jump buffer of 0.1 s".
statements.explanation: A jump buffer remembers an early press and applies it when the character lands.

statements.label: E
statements.text: "Players who walk off a ledge can still jump for a split second" is compressed by "add a jump buffer".
statements.explanation: A buffer remembers an early press; the ledge case needs coyote time, so the wrong feature would be built.

questions.stem: A designer asks for variable jump height. Check each statement that is a correct unpacking of it for a character that jumps by setting an upward velocity.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The apex height stays the same and the time in the air changes.
statements.explanation: Apex height is what varies with the hold length, so a fixed height would fail the spec.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Releasing the button while the character is already falling cuts the fall speed.
statements.explanation: The cut applies while rising; reducing a fall speed would make the character float instead of shortening the jump.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A tap and a full hold of the button produce different apex heights.
statements.explanation: That difference in apex height is the observable result a test can check.

statements.label: D
statements.text: If the jump button is released while the character is still rising, the upward velocity is cut to a smaller value.
statements.explanation: Cutting the rising velocity on release is the usual implementation, ending the jump early at a lower apex.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Releasing the button after the apex has been reached changes nothing about the jump.
statements.explanation: The character is already falling, so the height is fixed and release has no effect.

questions.stem: An agent is asked to build a player state machine with Idle, Run and Jump. Check each statement that is a correct unpacking of "state machine" into constraints that can be tested.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Run and Jump are both active while the character runs and jumps at once.
