statements.explanation: In a basic state machine one state is current; a jump while running is a transition from Run to Jump.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A state with no transition into it does not become active unless it is the starting state.
statements.explanation: Without an incoming transition or start role the state is unreachable.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Exactly one state is active at a time.
statements.explanation: A single current state is what separates a state machine from a pile of independent flags.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Taking a transition makes the new state current, and the old state stops being active.
statements.explanation: Moving between states replaces the current state, which keeps exactly one active.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Each transition names the state it leaves, the state it enters and the condition that triggers it.
statements.explanation: Transitions are the checkable part: a source, a target and a trigger condition.

questions.stem: A designer wants walk-to-run to change smoothly with speed, and wants an attack to interrupt movement. Check each statement that correctly maps the behaviour to an AnimationTree tool.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A blend tree stores which state is current and the rules for leaving it.
statements.explanation: Tracking the current state and its transition rules is the state machine's job, not the blend tree's.

statements.label: B
statements.text: If the speed parameter is set once in _ready, the walk-to-run blend keeps following the speed.
statements.explanation: The parameter must be updated as speed changes, otherwise the blend stays at its initial position.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A longer blend time between walk and run handles the attack interruption.
statements.explanation: Blend time only smooths a transition; interrupting movement needs a state machine transition into an Attack state.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A blend space driven by a speed parameter blends walk into run continuously.
statements.explanation: A blend space mixes clips smoothly according to a parameter value, which suits a speed-driven change.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A blend space is the right tool for choosing one attack clip when the attack button is pressed.
statements.explanation: Picking one clip on a button press is a discrete change of state, which a state machine handles.

questions.stem: A designer says: "Slide the menu panel in to x = 200 over 0.5 seconds, slowing as it arrives." Check each statement that is a correct unpacking into a tween.

statements.label: A
statements.text: "Make the panel move smoothly" is as complete a tween spec as the one above.
statements.explanation: It names no property, target value or duration, so an agent would have to guess them.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A finished tween returns the property to its starting value.
statements.explanation: The property stays at the final value unless another tween or script moves it.

statements.label: C
statements.text: "Slowing as it arrives" is an ease-out curve.
statements.explanation: Ease-out decelerates toward the end of the motion, which matches a panel that slows as it arrives.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The tween needs a property (position), a final value (x = 200) and a duration (0.5 s).
statements.explanation: Those three values are the constraints a tween call needs to be fully specified.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Easing changes the final value the property reaches.
statements.explanation: Easing shapes the speed curve over time; the end value and duration stay what was set.

questions.stem: A Godot script has `signal died` and a UI script that should react. Check each statement that is a correct unpacking of "use a signal".

statements.label: A
statements.text: The connected function's return value is sent back to the emitter.
statements.explanation: Signals are one-way notifications, so the emitter receives no result from listeners.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The emitter declares the signal and calls emit; the listener connects one of its own functions to it.
statements.explanation: The two ends are declaring and emitting on one side and connecting a function on the other.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Values passed in emit are ignored; the connected function reads them from the emitter.
statements.explanation: Parameters travel with the signal and arrive as arguments of the connected function.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Emitting a signal that has no connected function raises an error.
statements.explanation: Emitting with no listeners simply does nothing, since the emitter does not know or depend on its listeners.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A signal accepts a single connected function.
statements.explanation: Many functions can connect to one signal, and all of them are called when it is emitted.

questions.stem: A designer says "the child should tell its parent, not reach into it". Check each statement that correctly applies "call down, signal up" to a Door scene that sits inside a Level scene.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The Door can be tested alone because it does not need to know which nodes listen.
statements.explanation: Signals decouple the sender from its receivers, so the Door runs without a Level.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The Door's signal carries a notification and arguments, and the Level's connected function decides what changes.
statements.explanation: The Level reacts in its own function, so the Door never edits the Level's properties directly.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The Door calls get_parent() and runs a method of Level directly.
statements.explanation: That ties the Door to one specific parent and breaks when the Door is reused elsewhere.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The Level can connect to the Door's signal after the Door is added to the scene tree.
statements.explanation: Connections can be made at runtime whenever both nodes exist, so ordering against add_child is flexible.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The Level calls methods on the Door, and the Door emits a signal when it is opened.
statements.explanation: Parents call down into children and children signal up, keeping the child independent.

questions.stem: An Area2D has the properties monitoring and monitorable. A coin Area2D must detect the player body. A hurtbox Area2D must be detectable by enemy hitbox areas. Check each statement that is correct.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A hurtbox that enemy hitbox areas must detect needs monitorable on.
statements.explanation: The hurtbox is the detected side, so other areas can only see it when monitorable is on.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Monitoring is whether this area detects others.
statements.explanation: Monitoring controls the detecting side: whether this area reports overlaps with bodies and areas.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Monitorable is whether other areas can detect this area.
statements.explanation: Monitorable controls the detected side: whether other areas can see this one.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Turning monitoring off makes the area block bodies like a wall.
statements.explanation: Areas do not block movement; turning monitoring off just stops the area from reporting overlaps.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Setting the coin's monitorable to false stops the coin from detecting the player.
statements.explanation: The coin's detection depends on its monitoring flag; monitorable affects only whether other areas see the coin.

questions.stem: Four game objects need physics bodies: a wall, a player moved by input code that slides along walls, a crate shoved around by forces, and a moving platform driven by an animation that must push the player. Check each statement that is a correct match.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The moving platform is a StaticBody2D, because the animation moves it.
statements.explanation: A body that is moved by animation yet must push others is an AnimatableBody2D.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The player is a RigidBody2D so that the engine handles walking.
statements.explanation: RigidBody2D is driven by forces and gives imprecise walking control, unlike the scripted control of CharacterBody2D.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The player is a StaticBody2D, because its movement is written in code.
statements.explanation: Static bodies are not meant to be moved; code-driven sliding movement uses a CharacterBody2D with move_and_slide.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The wall is a StaticBody2D.
statements.explanation: A wall does not move, which is exactly what a static body is for.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The crate is a CharacterBody2D.
statements.explanation: A crate pushed around by forces and tumbling needs a RigidBody2D, which simulates forces and mass.

questions.stem: An enemy must know whether the player is in line of sight. A tower must find every enemy within 3 metres. Check each statement that is a correct choice and unpacking.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A ray has no width, so it can pass through a gap a wide body could not.
statements.explanation: A line of zero thickness slips through narrow openings that a wider shape would be blocked by.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Finding everything within 3 metres is a shape query or an area with a circle shape.
statements.explanation: A shape query reports overlaps across a region instead of along one line.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Line of sight is a raycast from the enemy toward the player, and the first thing hit must be the player.
statements.explanation: If a wall is hit first it blocks the view, so the first hit must be the player.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Line of sight is a raycast, and a hit on something means the enemy sees the player.
statements.explanation: The ray may hit a wall, so the hit object must be checked to be the player.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A raycast returns the first object along one line, so it is the wrong tool for finding everything within 3 metres.
statements.explanation: One line misses bodies off to the side and hidden behind the first hit, so a region query is needed.

questions.stem: A RigidBody2D needs a one-time knockback of 400 pixels per second away from a hit, and also a constant thruster push. Check each statement that is correct.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The knockback is a force applied for a single physics step.
statements.explanation: A force acts over time, so one step gives a small, frame-dependent change instead of a fixed 400 pixels per second kick.

statements.label: B
statements.text: For a body with mass, an impulse gives a smaller velocity change to a heavier body.
statements.explanation: An impulse changes momentum, so the velocity change is the impulse divided by mass.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The knockback is an impulse, an instant change of velocity.
statements.explanation: A one-time kick is an impulse, applied once to change the body's velocity immediately.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The thruster is a force applied on every physics step, changing velocity gradually.
statements.explanation: A continuous push is a force applied each step, building speed over time.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Multiplying the impulse by delta makes the knockback weaker and dependent on frame rate.
statements.explanation: An impulse is not a per-second quantity, so scaling it by delta shrinks it and varies it with frame rate.

questions.stem: A designer writes: "The popup eases out, the falling crate eases in." Check each statement that is a correct unpacking.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Ease-in-out starts slowly, moves fastest in the middle and slows again at the end.
statements.explanation: It combines both curves, so the speed is low at both ends and peaks mid-way.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Ease-in starts slowly and speeds up, which suits an object starting to fall.
statements.explanation: Ease-in accelerates from rest, resembling a crate that gains speed as it falls.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Ease-in and ease-out reach different end values.
statements.explanation: Both reach the same end value; only the speed curve along the way differs.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Ease-out makes the animation take longer than a linear one of the same set duration.
statements.explanation: The duration is fixed by the setting; easing only reshapes how the speed varies within it.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Ease-out starts fast and slows at the end, which suits a popup that settles.
statements.explanation: Ease-out decelerates into rest, so the popup comes gently to its final position.

questions.stem: A camera follows with `position = position.lerp(target, 0.1)` once per rendered frame. Check each statement that is correct.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A weight of 0.1 means the camera reaches the target in 0.1 seconds.
statements.explanation: It closes a tenth of the remaining gap each frame and approaches the target gradually.

statements.label: B
statements.text: At a higher frame rate the camera catches up faster in real time.
statements.explanation: More lerp steps happen each second, so the gap closes sooner.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A frame-rate independent version scales the weight with delta, for example 1 minus exp(-k times delta).
statements.explanation: A time-based weight gives the same catch-up per second regardless of frame rate.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The amount of catch-up per second depends on the frame rate.
statements.explanation: A fixed weight applies once per frame, so more frames per second mean more catch-up per second.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Doubling the frame rate leaves the real-time catch-up speed unchanged.
statements.explanation: Doubling the frame rate doubles the lerp steps per second, which speeds up the catch-up.

questions.stem: A bullet is fast and thin and sometimes passes through thin walls. Check each statement that is a correct unpacking.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A raycast from the bullet's start to its end position each step misses a wall lying between them.
statements.explanation: A ray covers the whole distance between its endpoints, so it finds the wall even when the bullet would skip over it.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Making the sprite larger stops tunnelling.
statements.explanation: Physics uses the collision shape, not the picture, so a larger sprite changes nothing about collisions.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Continuous collision detection checks the whole path of the move instead of only the end position.
statements.explanation: Checking the swept path catches thin obstacles between steps, which stops tunnelling.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Teleporting the bullet to its new position by setting its position is a safe way to avoid tunnelling.
statements.explanation: Setting position skips the path in between, so the thin wall is never tested.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Tunnelling happens when the move per physics step is longer than the thing it should hit.
statements.explanation: The body is on one side of the wall at one step and the other side at the next.

questions.stem: A designer separates the terms "hitbox", "hurtbox" and "body collider" for a fighting game. Check each statement that is correct.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A hurtbox is the area that deals damage when it overlaps a hitbox.
statements.explanation: The roles are swapped: the hurtbox receives damage and the hitbox deals it.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A hitbox blocks the other fighter's movement.
statements.explanation: Blocking is the body collider's job; hitboxes just detect overlaps and do not push bodies.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Making the character's sprite bigger enlarges the hurtbox.
statements.explanation: Collision shapes, not the picture, define the hurtbox, so scaling the sprite leaves it unchanged.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A hitbox is an area that deals damage when it overlaps a hurtbox.
statements.explanation: The hitbox is the attacking side, detecting overlap with the hurtbox that receives the hit.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Hitbox and hurtbox are the same area under two names.
statements.explanation: They have different roles, attack versus receive damage, and are usually separate shapes.

questions.stem: An AnimatedSprite2D plays an 8-frame idle loop, and a 6-frame jump that must play once and stay on the last frame. Check each statement that is a correct unpacking.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Eight frames at 8 frames per second last 1 second.
statements.explanation: Duration is frame count divided by frames per second, which gives 1 second here.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Looping is on for idle.
statements.explanation: An idle animation repeats continuously, so its loop setting is enabled.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Raising the game's frame rate to 144 makes the sprite animation play faster.
statements.explanation: The animation has its own frames-per-second setting, independent of the display frame rate.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Looping is off for jump, so it stops on the last frame.
statements.explanation: With looping off the animation plays once and holds its last frame.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Doubling an animation's frames-per-second setting doubles its duration.
statements.explanation: Doubling the speed halves the duration, since the same frames are shown in half the time.

questions.stem: A designer asks for a waving flag that moves in the world and a tint that fades on every pixel by a value set from a script. Check each statement that is correct.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A varying carries a value from a script into the shader.
statements.explanation: A varying passes values from the vertex stage to the fragment stage, while uniforms bring in script values.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A uniform is computed separately for each pixel by the fragment shader.
statements.explanation: A uniform is set from outside and is the same for the whole draw, not computed per pixel.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A uniform is a value set from outside the shader, for example by a script, and read by the shader.
statements.explanation: A uniform is how a script passes the fade amount into the shader.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Moving the flag's corners is a fragment shader job.
statements.explanation: Corner positions are handled in the vertex stage; the fragment stage outputs per-pixel colour.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Tinting each pixel is a vertex shader job, run once per corner.
statements.explanation: Per-pixel colour comes from the fragment stage, which runs for each pixel.

questions.stem: A game has a Score value that must survive scene changes. Check each statement that is correct about using an autoload (singleton) for it.

statements.label: A
statements.text: An autoload is the right place for the player's sprite, because it keeps it between levels.
statements.explanation: Scene content belongs in scenes; an autoload suits global state and services, not level visuals.

statements.label: B
statements.text: An autoload creates a separate copy for each scene.
statements.explanation: There is one autoload instance shared by the whole game.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Other scripts can reach it by its autoload name.
statements.explanation: Godot registers the autoload under the name given in project settings, giving global access.

statements.label: D
statements.text: An autoload node is loaded at startup and stays alive while scenes change.
statements.explanation: It sits outside the current scene, so changing scenes does not free it.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The score resets to zero each time the current scene is changed, because autoloads belong to the scene.
statements.explanation: Autoloads do not belong to the current scene, so their values persist across scene changes.

questions.stem: A designer wants each enemy to have its own health, but all from one enemy scene. Check each statement that is correct.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Instancing the scene creates a separate copy of its node tree for each enemy.
statements.explanation: Each instance is its own node tree, so state is kept per enemy.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Editing a property on one instance changes the other instances of the scene.
statements.explanation: Instances keep their own values, so an edit on one does not touch the others.

statements.label: C
statements.text: An instance must be added to the scene tree, for example with add_child, to run.
statements.explanation: An instantiated node that is not in the tree is not processed or drawn.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Calling instantiate edits the saved scene file.
statements.explanation: It creates a node tree in memory and leaves the scene file as it was.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Two instances share one health variable because they share a script.
statements.explanation: Variables belong to each instance, so each enemy has its own health even with the same script.

questions.stem: An enemy uses NavigationAgent2D to walk to the player. Check each statement that is a correct unpacking.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The walkable area comes from the NavigationAgent2D's own radius setting.
statements.explanation: The walkable area comes from the navigation region; the agent's radius only affects clearance and avoidance.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The agent finds a path without a navigation region set up.
statements.explanation: The navigation map must be provided first, or the agent has nothing to path through.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The script sets the agent's target position and then reads the next path position each physics step to move toward it.
statements.explanation: The agent plans the path; the script is what actually moves the body along it.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The NavigationAgent2D moves the enemy's body by itself once a target is set.
statements.explanation: It only computes the path, so the body must be moved by code each step.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Collision layers decide where the enemy can walk.
statements.explanation: Navigation data decides the path; layers decide physics collisions, which are a separate system.

questions.stem: A one-shot explosion uses a particle node. Check each statement that is a correct unpacking of its settings.

statements.label: A
statements.text: With one-shot off, the effect plays once and stops.
statements.explanation: With one-shot off the emitter repeats continuously, which would make the explosion loop.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Lifetime is how long each particle lives.
statements.explanation: Lifetime is a per-particle duration, after which that particle disappears.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Amount is how many particles are emitted.
statements.explanation: Amount sets the number of particles the emitter creates, as distinct from how long each one lives.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Lifetime is how long the emitter keeps running.
statements.explanation: It describes the life of a single particle, not the time the emitter keeps emitting.

statements.label: E
statements.text: One-shot makes the emitter release one burst and then stop.
statements.explanation: With one-shot on, the particles are emitted once instead of continuously.

questions.stem: A weapon has a cooldown of 0.5 seconds. The agent uses a Timer node. Check each statement that is a correct unpacking.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Starting the timer at fire time, not at button-press time, keeps a refused shot from extending the cooldown.
statements.explanation: A refused shot should not restart the timer, or the player would wait longer than 0.5 seconds.

statements.label: B
statements.text: wait_time is in seconds.
statements.explanation: The Timer's wait_time property is measured in seconds, not frames, so 0.5 means half a second.

statements.label: C
statements.text: One-shot off makes the timer fire once and stay stopped.
statements.explanation: With one-shot off the timer restarts and times out repeatedly, so it would not stay stopped.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The weapon can fire again as soon as the timer node exists.
statements.explanation: The timer must finish counting down first, so merely having the node does not end the cooldown.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Starting the timer when the weapon fires, and refusing to fire while the timer is running, gives a cooldown.
statements.explanation: That is the core logic: the running timer blocks firing until it finishes.

questions.stem: An agent reports: "Made the jump frame-rate independent by multiplying the jump impulse by delta." The jump is a single upward impulse applied at takeoff. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The claim is wrong: an impulse applied once is not a per-second rate, so scaling it by delta makes the jump weaker and still dependent on frame rate.
statements.explanation: A one-time velocity change has no per-second unit, so multiplying by the varying delta only makes the jump height fluctuate with frame time.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The frame-rate dependent part of a jump is usually gravity, which is scaled by delta when it changes the vertical velocity.
statements.explanation: Gravity is an acceleration in units per second squared, so each frame adds gravity times delta to the vertical velocity.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A follow-up that turns the claim into evidence is: run the jump at 30 and 144 frames per second and report the apex height for each.
statements.explanation: Comparing apex height at two frame rates directly measures frame-rate independence, and matching heights would confirm the fix.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The corrected code sets the jump as a one-time velocity change such as velocity.y = jump_velocity, with no delta factor.
statements.explanation: A single velocity assignment at takeoff is the same at any frame rate, so delta does not belong in it.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A follow-up that turns the claim into evidence is: ask the agent to explain in words why the change is correct.
statements.explanation: An explanation is more claim, not a measurement, so a jump that still varies with frame rate would pass unnoticed.

questions.stem: An agent reports: "Fixed the wall clipping by moving the movement code from _physics_process to _process so it updates more often." Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The reasoning is right, because more frequent updates mean smaller steps and so the clipping goes away.
statements.explanation: _process does not add physics steps, and its delta is irregular, so the body can still jump past thin colliders.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A follow-up that gives evidence is: confirm the code now runs in _process and that the project still compiles.
statements.explanation: Compiling and running in _process say nothing about whether the body still passes through walls, so the bad claim would be accepted.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A follow-up that gives evidence is: replay the same fast move into the thin wall 100 times and report how many times the body passed through.
statements.explanation: A repeated identical test gives a pass-through count that can be compared before and after the change.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The reasoning is wrong: _process follows the display, so its delta varies, while physics-based movement is meant to run on the fixed physics tick.
statements.explanation: Collision handling is tuned to the fixed physics step, and a variable display delta makes per-step distances uneven and unpredictable.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Clipping through thin walls is better addressed with continuous collision detection or a limit on how far a body moves per step.
statements.explanation: Both options check or restrict the path travelled in a step, which is what stops a fast body from skipping a thin collider.

questions.stem: An agent reports: "Added coyote time. The player can now jump when is_on_floor() is true." Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The claim is right, since checking is_on_floor() before jumping is what coyote time means.
statements.explanation: That check was already how normal jumping worked, so accepting the claim would ship a feature that was never built.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A follow-up that gives evidence is: simulate a jump press 0.05 s after leaving a ledge and report whether the jump happened.
statements.explanation: A press just after leaving the floor is exactly the case coyote time must allow, so the result shows whether it works.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A follow-up that gives evidence is: confirm is_on_floor() returns true while standing and that the jump works there.
statements.explanation: Jumping while grounded worked before the change, so this check passes whether or not coyote time exists.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A correct implementation stores a timer that starts when the character leaves the floor without jumping, and allows the jump while the timer is above zero.
statements.explanation: The timer creates the grace window, and it must start only on walking off, not on jumping, or double jumps appear.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The claim is wrong: is_on_floor() being true is ordinary jumping; coyote time lets a jump work for a short window after is_on_floor() turns false.
statements.explanation: Jumping while grounded already worked before, so the claim describes no new behaviour; the feature is the grace window after leaving a ledge.

questions.stem: An agent reports: "Added jump buffering: jump_pressed is set to true when the button is pressed and stays true until the player lands." Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The implementation is correct, because it remembers the press until the character lands.
statements.explanation: Remembering indefinitely is the bug, since a stale press fires an unwanted jump instead of a forgiving short buffer.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A follow-up that gives evidence is: press jump 0.05 s before landing and then 1 s before landing, and report which of the two jumps on landing.
statements.explanation: A correct buffer jumps for the near press and ignores the early one, so the two cases expose a missing expiry.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A correct version records the time of the press, or runs a short timer, and clears the flag when it expires.
statements.explanation: Expiry limits the buffer to a fraction of a second, so only presses just before landing count.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A follow-up that gives evidence is: ask the agent to rename the flag to jump_buffer.
statements.explanation: Renaming changes the label but not the missing expiry, so a flag that persists would still be accepted.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The implementation lacks an expiry, so a press made long before landing still causes a jump on landing.
statements.explanation: A buffer should be a short window; a flag that persists until landing turns an early press into a surprise jump seconds later.

questions.stem: An agent reports: "Fixed the coin pickup by setting the coin's collision layer to 1 so it overlaps the player." The coin is an Area2D and the player is on layer 1. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The change may have side effects, since other things whose masks include layer 1 will now see the coin as part of the player's layer.
statements.explanation: Layer membership has consequences: enemies or walls that scan layer 1 may now react to the coin.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The fix is right because the coin must be on the same layer as the player to touch it.
statements.explanation: Detection depends on one object's mask matching the other's layer, so objects do not need to share a layer.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The fix targets the wrong property: the coin detects the player through its collision mask, not its collision layer.
statements.explanation: An Area2D detects bodies whose layer appears in its own mask, so changing the coin's layer does not help it see the player.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A follow-up that gives evidence is: print the coin's layer and mask values and run the pickup, reporting whether body_entered fired.
statements.explanation: The printed values show the actual setup, and the signal result shows whether the pickup works in play.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A follow-up that gives evidence is: ask the agent to re-read the coin's scene file.
statements.explanation: Rereading the file reports the same settings but runs nothing, so a pickup that still fails would go unnoticed.

questions.stem: An agent reports: "Smoothed the camera with lerp(position, target, 0.1) each frame. It's now frame-rate independent." Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A delta-aware weight, such as 1 minus exp(-k times delta), makes the catch-up depend on time rather than frames.
statements.explanation: The exponential form gives the same smoothing per second at any frame rate, because delta enters the weight directly.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A follow-up that gives evidence is: record how long the camera takes to close half the gap at 30 and at 144 frames per second.
statements.explanation: Equal half-gap times at both frame rates would show true independence; a difference exposes the per-frame weight.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The claim is wrong because lerp is not suited to cameras.
statements.explanation: lerp works fine for camera smoothing; the defect is the per-frame weight, so dropping lerp would not address the actual claim.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The claim is wrong: a fixed weight applied per frame catches up faster at higher frame rates.
statements.explanation: A weight of 0.1 closes ten percent of the gap per frame, so more frames per second means faster catch-up.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The claim is right because lerp is a time-based function.
statements.explanation: lerp interpolates by a weight between zero and one, not by elapsed time, so it ignores delta unless the weight uses it.

questions.stem: A request said: "Fix the HUD health bar. Do not modify player.gd." The agent reports: "Fixed the health bar. I also cleaned up player.gd while I was there." Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A follow-up that gives evidence is: run the game and confirm the health bar updates, then accept the work.
statements.explanation: A working health bar does not address the scope violation, so the player.gd edits would slip through.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A follow-up that gives evidence is: show the diff limited to files changed and confirm player.gd is not in it.
statements.explanation: A file-level diff directly shows whether the forbidden file was touched, so it checks the constraint.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The agent went outside its scope, and the player.gd change should be reviewed or reverted before the HUD fix is accepted.
statements.explanation: The instruction named the file as off limits, so the edit breaks an explicit constraint regardless of how small it looks.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Cleaning up a file keeps behaviour the same, so the report can be accepted.
statements.explanation: The constraint was explicit, and a claimed same-behaviour cleanup is unverified, so accepting it would let a scope violation through.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The player.gd edits can stay in the commit and be reviewed later.
statements.explanation: The file was off limits, so keeping edits in the commit ships a violation that a later review may miss.

questions.stem: An agent reports: "Fixed the jump bug. While there I raised the project's physics ticks per second from 60 to 120 for smoother motion." The request was only to fix the jump bug. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The setting change should be reverted or approved separately, since the request named the jump bug alone.
statements.explanation: A project-wide change outside the request needs its own review instead of riding along with an unrelated fix.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The change is acceptable because a higher physics rate is a smoother physics rate.
statements.explanation: Higher rates cost more CPU and can change tuned behaviour, so the change should not pass just because it sounds smoother.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The jump fix can be evaluated alone by reverting the project setting and rerunning the jump test.
statements.explanation: Reverting the extra setting isolates the requested change, so the jump result is attributable to the fix itself.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A follow-up that gives evidence is: list the project settings changed in the commit.
statements.explanation: A settings list reveals scope creep like the tick rate, which a gameplay test would not show.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Changing physics ticks per second is a project-wide setting that was not requested, and it can change every body's behaviour and the timing of all timers in physics code.
statements.explanation: The tick rate affects how all physics code steps, so it alters tuned behaviour well beyond the jump fix.

questions.stem: An agent reports: "Fixed the stutter. Frame time is 40% better." No numbers, scene, or baseline were given. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A percentage improvement means little until the metric is named, such as average frame time or worst frame time.
statements.explanation: Stutter is about spikes, so an improved average can hide an unchanged worst case.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The claim can be accepted because a percentage is a precise measurement.
statements.explanation: A percentage of an unstated quantity is vague, and it could describe average time, a best case or one lucky frame.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A follow-up that gives evidence is: profile the same scene on the same machine before and after and report average and worst frame times.
statements.explanation: Same scene, same machine and both metrics make the comparison repeatable and fair.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The claim should not be accepted yet because it has no before value, after value, scene or hardware.
statements.explanation: A percentage without a baseline, scene and machine cannot be reproduced or checked, so it is not evidence.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Worst-case frame time is useful for stutter, because an average can hide spikes.
statements.explanation: Stutter appears as occasional long frames, which show up in the worst-case figure but get diluted in the average.

questions.stem: An agent reports: "All tests pass." The project has no test files. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A test framework such as GUT must be installed and at least one test written before a passing run means anything.
statements.explanation: Without a framework and test cases the runner has nothing to execute, so a pass is meaningless.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The claim shows the code works, since a test run reported zero failures.
statements.explanation: Zero failures from zero tests is an empty pass, so it gives no assurance about behaviour.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The claim should be questioned, because with zero tests there is nothing that could have failed.
statements.explanation: A run that executes zero tests passes trivially, so it says nothing about whether the code works.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A follow-up that gives evidence is: write one test that fails on the old code and passes on the new code.
statements.explanation: A test that flips from fail to pass proves the change fixed the specific behaviour.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A follow-up that gives evidence is: show the command run and its full output, including the number of tests executed.
statements.explanation: The executed-test count reveals at once whether any tests actually ran.

questions.stem: An agent reports: "Changed the enemy's knockback to a force of 500 applied once on hit." The enemy is a RigidBody2D. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A follow-up that gives evidence is: apply the knockback and report the enemy's velocity on the frame after the hit.
statements.explanation: The velocity right after the hit shows whether the push is the intended size.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A force applied once is the same thing as an impulse, so the claim is right.
statements.explanation: A force acts over a time step, so a single step gives a small push, while an impulse changes velocity instantly.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A one-time instant change in velocity is an impulse, so the term should be impulse.
statements.explanation: Impulse is the correct physics term for a single instantaneous velocity change, and the code should use it.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Calling apply_central_impulse once gives the intended one-time velocity change, scaled by the body's mass and not by step length.
statements.explanation: An impulse is applied as a velocity change divided by mass, so it behaves the same at any frame rate.

statements.label: E
statements.text: With a force applied for one physics step, the result depends on the step length and so is weaker than expected.
statements.explanation: A force of 500 over a short physics step yields a small velocity change, so the knockback looks feeble.

questions.stem: An agent reports: "Used move_and_collide for the player so it slides along walls." Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A fix is to keep move_and_collide and raise the player's speed so the body slides along the wall.
statements.explanation: Speed does not change the stopping behaviour, so the body would still halt at the wall with extra force.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A follow-up that gives evidence is: walk the player diagonally into a wall and report whether it keeps moving along the wall.
statements.explanation: A diagonal approach shows sliding or stopping directly, which settles whether the claim is true.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The claim is right, because collide means the body reacts to walls and so slides.
statements.explanation: The body halts at contact, because move_and_collide leaves any sliding response to code written by the user.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A follow-up that gives evidence is: ask the agent to print the word slide in the log.
statements.explanation: A printed word is not a movement result, so a body that stops dead would still pass.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The claim is wrong: move_and_collide stops at the first hit and reports it; sliding is what move_and_slide does.
statements.explanation: The two methods differ exactly here: move_and_collide returns the collision and halts, while move_and_slide deflects the motion along the surface.

questions.stem: An agent reports: "Enemy movement is now frame-rate independent: velocity = direction * speed * delta, then move_and_slide()." Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The claim is right, because multiplying by delta is the standard step for movement.
statements.explanation: With move_and_slide the multiplication is redundant, because the function already uses velocity as a per-second value.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The claim is wrong: move_and_slide already applies the time step to the velocity, so scaling by delta as well makes the enemy move much too slowly.
statements.explanation: Double scaling shrinks the per-second speed by the delta value, roughly a sixtieth, so the enemy crawls.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A follow-up that gives evidence is: report the distance the enemy covers in one second at 30 and 144 frames per second.
statements.explanation: Equal distances per second at both rates, at the intended speed, confirm the fix directly.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A follow-up that gives evidence is: confirm the enemy moves toward the player at one frame rate.
statements.explanation: The enemy moves toward the player either way, so a slow enemy at one frame rate would still pass.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Keeping delta in the velocity and raising the speed value to compensate makes the movement frame-rate independent.
statements.explanation: Delta varies per frame, so a fixed compensation fits only one frame rate and the enemy speed still changes.

questions.stem: An agent reports: "Variable jump height done: on button release I set velocity.y to 0." Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A follow-up that gives evidence is: release the button in the middle of the descent and report the vertical speed on the next frame.
statements.explanation: A release during descent exposes the hover bug, since the vertical speed would wrongly read near zero.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The claim has a bug: if the button is released while the character is already falling, setting velocity.y to 0 makes it stop in the air briefly.
statements.explanation: Zeroing a downward velocity cancels the fall, producing a visible hover before gravity restarts it.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The claim is correct, because zero vertical velocity ends the jump cleanly, including while falling.
statements.explanation: Zeroing the velocity during descent halts the fall, so the claim only holds while rising.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A correct version halves velocity.y on release regardless of direction of travel.
statements.explanation: Halving during a fall slows the descent, so the same release-in-descent glitch remains and the bug is kept.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A follow-up that gives evidence is: confirm that tapping the button gives a lower jump than holding it, and stop there.
statements.explanation: That test covers only the rising case, so the hover bug during descent would pass.

questions.stem: An agent reports: "Walk-to-run blending works. I set the AnimationTree speed parameter once in _ready." Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The claim is right, because a blend parameter keeps tracking the speed once set.
statements.explanation: A parameter keeps the last value written to it and does not follow the character's speed by itself.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The claim is doubtful: a value set once in _ready does not follow the character's changing speed, so the blend stays put.
statements.explanation: The parameter holds its initial value until code updates it, so walking faster does not change the blend.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The parameter can be set once in _ready to the maximum speed so the blend runs fully.
statements.explanation: A fixed maximum would play the run animation constantly, so walking would never appear.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A follow-up that gives evidence is: ask the agent whether the AnimationTree node exists.
statements.explanation: A node existing says nothing about whether the blend value changes with speed.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A follow-up that gives evidence is: start the game and report the blend value while the character stands still.
statements.explanation: A standing character reads the initial value either way, so this check passes the bad claim.

questions.stem: An agent reports: "The pickup works: I connected the coin's body_entered signal to _on_body_entered in the editor." No output was shown. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The claim is enough, because a connected signal means the handler runs.
statements.explanation: The handler runs when the signal is emitted, and that depends on monitoring, mask and the player's layer.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A follow-up that gives evidence is: report the coin's monitoring, layer and mask values.
statements.explanation: These inputs decide whether an overlap is detected, so wrong values would explain a silent handler.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A follow-up that gives evidence is: add a print in the handler, walk the player into the coin and show the output.
statements.explanation: A printed line in the handler shows the signal fired and the handler ran in play.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The Area2D's mask must include the player's layer for body_entered to fire.
statements.explanation: An area detects only bodies on layers in its own mask, so a mismatch leaves the signal silent.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A connection existing does not show that the signal fires, so the claim lacks evidence.
statements.explanation: A connection only lists a handler; the signal fires when an overlap occurs, which the setup may prevent.

questions.stem: An agent reports: "Fixed bullet tunnelling by doubling the bullet speed so it spends less time near the wall." Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A follow-up that gives evidence is: fire 200 bullets at the thin wall and report how many passed through, before and after.
statements.explanation: A pass-through rate over many shots shows whether the fix reduces an intermittent bug.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The reasoning is right because less time near the wall means less chance of passing through.
statements.explanation: Time near the wall is not the issue; distance covered per step is, and more speed raises it.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A fix that targets the cause is continuous collision detection or a raycast along the bullet's path.
statements.explanation: Both check the whole path travelled in a step instead of only the end position, so thin walls are caught.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A follow-up that gives evidence is: fire one bullet and report that it hit.
statements.explanation: One sample is not enough for a bug that happens sometimes, so a failing fix could still pass.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The reasoning is wrong: faster bullets move farther per physics step, which makes tunnelling more likely.
statements.explanation: Longer steps jump over thin colliders more easily, so doubling speed worsens the problem it claims to fix.

questions.stem: An agent reports: "Applied the normal map to the albedo slot so the bricks look bumpy." Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A follow-up that gives evidence is: render the wall with a light moved across it and show whether the highlights change with the light.
statements.explanation: Real bumps shade differently as the light moves, while a flat colour texture does not.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The claim is right, because both are textures that change how the surface looks.
statements.explanation: The two textures hold different data, so only the normal slot reads directions to bend the lighting.

statements.label: C
statements.text: In StandardMaterial3D the Normal Map feature must be enabled before the texture is read as surface directions.
statements.explanation: Without enabling the feature, the assigned texture is ignored and the bricks still look flat.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The normal map belongs in the material's normal slot.
statements.explanation: That slot reads the texture as surface directions, which produces the bump shading under light.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The claim is wrong: albedo is base colour, and a normal map stores surface directions, so in the colour slot it shows as purple-blue colour instead of bumps.
statements.explanation: The texture holds direction data, so used as colour it paints the surface blue and gives no lighting detail.

questions.stem: An agent reports: "Made the floor an Area2D so the player can stand on it." Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A follow-up that gives evidence is: drop the player onto the floor and report whether is_on_floor() becomes true.
statements.explanation: Landing on a real floor makes is_on_floor() true, so the result tests the claim directly.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A follow-up that gives evidence is: ask the agent to add a sprite to the floor.
statements.explanation: A sprite changes the look but not the physics, so a floor the player falls through would pass.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The claim is right because a collision node with a shape holds a character up.
statements.explanation: Only solid bodies block movement; an area with a shape just reports overlap, so the player still falls.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The claim is wrong: an Area2D detects overlaps and does not block, so the player falls through it.
statements.explanation: An Area2D reports overlaps but exerts no collision response, so a character passes straight through.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Matching the Area2D's layer to the player's mask is enough for the player to stand on it.
statements.explanation: Layers and masks control detection between objects, but an area stays non-solid, so the player still falls.

questions.stem: An agent reports: "Combined hitbox and hurtbox into one Area2D so one node handles both." Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The change creates a risk: an attack area on the player would overlap the player's own hurtbox and could damage the player.
statements.explanation: A merged node detects its own owner, so the attack can register as damage to the player.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The change is a tidy-up, because both are the same thing.
statements.explanation: They have different roles, dealing damage versus receiving it, and need different layers and masks.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A follow-up that gives evidence is: swing the player's attack in an empty room and report whether the player takes damage.
statements.explanation: An empty room isolates self-hits, so damage taken exposes the merged-node bug.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Keeping them separate lets each be on its own layer and mask so attackers hit only what they should.
statements.explanation: Separate nodes allow separate layer and mask settings, which control who can damage whom.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A hitbox can have monitoring switched off, because the hurtbox's own mask and monitoring detect the overlap.
statements.explanation: The hurtbox does the detecting, so the hitbox only needs to be on a layer the hurtbox's mask includes.

questions.stem: An agent reports: "Verified the export: the game runs correctly in the editor, so the exported build is fine." Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Running in the editor does not test the packaged build, which can differ in file paths, missing resources and export settings.
statements.explanation: The exported package has its own file layout and filters, so problems appear only after exporting.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The claim is enough because the editor runs the same files as the build.
statements.explanation: Exports apply filters, presets and packed paths, so the build can differ from the editor.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A follow-up that gives evidence is: list the resources the export excluded or failed to find.
statements.explanation: Missing resources are a common export failure, and a list shows them before the player does.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Resources loaded by a built string path may be missing from the export unless the preset includes them.
statements.explanation: The export scans references it can see, so a path assembled at run time can be skipped.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A follow-up that gives evidence is: export the build, launch the exported executable and report what happens on the first level.
statements.explanation: Running the real artefact tests what ships and exposes export-only failures.

questions.stem: An agent reports: "Line of sight works: the enemy's raycast returns a hit, so the enemy can see the player." Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A follow-up that gives evidence is: put a wall between enemy and player and report whether the ray still hits something.
statements.explanation: The ray hits the wall, so it reports a hit anyway, and the enemy that sees through cover would pass.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The claim is right, since the ray goes toward the player and so a hit is the player.
statements.explanation: The ray stops at the first collider it meets, which can be a wall between enemy and player.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Setting the ray's mask to the player's layer alone is right, because walls are then ignored.
statements.explanation: Ignoring walls lets the ray reach the player through them, so the enemy sees through solid cover.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A follow-up that gives evidence is: confirm line of sight is true with the player standing in plain view, and nothing else.
statements.explanation: This tests the positive case alone, so an enemy that sees through walls would pass.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The claim is incomplete: a ray hit may be a wall, so the code must check that the first thing hit is the player.
statements.explanation: A ray reports the first collider along its path, so a hit alone does not tell what it was.

questions.stem: An agent reports: "Replaced the AnimationTree state machine with a blend tree so the attack plays when the button is pressed." Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The change fits poorly: an attack that interrupts movement is a discrete change of state, which a state machine with transitions expresses.
statements.explanation: A state machine switches between named states on events, which matches the attack interrupting movement.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A follow-up that gives evidence is: press attack while running and report which animation is playing on the next frame.
statements.explanation: The playing animation after the press shows whether the attack interrupts movement.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A follow-up that gives evidence is: ask the agent to explain the difference between the two in a paragraph.
statements.explanation: A written explanation is not a behaviour test, so a broken attack would pass.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A state machine suits mixing walk and run by a speed value, which is why it was replaced.
statements.explanation: Mixing by a continuous speed value is blend tree work; a state machine only switches between clips.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The change is right because a blend tree can trigger clips from button presses by itself.
statements.explanation: A blend tree mixes animations by parameters and has no transitions to react to an event.

questions.stem: An agent reports: "Used create_tween() inside _process to move the node smoothly each frame." Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The approach is wrong: it creates a new tween every frame, and many tweens fight over the same property.
statements.explanation: Overlapping tweens all write to the same property, so the node jitters between their targets.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Moving by code with move_toward(target, speed * delta) in _process suits a target that changes continually.
statements.explanation: A per-frame move toward the current target follows it smoothly without creating objects.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A follow-up that gives evidence is: report how many active tweens exist on the node after 5 seconds.
statements.explanation: A growing tween count shows the per-frame creation bug directly, while one active tween is healthy.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A tween should be created once with the target and duration, which suits a fixed destination.
statements.explanation: A single tween runs the move on its own, so creating it once avoids conflicts.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The approach is right, because a tween is created each frame to stay current.
statements.explanation: One tween covers the whole move, so a fresh one per frame only multiplies the conflicts.

questions.stem: A request said: "Add a double jump. Do not delete any files." The agent reports: "Double jump added. I deleted the unused enemy scenes to keep the project tidy." Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The deletion is fine because the scenes were unused.
statements.explanation: The agent could not know they were unused where scripts load them by path, and the constraint applied anyway.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A follow-up that shows the constraint was kept is: ask the agent to run the game once and report that it starts.
statements.explanation: Starting does not load the missing scene, so a broken reference would pass.

statements.label: C
statements.text: An unused file can be referenced by a path in a script, so deletion can break the game later.
statements.explanation: A scene loaded by a string path is invisible to the editor's reference view, so removal causes a runtime error.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The agent broke an explicit constraint, and the deleted scenes should be restored before the work is accepted.
statements.explanation: The request forbade deleting files, so the removal is a violation whether or not the scenes seemed unused.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A follow-up that gives evidence is: list the files removed in the change and check them against the constraint.
statements.explanation: A list of deleted files in the change shows the violation directly.

questions.stem: A request said: "Rename the Player node's script variable hp to health." The agent reports: "Renamed hp to health in player.gd. Done." Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A follow-up that gives evidence is: search the whole project for the old name and report each remaining match.
statements.explanation: A project-wide search lists remaining references, showing what the rename missed.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The claim is complete, since the variable is declared in player.gd.
statements.explanation: Other files can read or write the variable, so declaring it in one place does not cover its uses.

statements.label: C
statements.text: An exported variable renamed in a script loses its saved Inspector value in scene files, so those scenes need checking.
statements.explanation: The scene stores values by property name, so the old name's value is dropped.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The claim is incomplete: other scripts, scenes or animation tracks may still refer to hp.
statements.explanation: A rename in one file leaves other callers of hp broken until they are found and updated.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A follow-up that gives evidence is: run the game, take damage and report the health value.
statements.explanation: A play-through exercises the renamed variable and shows whether damage still reaches it.

questions.stem: An agent reports: "The test for the damage function passes. I generated the expected value by running the function and pasting its output." Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The test is strong, since it passes on the current code.
statements.explanation: It passes whatever the code does, because the expected value is the code's own output.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The test is weak: it asserts that the function returns what it returned, so it cannot find a wrong formula.
statements.explanation: The expected value comes from the code under test, so the assertion holds even when the formula is wrong.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The test becomes strong once the pasted value is moved into a named constant in the test file.
statements.explanation: A constant holds the same copied output, so a wrong formula still passes.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A follow-up that gives evidence is: change the damage formula on purpose and report whether the test then fails.
statements.explanation: A test that stays green after a deliberate break cannot detect faults, so this check exposes it.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A follow-up that gives evidence is: run the same test a second time.
statements.explanation: The same test passes again for the same reason, so it adds no independent check.

questions.stem: An agent reports: "Edited the .tscn file by hand and renamed several nodes to match the new naming scheme. Everything still works." The request was to add a light. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Renaming nodes changes node paths, which scripts and signals use, so it can break references that are not tested.
statements.explanation: Calls such as get_node and signal connections store paths, and a renamed node leaves them pointing nowhere.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A follow-up that gives evidence is: open the scene in the editor and report that it loads.
statements.explanation: A scene that loads does not prove scripts and signals still find their nodes.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The rename can stay in the commit since the scene still loads and the light works.
statements.explanation: The rename was outside the request and carries hidden risk, so it should be reverted or approved.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A follow-up that gives evidence is: ask the agent to restate that everything works.
statements.explanation: Restating repeats the unverified claim, so a broken reference would pass.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Renaming nodes is cosmetic, so it does not affect scripts or signals.
statements.explanation: Paths are used in code and connections, so renames can break behaviour.

questions.stem: An agent reports: "Fixed the global score: I reload the scene to reset it, and the score now persists across levels because it is an autoload." Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A follow-up that gives evidence is: ask if the autoload is registered in the project.
statements.explanation: Registration does not show whether the score resets or persists.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Both claims hold, because reloading the scene resets scene nodes and the autoload together.
statements.explanation: The autoload sits outside the scene tree, so a reload cannot reset it.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A follow-up that gives evidence is: collect a coin, reload the scene and report the score before and after.
statements.explanation: The before and after values show whether the score survives the reload.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The two claims conflict: an autoload survives scene reloads, so reloading the scene does not reset the score.
statements.explanation: An autoload lives outside the current scene, so changing or reloading scenes leaves its values untouched.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Resetting the score needs an explicit reset in the autoload, for example a function called on a new run.
statements.explanation: Only code that assigns the score can reset it, so the new-run path must call it.

questions.stem: A teammate says "the signal is not arriving". The bug report concerns a Coin node that should tell the HUD to add a point, and the agent has to know which meaning of "signal" is in use. Check each statement that is correct.

statements.label: A
statements.text: If the report is about a node's body_entered not reaching its handler, the places to check are the connection, the area's mask and monitoring.
statements.explanation: These are the Godot causes of a missing body_entered call, so the agent inspects the connection and physics settings.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A request that says "handle the signal" without saying which one leaves the agent guessing between event, OS signal and audio or electrical signal.
statements.explanation: The word has several meanings across software and hardware, so the agent may build the wrong kind of handler.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A signal emitted with nothing connected to it does nothing visible, so a missing handler call points the agent at the connection.
statements.explanation: Emitting without a connected function silently has no effect, which makes the missing connection the first thing to check.

statements.label: D
statements.text: In Godot, a signal is a named event a node emits, which other nodes connect functions to.
statements.explanation: This is the engine meaning, so the agent should look at connections between nodes rather than operating system messages.

statements.label: E
statements.text: In Godot, a signal is a message sent from the operating system to the running game process.
statements.explanation: That describes an OS signal, and an agent acting on it would write process-level handlers instead of node connections.

questions.stem: A designer says "make the forest scene" and also "build the forest level". Check each statement that is correct about the two words in Godot.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A level is a Godot file type with its own extension, so the forest should be saved as a level file.
statements.explanation: Godot has no level file type, so the agent would create a file the editor cannot open.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A level is a playable area, usually built as a scene in Godot.
statements.explanation: Level is a design word for a playable space, and the engine represents it with an ordinary scene.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A scene is a saved tree of nodes that can be reused or instanced inside another scene, whether it is a whole area or a single coin.
statements.explanation: Scene is the engine's container type, so a single pickup and an entire area are both scenes.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A coin should be placed in the levels folder because it is saved as a scene.
statements.explanation: A coin is a scene but not a level, so the agent would misfile reusable pieces among playable areas.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A game has fewer scenes than levels, because levels are made of scenes.
statements.explanation: A level is usually one scene, and the game also has scenes for menus, enemies and items, so scenes outnumber levels.

questions.stem: A request says "set the mask so the laser ignores glass". Check each statement that correctly separates the meanings of mask in a game project.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Setting a collision mask changes how the object is drawn.
statements.explanation: A collision mask is a physics setting, so an agent would be wrong to expect any visual change from it.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A light cull mask decides which bodies the laser ray ignores, so the agent edits the light node.
statements.explanation: A light cull mask picks which render layers a light affects, so editing it leaves the physics ray unchanged.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A collision mask and a collision layer are the same setting, so setting the glass's layer is enough to make the laser ignore it.
statements.explanation: Layer says what the object is while mask says what it checks, so changing the glass layer would not change the laser.

statements.label: D
statements.text: An alpha mask in the glass texture is where to make the laser ignore glass, so the agent edits the image.
statements.explanation: An alpha mask only controls which pixels are visible, so editing the texture would change looks and leave the laser blocked.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A collision mask lists the physics layers an object scans for or is blocked by.
statements.explanation: The laser's ray or body checks its mask, so removing the glass layer from that mask makes the laser ignore glass.

questions.stem: A build report says "the physics is stable". The next step depends on whether this means resting bodies stay still or something else. Check each statement that is correct about what an agent could be claiming.

statements.label: A
statements.text: It could mean the sort of a list is stable, which means the list is sorted in place.
statements.explanation: Stability in sorting concerns the order of equal items, so an agent confusing it with in-place sorting would build the wrong thing.

statements.label: B
statements.text: It means the physics solver is deterministic, so replays match exactly.
statements.explanation: Stable simulation means resting bodies do not jitter, and an agent assuming determinism would build replay checks instead of testing resting stacks.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A stable sort keeps items with equal keys in their original relative order.
statements.explanation: This is a third meaning of the word, unrelated to physics, and matters when sorting a leaderboard by score.

statements.label: D
statements.text: It could mean no jitter or drift when bodies rest on each other.
statements.explanation: This is simulation stability, and the check is to stack bodies in a scene and watch whether they settle.

statements.label: E
statements.text: "Stable" here is a precise measurement, so the claim needs no follow-up.
statements.explanation: The report does not say which meaning or how it was measured, so the agent should ask before accepting it.

questions.stem: An agent says "the edit is atomic" after changing three script files for one feature. Check each statement that is correct.

statements.label: A
statements.text: An atomic edit means the change is small, such as one line.
statements.explanation: Atomic describes completeness of application rather than size, so an agent treating it as small would accept a half-applied large edit.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A claim that the edit is atomic does not say the edit was tested, so the agent still runs the tests.
statements.explanation: Atomicity and testing are separate properties, and relying on the word alone would let broken code be accepted.

statements.label: C
statements.text: An atomic commit groups one logical change, which may touch several files.
statements.explanation: Here atomic refers to a single coherent change, so three related scripts can belong in one atomic commit.

statements.label: D
statements.text: An atomic edit is applied completely or not at all, with no half-applied state left behind.
statements.explanation: Atomic means all or nothing, so a failed edit must leave the project exactly as it was.

statements.label: E
statements.text: If an atomic multi-file change fails on the third file, the first two files are restored.
statements.explanation: All-or-nothing behaviour means partial results are rolled back, so the project does not end in a mixed state.

questions.stem: A load-time report says "the cache was cleared and loading got slower". Check each statement that is correct.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A stale cache can show an old result after a source file changed.
statements.explanation: When a cached result is out of date, clearing it is a sensible first fix for odd behaviour.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Clearing a cache costs time once, since the stored results must be rebuilt.
statements.explanation: The slower load is a one-time rebuild cost, so an agent should not treat it as a permanent regression.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A cache is the source of truth for the project, so deleting it loses work.
statements.explanation: A cache can be regenerated from the sources, so an agent that refuses to delete it would waste effort.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A cache holds results that were already computed, such as imported assets or compiled shaders, so they need not be computed again.
statements.explanation: A cache saves repeated work, which is why clearing it makes the next load slower.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A CPU cache and a project import cache are different stores that share a name.
statements.explanation: One is hardware memory near the processor and the other is a folder of converted assets, so clearing one does not affect the other.

questions.stem: A designer asks for "a 12 frame walk cycle with keyframes on frames 1, 4 and 7". Check each statement that is correct.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Keyframes on frames 1, 4 and 7 mean frames 2, 3, 5 and 6 stay blank until the agent adds keyframes there.
statements.explanation: The in-between frames get values by interpolation, so adding more keyframes would change the requested animation.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A keyframe is a stored value at a specific time, and the frames between come from interpolation in an animation track.
statements.explanation: Keyframes are the stored values, so the agent adds three keys to the track and lets playback fill in the rest.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A frame is one displayed image in time, and a sprite sheet cell holds one.
statements.explanation: The agent should plan twelve cells in the sheet because each frame is one displayed image.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Counting an animation's length in frames tells you how many keyframes it holds.
statements.explanation: Keyframes are only the stored values, so a twelve frame animation can hold three keyframes and an agent counting frames would add too many.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A frame and a keyframe are the same thing, so 12 frames means 12 keyframes.
statements.explanation: They are different, and an agent treating them as equal would build twelve keys instead of three.

questions.stem: A material request says "use the normal on this surface" in one line and "use the normal map" in another. Check each statement that is correct.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Flipping the normal changes the surface's albedo colour, so the agent edits the colour texture.
statements.explanation: Flipping a normal reverses the direction a surface faces for lighting, so editing colour would leave the lighting error in place.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A normal map is an ordinary map for the surface's colour.
statements.explanation: Colour belongs to the albedo texture, and an agent putting a normal map there would produce a strange purple surface.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A normal map is a texture that stores a normal for each texel.
