statements.explanation: A normal map is an image file, so the agent assigns it to a texture slot rather than computing a vector.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A normal is a direction perpendicular to a surface at a point.
statements.explanation: A normal is a vector used for lighting, so the agent reads or writes it as a direction.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A normal is the usual, default value of a parameter.
statements.explanation: That is the everyday sense of the word, and an agent using it would reset a parameter instead of reading a surface direction.

questions.stem: A report says "the static light is baked". Check each statement that is correct about the word static in a game project.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Static lighting means light that is recomputed each frame, so the agent skips baking it.
statements.explanation: Static lighting does not change at run time and may be baked, so skipping the bake would leave the scene unlit.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Static typing makes objects unable to move.
statements.explanation: Static typing concerns variable types in scripts, so an agent confusing it with physics would freeze objects needlessly.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Static typing in a script means declaring the types of variables.
statements.explanation: This is the language meaning, so the agent adds type annotations rather than changing physics bodies.

statements.label: D
statements.text: StaticBody is a physics body that is not moved by forces.
statements.explanation: A static body stays put under collisions, so an agent uses it for walls and floors.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A StaticBody2D is pushed around by forces like a RigidBody2D.
statements.explanation: A static body ignores forces, and an agent using it for a crate that should be pushed would build a crate that never moves.

questions.stem: A log line says "process finished with errors". The agent has to decide whether to debug a node or the program run. Check each statement that is correct about the word process.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A _process function is a separate operating system process.
statements.explanation: It is a function inside the game process, and an agent treating it as a separate program would look for the wrong thing.

statements.label: B
statements.text: In an operating system, a process is a script function the engine calls each frame.
statements.explanation: An OS process is a running program, and mixing it up with _process leads to the wrong fix.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Each node's process runs on its own processor core by default.
statements.explanation: Godot runs _process on the main thread by default, so an agent expecting parallelism would skip needed safety checks.

statements.label: D
statements.text: In Godot, _process is a function called each rendered frame.
statements.explanation: This is the engine meaning, so an error in it would show up repeatedly while the game runs.

statements.label: E
statements.text: In a terminal, "Process finished" means the node's _process stopped being called, so the agent debugs the game loop.
statements.explanation: The message normally refers to the whole program run ending, so the agent should read the exit code and earlier errors.

questions.stem: A build request mentions "export" in three ways: an exported variable, an exported project, and an export from Blender. Check each statement that is correct.

statements.label: A
statements.text: An exported variable (@export) shows a script property in the Inspector.
statements.explanation: This is the script meaning, so the agent adds an annotation to the variable rather than configuring a build.

statements.label: B
statements.text: An exported variable and an exported project are unrelated features that share a word, so editing @export does not create a build.
statements.explanation: Adding an annotation changes the Inspector only, and an agent expecting a build from it would never produce one.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Exporting a project packages the game into a build for a platform.
statements.explanation: This uses an export preset to produce a shippable build, which has nothing to do with Inspector properties.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Exporting from Blender writes the model to a file format such as glTF.
statements.explanation: This is the asset meaning, and the file produced is what Godot later imports.

statements.label: E
statements.text: An exported variable is the build file that is shipped.
statements.explanation: The shipped file comes from exporting the project, and an agent mixing them up would look for the wrong output.

questions.stem: A designer says "spawn ten instances". An agent should keep separate the senses of instance. Check each statement that is correct.

statements.label: A
statements.text: GPU instancing and scene instancing are the same feature.
statements.explanation: They differ, and an agent that treats them as one would use the wrong tool to spawn gameplay objects.

statements.label: B
statements.text: GPU instancing draws many copies of one mesh in one draw call.
statements.explanation: This is the rendering meaning, used for efficient drawing of grass or crowds.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Instancing a scene in Godot creates a new copy of its node tree.
statements.explanation: Each instance_ call builds a fresh node tree, which the agent then adds to the scene.

statements.label: D
statements.text: An instance of a script class is the class definition in the .gd file, so spawning ten instances means writing ten script files.
statements.explanation: An instance is an object created from the class, and the agent should call new on one class ten times.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Instancing a scene gives copies that share one set of variable values.
statements.explanation: Each instance has its own values, and an agent assuming sharing would write code that fails to update the others.

questions.stem: A texture request says "give the crate a metal material" while a physics request says "give the crate a bouncy material". Check each statement that is correct.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A physics material controls friction and bounce.
statements.explanation: The bouncy request is about motion, so the agent sets bounce on a physics material on the body.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A render material controls how a surface looks, for example colour and shininess.
statements.explanation: The metal request is about appearance, so the agent edits the render material on the mesh.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A shiny render material makes the crate slide more easily, so the agent edits the render material for slipperiness.
statements.explanation: Render materials affect appearance, and slipperiness comes from the physics material's friction.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The two settings live on different parts of the object.
statements.explanation: The render material is on the mesh and the physics material is on the body, so both requests need separate edits.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A bouncy physics material changes the crate's colour.
statements.explanation: Physics materials set friction and bounce, so an agent editing them would not change the look.

questions.stem: A designer asks for "a trigger on the door" without saying what kind. Check each statement that is correct.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A trigger zone blocks the player like a wall.
statements.explanation: A trigger detects overlaps and lets bodies pass, so an agent building a wall would stop the player at the door.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A trigger means the same setting in Godot, Unity and Unreal.
statements.explanation: The terms differ between engines, and an agent copying a Unity tutorial would look for a setting that Godot does not have.

statements.label: C
statements.text: In an animation system, a trigger can be a parameter that starts a transition.
statements.explanation: This third meaning is a one-shot parameter in an animation state machine rather than a physical zone.

statements.label: D
statements.text: In Unity, Is Trigger makes a collider detect overlaps instead of blocking.
statements.explanation: This is the Unity setting, and it explains why Unity tutorials describe triggers differently than Godot ones.

statements.label: E
statements.text: In Godot, a trigger zone is usually an Area2D or Area3D that detects overlaps and does not block.
statements.explanation: The agent builds an Area node with a collision shape and connects its body_entered signal.

questions.stem: A request says "scale the enemy", "scale the time" and "scale the texture". Check each statement that is correct.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Changing texture scale makes the mesh larger, so the agent uses it to resize the crate.
statements.explanation: Texture scale or UV tiling repeats or stretches the pattern, and leaves the mesh size the same.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Changing a sprite's scale resizes a sibling collision shape automatically.
statements.explanation: A sibling shape is a separate node, so the agent must scale it too or the hitbox will not match.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Time scale changes how fast game time runs, such as for slow motion.
statements.explanation: This is the engine setting Engine.time_scale, which affects everything driven by delta.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Scaling a node by 2 changes the time scale of the game.
statements.explanation: Node scale and time scale are separate, and an agent mixing them up would double the size when speed was wanted.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Scaling a node changes its size, and its children inherit the scale.
statements.explanation: The agent sets the node's scale property and children, including collision shapes, grow with it.

questions.stem: A rig request says "put the origin at the feet" and also "move the pivot". Check each statement that is correct.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Moving the pivot of a sprite changes the point it rotates around while its position stays fixed.
statements.explanation: A pivot shifts the rotation centre, so the agent uses it for a spinning pickup without changing where it stands.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Setting the origin at the feet makes placing the character on a floor line simple.
statements.explanation: With the origin at the feet, setting the y position to the floor height puts the character on the ground.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The world origin is the zero point of the scene's coordinates.
statements.explanation: All positions are measured from it in global space, so the agent uses it as a reference when placing the rig.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The origin and the world origin are the same thing.
statements.explanation: A node origin is local to the node while the world origin is the scene's zero point, so an agent mixing them would misplace objects.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A node's origin is the point its position refers to, and rotation happens around it unless an offset is set.
statements.explanation: The agent places the node's origin at the feet, so position values describe where the feet stand.

questions.stem: A report says "lighting is baked", a rig note says "animation baked", and a navigation note says "navmesh baked". Check each statement that is correct.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A baked lightmap updates when a light is moved at run time.
statements.explanation: A baked lightmap stays fixed, so an agent expecting live shadows from it would see stale lighting.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Baking a navigation mesh stores the routes each agent will walk, so a moved obstacle changes the route without a rebake.
statements.explanation: Baking precomputes the walkable area from level geometry rather than routes, so a moved obstacle needs a rebake or dynamic obstacle handling.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Baking animation turns procedural or constraint-driven motion into stored keyframes.
statements.explanation: This freezes the motion into keys, so the clip plays back without the original rig logic.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Baked means the result can be edited by changing the original settings alone.
statements.explanation: The result must be baked again, and an agent that only edits settings would leave the old baked data in place.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Baking light precomputes lighting into textures so it is not computed at run time.
statements.explanation: The result is a lightmap, which makes lighting cheap but means it must be baked again after changes.

questions.stem: A 2D level request mixes tile, TileSet and TileMap. Check each statement that is correct.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Changing a tile's collision shape in the TileSet affects each cell that uses that tile.
statements.explanation: The shape is shared by the tile, so one edit updates every placed copy of it.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A TileSet is the node that holds the level layout, so the agent paints the level on it.
statements.explanation: The TileMap holds the layout, and painting on the TileSet would change the palette rather than the level.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A TileMap is the node that places tiles from a TileSet into a grid.
statements.explanation: The TileMap holds the level layout, so the agent paints cells on it using the TileSet.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A TileMap is the image file with the tile pictures, so the agent imports it as a texture.
statements.explanation: The image is the atlas texture used by a TileSet, and importing a TileMap as a picture would give the agent nothing to paint.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A TileSet is the collection of tiles, with their images and collision shapes, that can be used.
statements.explanation: The TileSet is the palette resource, so the agent defines tile images and collisions there.

questions.stem: A rendering note says "shader" and a design note says "material". Check each statement that is correct.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A material is an asset that holds a shader and the parameter values, such as textures and colours.
statements.explanation: The material supplies the settings, so the agent assigns textures and colours on it.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A shader is a program that runs on the GPU to compute vertex positions or pixel colours.
statements.explanation: The shader holds the code, so the agent writes GPU logic there.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A shader holds the specific textures for one crate.
statements.explanation: The material holds those values, and an agent storing textures in a shader would break reuse across objects.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A material is a program that runs on the GPU.
statements.explanation: That describes the shader, and an agent writing code into a material would find nowhere to put it.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Each material needs its own copy of the shader, so ten crate colours mean ten shader programs.
statements.explanation: Materials can share one shader with different parameter values, and copying the shader would multiply the code to maintain.

questions.stem: A Godot task says "load the resource" and a profiling note says "the resource usage is high". Check each statement that is correct.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A Godot Resource is the memory the game is using.
statements.explanation: A Resource is a data object, and an agent treating it as memory use would profile when a file load was wanted.

statements.label: B
statements.text: An agent asked to "reduce resources" could mean files or system load, and should be told which.
statements.explanation: The phrase is ambiguous, and guessing could delete data files when the goal was to lower memory use.

statements.label: C
statements.text: In Godot, a Resource is a data object that can be saved to a file, such as a texture or an animation.
statements.explanation: This is the engine meaning, so "load the resource" calls the load function on a file path.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Loading a Resource file lowers the processor usage.
statements.explanation: Loading a file adds work, so an agent expecting a performance gain from loading would not fix the profiling issue.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Resource usage in a profiling note usually means memory or processor time used by the game.
statements.explanation: This is the system meaning, so the agent should open the profiler rather than load a file.
